full_text:
IFPI Position on the European Commission's Proposal for a Regulation on Digital Services Act (DSA)

31 March 2021
I. IFPI IFPI is the organisation representing the interests of the recording industry worldwide. IFPI and its National Group network has over 8,000 members across more than 70 countries. IFPI's mission is to promote the value of recorded music, campaign for the rights of record producers and expand the commercial uses of recorded music in all markets where its members operate. II. INTRODUCTION The European Commission's (the 'Commission') proposal for a Regulation on Digital Services Act ( the 'DSA proposal') confirms the Commission's clear intent ion to ensure greater accountability and transparency of digital services and to introduce effective obligations to tackle illegal content online. We wholeheartedly agree with the Commission's goals, and we believe that the proposed legislation provides a starting point for achieving them. We recognise that the DSA proposal is a horizontal instrument which covers all types of illegal content and which aims inter alia to clarify general concepts that are relevant to the intermediary liability regime and to harmonise processes aimed at effectively tackling illegal content. We stress, however, that it is crucial to ensure that any proposed rules do not make the situation worse in any area or with respect to any type of illegal activity, for example with respect to copyright infringements. We agree with the Commission's aim to preserve in the DSA the framework and key principles set out in the EU E-Commerce Directive 2000/31/EC (the 'E-Commerce Directive'). It is therefore essential not to adopt any interpretations or approaches that could risk inadvertently altering the current limited liability framework. The Commission aims further to enhance the accountability of all types of information society services and to update their responsibilities and obligations to tackle illegal content online more effectively. However, as it currently stands, the DSA proposal fa lls short of meeting these goals and therefore it would benefit from certain improvements in these areas.

III. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
1. The DSA must preserve the scope of the liability regime as set out in Articles 12-14 of the E-Commerce Directive. Although the DSA proposal does maintain the categories of services that may be eligible for 'safe harbour' protection (caching, mere conduit, and hosting), recital 18 of the DSA proposal imply a higher threshold for establishing that a service is playing an "active role" and therefore not eligible for the liability privileges. This would be inconsistent with the EU acquis. Any clarification of the distinction between "technical, automatic and passive" intermediaries and those that play an "active role" must be strictly in line with the existing EU acquis, so as to avoid broadening the application of 'safe harbours'.
2. The DSA must not dilute the conditions for 'safe harbour' eligibility.

Once a service has satisfied the threshold eligibility criteria, it must comply with certain conditions to enjoy the 'safe harbour' liability privileges. These conditions must not be diluted.

A crucial existing condition concerning hosting providers and set out in Article 14 of the E-Commerce Directive is that the service provider must have no actual knowledge or awareness of illegal activities. Actual knowledge is clearly a different standard from awareness, or so called "constructive knowledge". It is essential that these standards are not conflated.

The DSA proposal appears to conflate actual knowledge with awareness, with the effect of increasing the threshold for establishing that a service has awareness of illegal activity. This would broaden the application of 'safe harbours', which would be against the Commission's stated goals and highly detrimental to any individual or entity seeking to prevent the dissemination of illegal content.

3. The DSA should include meaningful positive obligations for all information society services. To enhance the effectiveness of measures to stop and prevent illegal content online, all digital services must do more. To achieve this, the DSA proposal should:
- Apply the appropriate positive obligations to all information society services which enable or facilitate the operation of illegal websites by providing them with services or means to operate.
- Introduce a 'Stay Down' Obligation for hosting services. 'Notice and takedown' is ineffective to protect right holders. A 'stay down' obligation is necessary to strike the right balance between the need to stop illegal activities online and online intermediaries' need for commercial certainty.
- Improve the 'trusted flaggers' provisions to provide meaningful benefits to 'trusted flaggers', including obliging services, including micro and small ones, to accept their

notices "at face value", to act upon them immediately, and where available, to provide access to free tools to help locate illegal content a t scale (for example, an Application Programming Interface ('API')).
- Improve the "repeat infringer" provisions to require all information society services that enable or facilitate illegal activities to adopt and effectively implement an adequate repeat infringer policy.
- Broaden the 'Know Your Business Customer ' obligation to all information society services (not only online marketplaces and covering micro and small companies) and provide a mechanism for interested persons to access th at information, in a timely manner and at scale, for the legitimate purpose of investigating perpetrators of illegal activity and enforcement of their rights.

4. The DSA should clarify that the provision on voluntary proactive measures (Article
6) applies to activities solely taken to detect, identify and take action against illegal content. While we agree with the Commission's proposed approach to remove disincentives for services to take proactive measures to identify and remove illegal content, such a provision must be clearly defined as to its scope and effect, to avoid it being abused by the services and becoming a new 'safe harbour'.
5. The positive obligations under the DSA should be coupled with effective enforcement measures. While pirate websites operate indiscriminately across Europe, right holders have to take action country by country based on e ach Member State's legal system. Right holders and other injured parties should have access to effective enforcement mechanisms across the EU, without the need for any individual or an y entity, who are seeking to stop or prevent the dissemination of illegal content, to bring actions in each individual Member State against the same illegal service, the same infringing activity or infringing content. The proposal fails to include any meaningful provisions regarding the mentioned issue. We look forward to working with the EU co-legislator to improve the proposal in that respect. IV. DETAILED COMMENTS
1. The DSA must maintain the existing qualifying criteria for the liability privileges. Although the DSA proposal does not substantively change the scope of the liability regime, which has been set out in the E-Commerce Directive, it does imply a reduced threshold for establishing that a service is eligible for 'safe harbour' liability privileges, thereby potential extending their scope. These elements, which are described below, must be addressed, so as to maintain the existing balance in the EU acquis. 1.1 The DSA should maintain categories of services that may be eligible for th e intermediary liability regime.

As a starting point, we agree with the Commission's proposal not to change the categories of intermediary services eligible for 'safe harbours' ('mere conduit', 'caching', and 'hosting' services) (Chapter II, Art icles 3 - 5 of the DSA proposal), as currently established in the E - Commerce Directive. 1.2 The DSA must not alter the scope or application of the intermediary liability regime. The E-Commerce Directive sets out liability privileges for certain types of services ('mere conduit', 'caching', and 'hosting' services), but eligibility for the liability limitations does not arise merely because the service falls within 'mere conduit', 'caching', and 'hosting services' categories. To be eligible, the activities of a service must be, as stated in recital 42 of the E-Commerce Directive and reflected in recital 18 of the DSA proposal, of a "mere technical, automatic and passive nature, which implies that the information society service provider has neither knowledge of nor control over the information which is transmitted or stored", i.e. the service should not play an active role. In the Google France cases (Joined cases C-236/08 to C-238/08), the CJEU held that Article 14 of the E-Commerce Directive applies where the service provider "has not played an active role of such a kind as to give it knowledge of, or control over, the data stored ". The CJEU also ruled in L'Oréal v eBay (C-324/09) that a service playing an " active role of such a kind as to give it knowledge of, or control over, the data relating to those offers for sale [ ] cannot then rely, in the case of those data, on the exemption from liability referred to in Article 14(1) of Directive 2000/31/EC". These principles have also been applied by courts of Member States. 1 It is essential that the DSA maintains the "technical, automatic and passive" eligibility criterion and in no way alters the threshold for establishing that a ser vice provider's activities are not merely technical, automatic and passive. Changing the threshold could effectively expand the scope of the liability privileges, which would go against the aim of the DSA proposal to preserve the liability regime established in the E-Commerce Directive and would eventually lead to less not more accountability of the services. 1.3 Certain aspects of the DSA proposal could be understood as implying a higher threshold for establishing that a service is playing an "active role". Recital 18 of the DSA proposal. We support the first part of recital 182, which reflects recital 42 of the E-Commerce Directive

1 For example, by the Civil Court of Rome in Reti Televisive S.p.a v Vimeo LLC (23732/2012) 10 January 2019; Reti Televisive S.p.a v Daily Motion S.A. (62326/2015), 10 January 2021. 2 "The exemptions from liability established in this Regulation should not apply where, instead of confining itself to providing the services neutrally, by a merely technical and automatic processing of the information provided by the recipient of the service, the provider of intermediary services plays

and the CJEU's decision in L'Oréal v eBay and intends to confirm which services would be eligible for the liability regime by keeping the distinction between active and passive services. However, the second part of recital 18 3 is concerning because it could - unintentionally -- raise the threshold for establishing an " active role". While the statement in this part is evidently correct in that it gives two examples of activities which would undoubtedly impute an "active role", it is easily misunderstood as setting a high threshold for establishing when a service plays an active role. The CJEU has already confirmed what type of engagement with the uploaded content is sufficient to impute the service with an active role and therefore to disqualify it from eligibility for the safe harbour privileges. In L'Oreal v eBay, the provision of "assistance which entails, in particular, optimising the presentation of the offers for sale in question or promoting those offers " was found by the Court to constitute an active role. If the DSA proposal is to give examples of activities which would preclude the application of the liability regime, it should do so by codifying relevant parts of the CJEU's jurisprudence (notably L'Oréal v eBay). It should not give examples which could be mistakenly understood as implying a higher threshold for establishing an active role. The Commission's proposed clarifications in recital 18 of the DSA proposal are based on a flawed analysis in the Commission's Impact Assessment ('IA'). When seeking to address the perceived problem that the distinction between active and passive roles is not clear, the Commission seems to rely on the following analysis, which illustrates a misunderstanding of the distinction between active and passive activities: "[ ] there is still an important uncertainty as to when it is considered that an intermediary, and in particular, a hosting service provider, has played an active role of such a kind as to lead to knowledge or control over the data that it hosts. The fact that there is no such thing as an "active host", but that a provider might play an active role regarding some listings, but not others (for instance because it presents it or recommends it in a special manner) does not lead to the necessary legal certainty to provide legal intermediation services without risking claims for damages or even criminal liability." (IA, Annex 9, p 159, emphasis added) The Commission then makes assertions about the distinction that have no basis in the EU acquis: "the Court has interpreted the condition for hosting services to 'a passive and neutral role', as referred to in Recital 42 of the E-Commerce Directive for mere

an active role of such a kind as to give it knowledge of, or control over, that information " (emphasis added). 3 "Those exemptions should accordingly not be available in respect of liability relating to information provided not by the recipient of the service but by the provider of intermediary service itself, including where the information has been developed under the editorial responsibility of that provider."

conduits and caching services - and national courts have later on applied this caselaw in contr adicting ways. In this context, some national courts have equalled 'active role (of such a kind as to give it knowledge or control)' with a sort of 'appropriation' of the content ('zu eigen machen') to the extent that a reasonably informed user could conclude that the platform is the author or responsible for such content. Similar interpretation has been also proposed very recently by Advocate General Saugmandsgaard in a c ase which is currently pending before the Court. When applied to hosting service providers, it is important to create legal certainty and ensure that this requirement cannot imply that automatic, algorithmic ordering, displaying, and tagging or indexing of the content it stores, activities that are today necessary to make such content findable at all, imply an active role." (IA,
p. 112, emphasis added). We strongly disagree with this interpretation. First, the Commission places undue reliance on the decision of the German Court (OLG Munich) in GEMA v YouTube case, and the Opinion of the Advocate-General in the Peterson v YouTube CJEU reference. This "appropriation" test is not part of the EU acquis and therefore should not be included in the DSA (as it seemingly is by way of the second part of the proposed recital 18). Instead, the DSA should follow the CJEU case law, in particular the L'Oreal v eBay decision4, in which the Court confirmed that services that have knowledge or control of the content -- which is manifested for instance by optimising the presentation of the content or by promoting it -- play an active role and cannot benefit from the liability privileges in the E-Commerce Directive. The Court makes no mention of reference in its decision to the "appropriation" test. The attempt to exclude " automatic, algorithmic ordering, displaying, and tagging or indexing of the content it stores, activities that are today necessary to make such content findable at all " from implying an active role is highly objectionable. These activities may indeed be necessary to render content "findable", but they are not consi stent with the merely technical, automatic and passive activities of a mere host provider. On the contrary, they are activities that more effectively optimise the presentation of content, which according to the CJEU should disqualify a service prov ider from eligibility for the liability privilege.5

4 In Para 116 of Judgement of the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Justice in L'Oreal v eBay (C-324/09), 12 July 2011 5 In Stichting Brein v Ziggo BV, XS4ALL Internet BV (Case C‐610/15), the CJEU held (at para 38) that the operators of the online sharing platform T he Pirate Bay ("TPB") could not be considered to be making a 'mere provision' of physical facilities for enabling or making a communication, within the meaning of recital 27 of Directive 2001/29 which is analo gous to precluding a finding that the service's activities are technical, automatic and passive (the CJEU did not even consider whether TPB could be eligible for the hosting safe harbour). In reaching this decision, the CJEU referred to the fact that TPB, inter alia, indexed torrent files in such a way that the works to which the torrent files refer may be easily located and downloaded by the users of that sharing platform.

2. The DSA must not dilute the conditions for 'safe harbour ' eligibility for hosting services. 2.1 Knowledge and awareness of illegal activity or illegal content. As a condition for eligibility for the liability privileges, the E-Commerce Directive and the DSA proposal each provide that the hosting service provider must not have actual knowledge of illegal activity or illegal content and, as regards claims for damages, is not aware of facts or circumstances from which the illegal activity or illegal content is apparent, or upon obtaining such knowledge or awareness, acts expeditiously to remove or to disable access to the illegal content (Article 5 of the DSA proposal). In the first section of this paper, we address the issue of "knowledge or control" in the context of the distinction between active and passive services. In this section we address the circumstances in which actual knowledge or awareness may arise for the p urposes of triggering the requirement in proposed Article 5 to act expeditiously to remove or to disable access to the illegal content. Actual knowledge is clearly a different standard to awareness. It is essential that these standards are not conflated, since to do so would likely raise the threshold for establishing that a service provider has "awareness" such as to trigger the obligatio n to remove the infringing content, failing which it will be deprived it of 'safe harbour' eligibility. However, the proposed recital 226 does appear to conflate these standards to the detriment of right holders. This recital cites two examples of events that could trigger actual knowledge or awareness - an investigation or a notice. As with recital 18, these examples imply a high threshold for establishing awareness. On proper construction, awareness could arise without an investigation or a right holder's notice. Yet the Commission's statements in the Impact Assessment indicate that the Commission considers that a right holder's notification may be necessary to trigger awareness: "When a hosting service provider receives a notice about allegedly illegal content that it stores, it should not be held liable even if such notice has triggered "actual knowledge" or "awareness" of such illegality as long as it took expeditious action pursuant to the ECD. However, it is not clear what is necessary for a notice to trigger such awareness. There is also uncertainty around gaining actual knowledge or awareness of illegal c ontent as a result of the provider's voluntary actions, as explained above." "The wording of point (a) of Article 14(1) ECD indicates that, for the awareness test to be met, the facts and circumstances in question must be such that the illegality

6 "The provider can obtain such actual knowledge or awareness through, in particular, its own-initiative investigations or notices submitted to it by individuals or entities in accordance with this Regulation in so far as those notices are sufficiently precise and adequately substantiated to allow a diligent economic operator to reasonably identify, assess and where appropriate act against the allegedly illegal content."

is apparent; a case of borderline illegality does generally not seem sufficient to lead to 'awareness' within the meaning of Article 14(1)(a). A well-structured notice-andaction procedure should provide legal certainty to all parties involved in order to be effective and complete." (IA, Annex 9, page 161, emphasis added). To avoid conflating actual knowledge and awareness, we suggest removing the reference to awareness from the proposed recital 22.

2.2 Voluntary actions/the removal of disincentives. We broadly agree with the Commission's proposed approach of clarifying that a service provider should not be disqualified from eligibility for 'safe harbour' privileges by reason of the mere fact that a service provider undertakes activities to detect, identify and take action against "illegal content". However, it should be clarified that such activities should be solely for those purposes. This is important, so as to avoid activities that also have other purposes from automatically being disregarded from an assessment of the service provider's eligibility. 2.3 The DSA should allow for flexibility in the Notice & Action mechanism and ensure non-burdensome requirements for notices. The proposed notice and action mechanisms should provide more flexibility for the different types of services and content, to take account of the horizontal nature of the DSA framework. It should also specifically allow for notification of multiple contents. Furthermore, requirements for notifications of ille gal content should not introduce new and burdensome requirements, or requirements that would make the process unworkable. This should take into account the high volume of infringements reported by right holders. By way of illustration, IFPI has notified n early 200 million infringements since 2012 across all monitored platforms. Further, the requirements should be broad enough to encompass all types of content and insofar as possible, be future proof. These principles should apply to all the notification requirements under proposed Article 14. By way of example, a mandatory requirement to provide an URL (an address to a resource on the Internet) would place undue burden on the notifier to identify every instance of the same illegal content, and effectively let the hosting services off the hook to remove all infringing copies from their services (i.e. to perform a legacy scan for existing infringements) and implies that all that is required is removal of the infringement at the specific URL, when the service provider may be under an obligation to do more. In some cases, a URL will not give an accurate location for a specific infringement (e.g. in a live stream or on an App ). An URL should be sufficient, but not a necessary means of identifying the illegal content in a notice. Article 14(3) of the DSA proposal provides that notices that are compliant with the requirements in Article 14(2) shall be considered to give rise to actual knowledge or awareness for the purpose of Article 5 in respect of the specific item of information concerned. As noted in section 2.1 above, this should not lead to the conflation of the concepts of 'knowledge' and 'awareness'; it should be clear that a notice is not required to obtain awareness of illegal

content or activity and a notice may give rise to knowledge or awareness of illegal content or activity in a location other than at the URL(s) specified in a notice. The action required of providers of hosting services following receipt of a notice set out in Article 14(6) is to process notices and take decisions " in a timely, diligent and objective manner". This is inconsistent with and dilutes the criteria for eligibility for the hosting 'safe harbour' under Article 5(1)(b), i.e. " upon obtaining such knowledge or awareness, acts expeditiously to remove or disable access to the illegal content".
3. The DSA should include meaningful positive obligations for all information society services.

3.1 Positive obligations should apply to a broader category of services. The scope of the proposed DSA is limited to providers of intermediary services falling under Articles 3 - 5 of the DSA proposal (Articles 12-15 of the E-Commerce Directive respectively). However, there are several other digital services, which facilitate illegal activity online including copyright infringement, and which would fall outside its scope. To enhance the effectiveness of measures to stop and prevent illegal content online, which is the goal of the DSA, all digital services must do more. To achieve this, the DSA proposal should:
• Apply positive obligations not only to the intermediary services under the proposed DSA, but also to other services which enable or facilitate the operation of illegal websites by providing them services or means to operate. All information society services, which are being used to provide illegal content, for example, domain name registries/registrars, CDN service providers, payment providers, ad networks, should be obliged to take reasonable steps to stop, limit and prevent illegal activity. The content of those obligations should depend on the types of a service. However, some obligations are appropriate to apply to all types of intermediar ies such as 'repeat infringer' policies and 'Know Your Business Customer' (KYBC) obligations.

• The obligations concerning traceability ("Know Your Business Customer") an d "repeat infringers", as well as the Trusted Flaggers provision should be meaningful, and they should apply to micro and small companies. For example, some of the online intermediaries that are used by illegal services are relatively small and sometimes work in cahoots with other smaller facilitators of illegal activities. In the context of providers of hosting services, we have seen bulletproof hosts operate networks of smaller ISPs. Further, it is common for small niche ISPs to resell servers from larger ISPs and in some cases, operators of infringing services lease servers to effectively run their own ISP. 3.2 'Stay Down' obligation for hosting services.

The mere removal of specific infringing content is no longer sufficient to prevent the large - scale availability of illegal content and should not entitle providers of hosting services to the safe harbour privileges. To illustrate the point, according to IFPI data for 2018, 88 percent of the notices sent by IFPI refer to works that have already been notified to the same online service. Upon obtaining knowledge of illega l content or activity or awareness o f facts or circumstances from which the illegal activity or illegal content is apparent, providers of hosting services should be under an obligation to (i) expeditiously remove or disable access to all instances of the same illegal content; and (ii) ensure the same content does not reappear. The Commission acknowledges that 'stay down' orders issued by the courts is part of the EU jurisprudence7. National courts in in Italy8 and Germany9 and other EU member states10, as well as the CJEU11 have recognised a 'stay down' obligation in connection with different types of illegal content including content that infringes copyright and which is defamatory. This is an appropriate and proportionate obligation which could be implemented through a variety of means, including thorough already widely used Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) technologies. 3.3 Meaningful benefits for 'Trusted Flaggers'. The introduction of the concept of 'trusted flaggers' is welcome, but it should offer real benefits to those who are awarded this status and it should not diminish the obligations of service providers in respect of notices submitted outside this regime.

7 "Depending on the legal system of each Member State and the field of law at issue, national judicial or administrative authorities may order providers of intermediary services to act against certain specific items of illegal content. Such orders, in particular where they require the provider to prevent that illegal content reappears, must be issued in compli ance with Union law [ ]" (Commission's explanatory memorandum, p 3); " This proposal should constitute the appropriate basis for the development of robust technologies to prevent the reappearance of illegal information, accompanied with the highest safeguards to avoid that lawful content is taken down erroneously (Commission's explanatory memorandum, p 4); 8Delta TV vs Google & YouTube, Turin Court of First Instance, 7 April 2017, No. 38112/2013; Delta TV v Dailymotion, Turin Court of First Instance, 24 January 2018, No. 342/2018; RTI v Vimeo, Court of Rome, 10 January 2019, No. 693/2019; RTI v Yahoo!, Italian Supreme Court, 19 March 2019, No. 9133/2015, Court of Rome, 12 July 2019, No. 14757/2019. 9 GEMA v Rapidshare, Federal Court of Justice, 15 August 2013, No. I ZR 80/12; GEMA vs YouTube, Higher Regional Court of Hamburg, 1 July 2015, No. 5 U 87/12; GEMA v Rapidgator Limited, Regional Court of Hamburg, 12 June 2018, No. 308 O 224/18; Sony Music Entertainment Germany GmbH v Y-Flex LLP (operator of Rapidgator), Regional Court of Hamburg, 23 July 2019, No. 310 O 193/19. 10 SFP v Chomikuj12, Krakow Court of Appeal, 18 September 2017, Ref I ACa 1494/15. 11 L'Oreal v eBay (C-324/09), 12 July 2011; See also, Eva Glawischnig-Piesczek v Facebook (C-18/18) October 2019.

Article 19(1) of the DSA proposal provides that online platforms shall take the necessary technical and organisational measures to ensure that notices submitted by 'trusted flaggers' through the mechanisms referred to in Article 14 are processed and decided upon "with priority and without delay". 31 March 2021
I. IFPI IFPI is the organisation representing the interests of the recording industry worldwide. IFPI and its National Group network has over 8,000 members across more than 70 countries. IFPI's mission is to promote the value of recorded music, campaign for the rights of record producers and expand the commercial uses of recorded music in all markets where its members operate. II. INTRODUCTION The European Commission's (the 'Commission') proposal for a Regulation on Digital Services Act ( the 'DSA proposal') confirms the Commission's clear intent ion to ensure greater accountability and transparency of digital services and to introduce effective obligations to tackle illegal content online. We wholeheartedly agree with the Commission's goals, and we believe that the proposed legislation provides a starting point for achieving them. We recognise that the DSA proposal is a horizontal instrument which covers all types of illegal content and which aims inter alia to clarify general concepts that are relevant to the intermediary liability regime and to harmonise processes aimed at effectively tackling illegal content. We stress, however, that it is crucial to ensure that any proposed rules do not make the situation worse in any area or with respect to any type of illegal activity, for example with respect to copyright infringements. We agree with the Commission's aim to preserve in the DSA the framework and key principles set out in the EU E-Commerce Directive 2000/31/EC (the 'E-Commerce Directive'). It is therefore essential not to adopt any interpretations or approaches that could risk inadvertently altering the current limited liability framework. The Commission aims further to enhance the accountability of all types of information society services and to update their responsibilities and obligations to tackle illegal content online more effectively. However, as it currently stands, the DSA proposal fa lls short of meeting these goals and therefore it would benefit from certain improvements in these areas. III. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Although the DSA proposal does maintain the categories of services that may be eligible for 'safe harbour' protection (caching, mere conduit, and hosting), recital 18 of the DSA proposal imply a higher threshold for establishing that a service is playing an "active role" and therefore not eligible for the liability privileges. A well-structured notice-andaction procedure should provide legal certainty to all parties involved in order to be effective and complete." (IA, Annex 9, page 161, emphasis added). We broadly agree with the Commission's proposed approach of clarifying that a service provider should not be disqualified from eligibility for 'safe harbour' privileges by reason of the mere fact that a service provider undertakes activities to detect, identify and take action against "illegal content". However, it should be clarified that such activities should be solely for those purposes. This is important, so as to avoid activities that also have other purposes from automatically being disregarded from an assessment of the service provider's eligibility. 2.3 The DSA should allow for flexibility in the Notice & Action mechanism and ensure non-burdensome requirements for notices. The proposed notice and action mechanisms should provide more flexibility for the different types of services and content, to take account of the horizontal nature of the DSA framework. It should also specifically allow for notification of multiple contents. Furthermore, requirements for notifications of ille gal content should not introduce new and burdensome requirements, or requirements that would make the process unworkable. This should take into account the high volume of infringements reported by right holders. By way of illustration, IFPI has notified n early 200 million infringements since 2012 across all monitored platforms.

This should take into account the high volume of infringements reported by right holders. By way of illustration, IFPI has notified n early 200 million infringements since 2012 across all monitored platforms. Further, the requirements should be broad enough to encompass all types of content and insofar as possible, be future proof. These principles should apply to all the notification requirements under proposed Article 14. By way of example, a mandatory requirement to provide an URL (an address to a resource on the Internet) would place undue burden on the notifier to identify every instance of the same illegal content, and effectively let the hosting services off the hook to remove all infringing copies from their services (i.e. to perform a legacy scan for existing infringements) and implies that all that is required is removal of the infringement at the specific URL, when the service provider may be under an obligation to do more. In some cases, a URL will not give an accurate location for a specific infringement (e.g. in a live stream or on an App ). An URL should be sufficient, but not a necessary means of identifying the illegal content in a notice. Article 14(3) of the DSA proposal provides that notices that are compliant with the requirements in Article 14(2) shall be considered to give rise to actual knowledge or awareness for the purpose of Article 5 in respect of the specific item of information concerned. As noted in section 2.1 above, this should not lead to the conflation of the concepts of 'knowledge' and 'awareness'; it should be clear that a notice is not required to obtain awareness of illegal

content or activity and a notice may give rise to knowledge or awareness of illegal content or activity in a location other than at the URL(s) specified in a notice. The action required of providers of hosting services following receipt of a notice set out in Article 14(6) is to process notices and take decisions " in a timely, diligent and objective manner". This is inconsistent with and dilutes the criteria for eligibility for the hosting 'safe harbour' under Article 5(1)(b), i.e. " upon obtaining such knowledge or awareness, acts expeditiously to remove or disable access to the illegal content". 3. The DSA should include meaningful positive obligations for all information society services. 3.1 Positive obligations should apply to a broader category of services.

The DSA should include meaningful positive obligations for all information society services. 3.1 Positive obligations should apply to a broader category of services. The scope of the proposed DSA is limited to providers of intermediary services falling under Articles 3 - 5 of the DSA proposal (Articles 12-15 of the E-Commerce Directive respectively). However, there are several other digital services, which facilitate illegal activity online including copyright infringement, and which would fall outside its scope. To enhance the effectiveness of measures to stop and prevent illegal content online, which is the goal of the DSA, all digital services must do more. To achieve this, the DSA proposal should:
• Apply positive obligations not only to the intermediary services under the proposed DSA, but also to other services which enable or facilitate the operation of illegal websites by providing them services or means to operate. All information society services, which are being used to provide illegal content, for example, domain name registries/registrars, CDN service providers, payment providers, ad networks, should be obliged to take reasonable steps to stop, limit and prevent illegal activity. The content of those obligations should depend on the types of a service. However, some obligations are appropriate to apply to all types of intermediar ies such as 'repeat infringer' policies and 'Know Your Business Customer' (KYBC) obligations. • The obligations concerning traceability ("Know Your Business Customer") an d "repeat infringers", as well as the Trusted Flaggers provision should be meaningful, and they should apply to micro and small companies. For example, some of the online intermediaries that are used by illegal services are relatively small and sometimes work in cahoots with other smaller facilitators of illegal activities. In the context of providers of hosting services, we have seen bulletproof hosts operate networks of smaller ISPs. Further, it is common for small niche ISPs to resell servers from larger ISPs and in some cases, operators of infringing services lease servers to effectively run their own ISP. 3.2 'Stay Down' obligation for hosting services. The mere removal of specific infringing content is no longer sufficient to prevent the large - scale availability of illegal content and should not entitle providers of hosting services to the safe harbour privileges.

3.2 'Stay Down' obligation for hosting services. The mere removal of specific infringing content is no longer sufficient to prevent the large - scale availability of illegal content and should not entitle providers of hosting services to the safe harbour privileges. To illustrate the point, according to IFPI data for 2018, 88 percent of the notices sent by IFPI refer to works that have already been notified to the same online service. Upon obtaining knowledge of illega l content or activity or awareness o f facts or circumstances from which the illegal activity or illegal content is apparent, providers of hosting services should be under an obligation to (i) expeditiously remove or disable access to all instances of the same illegal content; and (ii) ensure the same content does not reappear. The Commission acknowledges that 'stay down' orders issued by the courts is part of the EU jurisprudence7. National courts in in Italy8 and Germany9 and other EU member states10, as well as the CJEU11 have recognised a 'stay down' obligation in connection with different types of illegal content including content that infringes copyright and which is defamatory. This is an appropriate and proportionate obligation which could be implemented through a variety of means, including thorough already widely used Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) technologies. 3.3 Meaningful benefits for 'Trusted Flaggers'. The introduction of the concept of 'trusted flaggers' is welcome, but it should offer real benefits to those who are awarded this status and it should not diminish the obligations of service providers in respect of notices submitted outside this regime. 7 "Depending on the legal system of each Member State and the field of law at issue, national judicial or administrative authorities may order providers of intermediary services to act against certain specific items of illegal content. Such orders, in particular where they require the provider to prevent that illegal content reappears, must be issued in compli ance with Union law [ ]" (Commission's explanatory memorandum, p 3); " This proposal should constitute the appropriate basis for the development of robust technologies to prevent the reappearance of illegal information, accompanied with the highest safeguards to avoid that lawful content is taken down erroneously (Commission's explanatory memorandum, p 4); 8Delta TV vs Google & YouTube, Turin Court of First Instance, 7 April 2017, No. 38112/2013; Delta TV v Dailymotion, Turin Court of First Instance, 24 January 2018, No.

Article 19(1) of the DSA proposal provides that online platforms shall take the necessary technical and organisational measures to ensure that notices submitted by 'trusted flaggers' through the mechanisms referred to in Article 14 are processed and decided upon "with priority and without delay". Due to their trusted status, they should be able to require immediate removal of content, and service providers should accept their notifications at face value and where available, provide access to free tools to help locate illegal content as scale (for example, an API). 3.4 Robust 'Repeat Infringer Policies'. Article 20 of the DSA proposal states that "[o]nline platforms shall suspend, for a reasonable period of time and after having issued a prior warning, the provision of their services to recipients of the service that frequently provide manifestly illegal content". The requirement to implement an effective 'repeat infringer' policy should apply to all intermediaries and not merely online platforms. Where an intermediary knows or becomes aware that a recipient of its services (whether a reseller or end-user) has repeatedly used its services in connection with infringing activity it must also, in appropriate circumstances, terminate the provision of their services to that recipient. This should apply to all instances of illegal content, without the additional requirement for it the "manifestly" illegal. The 'repeat infringer' policy should be applied with the genuine objective to prevent and deter the use of the services in connection with repeated and systematic illegal activities. Intermediaries must ensure they have adequate measures in place to detect repeat infringers.

Intermediaries must ensure they have adequate measures in place to detect repeat infringers. In assessing whether a user is a 'repeat infringer', account must be taken of all instances of illegal activity by that user, irrespective of whether the instances of illegality have been removed and in the context of Article 20(1), this should be by reference to the absolute amount of illegal content and not the relative proportion as per Article 20(3)(b). This verification process under Article 22(2) of the DSA proposal (see below) should ensure that any user that has been terminat ed pursuant 'repeat infringer' policy is not permitted to use the service, including under a different name. Online intermediaries' Terms of Service should allow and set out in a clear and transparent manner the intermediary's right and discretion to suspend and terminate repeat infringers in accordance with the principles set out above. 3.5 Broader 'Know Your Business Customer' ('KYBC') obligation. The application of the 'traceability of traders' obligation (Article 22 of the DSA proposal) to online marketplaces would be an incomplete solution. This is so because, firstly it is far too narrow in scope. To make the KYBC obligations truly effective, it should not be limited to platforms comprising online marketplaces. Illegal content is available via a range of online source s and is often not "sold" but rather monetised through advertising or subscriptions. Further, the provision of illegal digital content inevitably relies on the services of other intermediaries for infrastructure and

support, for example, domain registrars/registries, providers of hosting services, app stores, content delivery network and payment providers. Therefore, all such intermediaries should be subject to this obligation. It is also essential that the information provided pursuant to Article 22(1) of the DSA proposal is not only verified at the time of receipt, but also periodically for as long as the user continues to receive the intermediary's services. A KYBC obligation must be accompanied by a basis for interested persons to access that information, in timely manner and at scale, for the legitimate purpose of investigating perpetrators of illegal activ ity and enforcement of their rights (see section 3.6 below).

A KYBC obligation must be accompanied by a basis for interested persons to access that information, in timely manner and at scale, for the legitimate purpose of investigating perpetrators of illegal activ ity and enforcement of their rights (see section 3.6 below). Access to the information under Article 22(5) of the DSA proposal should not preclude an intermediary from providing access to information voluntarily, provided that it is able to do so in accordance with the applicable law. 3.6 Legal basis for a public register about domain registrants. Following GDPR coming into force, the Internet Cooperation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) 12 introduced a Temporary Specification for WHOIS requiring registrars and registries to redact the vast majority of WHOIS data pertaining to European domain registrants (irrespective of whether they are natural or legal persons). The result has been an almost total withdrawal of the public WHOIS register which has significantly impacted our ability to obtain data necessary for our enforcement and litigation actions. Discussions are ongoing at ICANN to develop an "access model" but there is a lack of confidenc e amongst stakeholders about this process and the prospects of it arriving at a workable solution. Legislative intervention is needed urgently to clarify the public interest in a public WHOIS registry. Therefore, the DSA should include an explicit legal basis for a public WHOIS registry which should, at a minimum, contain all data already required to be made publicly available under Article 5 of the E-Commerce Directive. Currently, there is also no proposed explicit basis for access to WHOIS information by interested individuals or entities (e.g. private sector organisations and companies) for the legitimate purpose of investigating and enforcing against illegal activity. 4. The DSA should maintain its confirmation that specific monitoring is allowed. We agree with the Commission's proposal to make clear that the prohibition on general monitoring obligations (a) does not preclude a service carrying out general monitoring on its own initiative and (b) does not preclude obligations upon services to carry out specific monitoring (Recital 28 of the DSA proposal). 4.1 Unnecessary and unhelpful reference to subsidiarity. 12 ICANN is a multi-stakeholder group that coordinates several databases relating to the internet. An essential feature of the intermediary liability regime in the E-Commerce Directive is that right holders or other victims of illegal activity may seek injunctive relief against an intermediary.

4.1 Unnecessary and unhelpful reference to subsidiarity. 12 ICANN is a multi-stakeholder group that coordinates several databases relating to the internet. An essential feature of the intermediary liability regime in the E-Commerce Directive is that right holders or other victims of illegal activity may seek injunctive relief against an intermediary. This is described in recital 45 of the E-Commerce Directive as well as in Articles 12-14 themselves13. This reflects the reality that the intermediary service provider is often best-placed to terminate or prevent illegal activit ies on its service and the practical difficulties involved in pursuing the operators of services engaged in illegal activity, as they will often deliberately conceal their identities using the many tools - including intermediary services - available in the online environment. While the draft DSA does not change existing rules in this respect, the statement in recital 26 that "where possible, third parties affected by illegal content transmitted or stored online should attempt to resolve conflicts relating to such content without involving the providers of intermediary services in question " could be misconstrued and interpreted as introducing a new condition for granting injunctions against online intermediaries. As such, the recital is not only unnecessary, it is also unhelpful. 5. Positive obligations under the DSA should be coupled with effective enforcement measures which have cross-border effect. 5.1 The issue. Injunctive relief is a key remedy for right holders both with respect to illegal services and the intermediary services that support the functionality of or access to illegal services, but the effectiveness of the remedy is currently undermined in many Member States because, while unauthorised websites ope rate indiscriminately across Europe, right holders have to take action Member State by Member State or if a single action is possible, to plead and prove illegality under the national law of each applicable Member State 14. This is slow and prohibitively co stly for most right holders. Furthermore, European legal systems do not uniformly allow right holders to seek "dynamic" or "catalogue wide" injunctions making it unreasonably difficult for right holders to effectively protect their rights across Europe.

This is slow and prohibitively co stly for most right holders. Furthermore, European legal systems do not uniformly allow right holders to seek "dynamic" or "catalogue wide" injunctions making it unreasonably difficult for right holders to effectively protect their rights across Europe. 13 (45): The limitations of the liability of intermediary service providers established in this Directive do not affect the possibility of injunctions of different kinds; such injunctions can in particular consist of orders by courts or administrative authorities requiring the termination or prevention of any infringement, including the removal of illegal information or the disabling of access to it. 14 The most compelling example to stress the importance of this issue is the notorious BitTorrent site "The Pirate Bay". The operators of The Pirate Bay have been subject to civil and criminal litigation in Sweden, and to criminal ac tions in Belgium and Finland. The cases were successful, and appeals were rejected by all instances including by the European Court of Human Rights. Actions against intermediaries, e.g. to block access to the site, have been successful in 20 countries arou nd the world including 13 EU Member States. The CJEU has also confirmed the operators of the websites are engaged in copyright restricted acts. However, in spite of these multiple actions, the site remains online and accessible in many EU countries. Not only does the current regime place tremendous burden on right holders as described above, but it also adds unnecessarily to the workload of the courts of Member States across the European Union, resulting in wasted time, costs and resource. Critically, the absence of cross-border injunctions is also inherently prejudicial to the proper functioning of the internal market. Although the draft DSA provides for sharing of orders and cross-border cooperation among Digital Services Coordinators in certain circumstances15, it does not provide a solution to the barriers to enforcement of rights within the EU. 5.2 Possible solutions. The DSA could improve the situation by introducing measures which could help to ensure cross-border effect of certain protective and preventive measures. In case of applications for "no fault" third party injunctions (available under applicable EU law) related to the same unauthorised service but different national respondent intermediaries, the DSA should empower Member States to introduce expedited procedures to ensure that the same category of online intermediaries will take the same measures in relation to the same infringing service.

In case of applications for "no fault" third party injunctions (available under applicable EU law) related to the same unauthorised service but different national respondent intermediaries, the DSA should empower Member States to introduce expedited procedures to ensure that the same category of online intermediaries will take the same measures in relation to the same infringing service. This could occur within a national court process where judgements from other EU Member States are used as the basis for granting similar injunctions.16 The same results could also be achieved through administrative procedures involving competent agencies ordering the relevant intermediaries to take such measures in their respective countries. By way of example, more effective cross-border enforcement could be achieved by developing further the provisions regarding cooperation among enforcement authorities (for example, under Article 8 of the DSA proposal ), including the Digital Services Coordinators, by establishing expedited procedures to use / recognise injunctive orders from other Member States. However, the immediate issue with that article is that it seems to focus on only specific items of illegal content 17, which makes the scope of the application of this provision very limited and will have to be changed. 15 For example, Articles 8(3) and 45 of the DSA proposal. 16 For example, if right holders were successful in obtaining a judgement against French ISPs requiring them to block access to The Pirate Bay, a German court should grant a similar order for German right holders against the same site in relation to German ISPs without the need to litigate the issue whether the underlying service is infringing. 17 Recital 29: "Depending on the legal system of each Member State and the field of law at issue, national judicial or administrative authorities may order providers of intermediary services to act against certain specific items of illegal content or to provide certain specific items of information. The national laws on the basis of which such orders are issued d iffer considerably and the orders are increasingly addressed in cross-border situations. [ ]" (emphasis added). Article 8(1): "Providers of intermediary services, shall upon receipt of an order to act against a specific item of illegal content, issued by t he relevant national judicial or administrative authorities "

Further, there is a danger in the 'one size fits all' approach to the content of orders by judicial authorities under Article 8(2) of the DSA proposal.

Article 8(1): "Providers of intermediary services, shall upon receipt of an order to act against a specific item of illegal content, issued by t he relevant national judicial or administrative authorities "

Further, there is a danger in the 'one size fits all' approach to the content of orders by judicial authorities under Article 8(2) of the DSA proposal. This is the case particularly given that the requirements are very prescriptive, for example, with respect to the inclusion of URLs which enable the identification of sp ecific illegal content. Due to the horizontal nature of the DSA, this provision would be applied to many different types of illegal activity and content. In the circumstances prescribing the content of the orders as proposed in Article 8(2), is not only unnecessary, but also unhelpful, as it fails to take into account the relevant differences between the activities and content involved. There is also a risk of creating confusion where there are already specific rules and procedures that apply to a partic ular area (for example, in the case of the enforcement of intellectual property rights). Article 8(2) of the DSA proposal must not limit the enforcement of intellectual property rights and scope of the remedies available in respect of infringements of such rights. Another example could be provisions concerning the Digital Services Coordinators' obligations and powers, which could be a basis to introduce more robust rules concerning measures having a 'cross-border' effect, in particular the use and/or recognition of evidence from other Member States.18 5.3 Dynamic and catalogue-wide injunctions. Right holders need to have recourse to measures that:
a. are sufficiently flexible to remain effective over time, i.e. injunctions or other measures that cover the provision of an infringing online service without being limited to specific online locations (URLs / domains) as these are easy to change; and
b. cover the right holder's entire catalogue (the infringer is enjoined from infringing works or recordings owned or controlled by the plaintiff/ applicant); and
c. are genuinely available on an expedited basis where the circumstances require 18 Article 8(3), Article 45, Recital 77 of the DSA proposal.

The European Publishers Council (“EPC”) welcomes the Commission’s Proposal for a Digital Services Act which represents an important step in updating the framework of liability exemptions for providers of intermediary services and in setting out of due diligence obligations that will help address harm arising out of the dissemination of illegal content online. Proportionate but uniform rules for a safe, predictable and trusted online environment where fundamental rights are effectively protected will create transparency and accountability. 
As the watchdogs of democracy, a free and independently funded media ensures that the democratic system remains healthy, uncorrupted and functional. The very essence of a free press is now a cherished freedom under threat by some key practices of very large online platforms especially search engines and social networks which take decisions that are determined and continually changed without any transparency or redress. European media companies have no control over how their content is presented and prioritised by algorithms on VLOPs - designed not to provide facts and diversity of opinion, but rather to maximise revenues for global platforms. This is a commercial issue but also a societal one if democratic debate and the right to be informed is mediated by the commercial policies of very large online platforms with no transparency to citizens as to how content appears where, combined all too often with inexplicable loss of visibility of professional journalism. 
It is essential to ensure that when updating and clarifying the law with regard to very large online platforms, professional publishers and news media are not subjected to new or disproportionate obligations beyond the general laws and editorial codes applicable to journalistic content. 
Publishers, unlike very large online platforms not only take responsibility and full legal liability for the content they publish but ensure their staff are trained and fully equipped to hold those in authority to account at home or abroad, insuring and protecting journalists in the field especially when they are working dangerous situations. Publishers 'go on the record' and defend their journalists, their views and positions in court if necessary. Unlike anonymous bloggers or commentators on social networks, publishers can be clearly identified and take responsibility for the content they publish and any updates thereafter. Publishers are additionally fully engaged in upholding self-regulatory codes for editorial and advertising content and of mechanisms for the public to seek speedy and effective redress free of charge.
Very large online platforms should be exempt from liability for professional journalistic content under the editorial control of a publisher or broadcaster. It is therefore essential that very large online platforms take measures to ensure they do not impose or implement policies that lead to the arbitrary removal or blocking of, legally uploaded content which is under the editorial responsibility of a publisher or broadcaster to ensure full protection of publishers and broadcasters’ journalistic content and copyrights.
A key principle to ensure a balanced DSA will be proportionality; in particular of the different levels of obligations which must apply to the different types of businesses contributing to the digital economy. 
Our full position paper and proposed amendments will follow in due course.

Digital Services Act Glassdoor, Inc. ("Glassdoor"), a U.S.-based company with European headquarters in Dublin, Ireland, welcomes the opportunity to provide feedback on the initial Digital Services Act ("DSA") proposal. Glassdoor particularly welcomes the expressed desire in the proposed legislation to enhance and expand consumer protections, particularly Freedom of Expression, as well as to maintain protections and immunities provided to platforms under the E-Commerce Directive. Glassdoor's mission is to help job seekers find a job and a company they will love. This mission is predicated on protecting workers' right to free speech, which we view as synonymous with the fundamental right of Freedom of Expression. We therefore respectfully request consideration that workplace experience reviews and ensuing allegations or instances of "defamation" or defamatory speech be explicitly removed from what is considered "illegal" content under the DSA proposal. Glassdoor hosts many tens of millions of online company reviews, providing a dynamic, effective and balanced platform on which EU workers can share their authentic experiences and legitimate opinions (both positive and negative) of their workplaces and how their employers have treated them. Companies, in turn, are able to respond to any review free of charge. The Glassdoor platform thus provides a significant and powerful resource to workers and amplifies workers' voices. This is particularly true with the rise of the "gig" economy and the resultant lessening of representation for workers through traditional channels such as trade unions or other representative bodies.This empowerment of workers' voices is particularly relevant given the current prevailing uncertainty surrounding the status of gig workers and whether they should be deemed employees or contractors. Glassdoor provides a platform for these workers to have a voice they would not otherwise have, while also providing companies the ability to easily and freely respond. The Glassdoor platform thus benefits both employees and thoughtful, forward-looking employers looking to improve themselves and do better by their workers. Research shows that organisations having a positive working environment tend to perform better 100 Shoreline Highway Mill Valley, California 94941

in terms of shareholder value https://www.glassdoor.com/research/stock-returns-bptw-2020/#, as well as in retaining staff and reducing employee turnover. https://www.glassdoor.com/research/app/uploads/sites/2/2017/02/GD_ResearchReport_ WhyWorkersQuit_Rebrand_Draft3-1.pdf At the same time, job seekers benefit immensely from having easy access to this previously hard-to-get and critically important information regarding what it is like to actually work at a company. Article 2 (g) (Definitions) Despite the draft legislation's stated aim of providing greater legal certainty, there is as yet no precise definition as to exactly what constitutes illegal content. Since the current legislation does not in our view sufficiently clarify or define "illegal content," there is a very real risk that increasingly varying interpretations of what exactly constitutes "illegal content" will continue to emerge in different jurisdictions. For example, what is regarded as illegal in Germany may not be illegal in France with regard to User Generated Content (UGC) in the form of job reviews posted on the Glassdoor site. This will result in significantly increased compliance, legal and technical costs, given the inevitably different interpretations presented across multiple EU jurisdictions. Since, for example, Article 25, provides illustrative examples of what would be regarded as illegal content, it would be very helpful to include similar descriptions instances applicable to the entirety of the DSA (and not just the Article 25 treatment of VLOPs). Above all, Glassdoor requests that the matter of defamation in the context of workplace experience reviews be explicitly removed from what is considered "illegal" content, particularly in light of the multiplicity of interpretations as to what precisely constitutes defamatory speech as a matter of national law across EU Member States. While the stated aim of the DSA proposal is to better protect EU consumers from illegal content (and legitimately so), our daily experience leads us to believe that organisations hoping to prevent the voicing of candid employee feedback will exploit the proposed legislation in an aggressive manner to stifle their employees' legitimate freedom of speech. We respectfully submit that this risk to employee free speech rights should be balanced with measures to curb illegal content. We therefore respectfully submit that EU consumers are best protected by having unfettered access to authentic workplace experience reviews posted on platforms such as Glassdoor, which provide much-needed transparency to actual workplace conditions and which should therefore not be at risk of being readily deemed to constitute "illegal" content.

Glassdoor also requests that consideration be given to further clarifying what is meant by "illegal activity," or to removing this reference entirely, since the term can be open to a wide range of interpretations lead to excessive takedowns in an effort to ensure strict compliance, which in turn would greatly impinge on Freedom of Expression. Glassdoor accordingly requests that workplace reviews be specifically carved out or excepted from this draft legislation, as legitimate worker speech and Freedom of Expression will inevitably be restricted. Glassdoor for years has sought to act responsibly by removing significant amounts of "lawful but harmful" or "lawful but awful" content before it is ever published or in response to content being flagged. We do so because hosting such content is not in keeping with our mission or compliance with our published Community Guidelines. We hope that, by moving to further protect employee speech, the DSA can serve to further protect workers' fundamental rights and the ability of EU job seekers to have a more beneficial online experience in being able to freely access this valuable and authentic information. Article 13 (Transparency reporting) Glassdoor requests that the requirement for public transparency of reporting not apply to platforms providing workplace reviews, as currently indicated in Article 13(2). We seek to ensure the future integrity of our platform against individuals and organisations that would seek to use such publicly available information to their own unscrupulous advantage, specifically for anti-consumer reasons such as facilitating the placement of fraudulent positive company reviews and/or removal under false pretenses of authentic negative reviews for anti-consumer reasons that directly harm job seekers. Article 14 (Notice and action) With respect to the requirement that there be actual knowledge of illegal content, Glassdoor believes that the current wording in Article 14 is not sufficiently robust and risks creating an outcome in which platforms such as Glassdoor must take extremely conservative, overly cautious approaches to regulating speech. The current proposal appears to presume that complainants are always acting appropriately, whereas in our experience complaints may sometimes be misguided or ill-intentioned. The net result is that significant amounts of workplace reviews that should not have to be removed would instead need to be removed because they are covered by any Notice received under Article 14, regardless of the quality of the complaint and/or underlying supporting evidence provided. This is directly counter to the desire to protect the fundamental right

of Freedom of Expression, and risks greatly restricting job seeker access to critical information shedding light on what it is really like to work at a company. Glassdoor accordingly requests that the procedural and evidentiary requirements in Article 14 be raised significantly so that it is readily possible to identify the particular content that is clearly or obviously illegal at face value. With respect to the many challenging and complex scenarios that will inevitably arise, including with respect to workplace experience reviews, Glassdoor respectfully requests that a complainant be required to obtain a court order or, as requested above, that defamatory speech or "defamation" specifically be excluded from the meaning of "illegal" content in the context of the DSA Article 18 (3) Costs Glassdoor requests that a mechanism be created for frivolous complaints or undue repeat complaints from the same source, so that in such cases the complaining party is not entitled, as of right, to avoid contributing to the costs being unilaterally and solely incurred by the platform provider. Article 19 (Trusted Flaggers) Glassdoor requests that further clarification be provided as to how the status of trusted Flagger is granted and revoked. Article 25 (VLOPs) Glassdoor requests that further clarity be provided as to the definition of a VLOP, rather than leaving this question to a future delegated act. Article 42 Glassdoor asks for further clarity on what triggers sanctions. While mentioned in Article 42, there is no specific wording or explanation as to what exactly triggers sanctions. Glassdoor requests that the legislation be more targeted in its aim of tackling illegal content and that any sanctions be made proportionate to the specific harm caused. For example, the imposition of significant fines should not be available in instances of

defamation or workplace reviews, or should at least be reduced to an amount relative to the harm caused. Signed Joe Freeman William Irwin Head of Legal Assistant General Counsel EMEA
