Vivendi - Feedback on the Digital Services Act - deepening the internal market and clarifying responsibilities for digital services

Introduction Vivendi is a European company based in France. Vivendi is one of the few companies to be at the crossroads of several cultural and creative industries: music, cinema, television, communications, books, video games and live performances. Promoting creation in all its diversity and revealing talent are at the heart of Vivendi's strategy. All businesses contribute to this objective, in particular Universal Music Group, Canal+ Group, Editis and Gameloft. The distribution platforms (Dailymotion and myCanal), the agreements signed with numerous telco operators and content aggregators ensure a large distribution of content and talent. Havas Group possesses a unique creative exp ertise to make a meaningful difference to brands, businesses and people. In addition, through Vivendi Village, Vivendi develops complementary activities in live performance, ticketing and franchise developments. Overall, Vivendi group has more than 40,000 employees in 82 countries, including 12,420 in Europe. In 2020, the Group invested 4 Bn Eur in content. This position paper sets out Vivendi's initial views on the Proposal for a Regulation on a Single Market for Digital Services (the Digital Services Act or DSA). Vivendi supports the objective of strengthen ing the existing EU legal framework through clearer, more stringent and harmonised rules on the liability of intermediary service providers in order to ensure online accountability while protecting fundamental rights, promoting innovation and ensuring online safety. We are also supportive of the overall structure which aims to: (i) clarify the conditional liability framework for intermediary services providers; (ii) introduce proportionate due diligence obligations; and, (iii) establish rules on the implementation and enforcement of the DSA. However, our support is conditioned upon the introduction of a number of clarifications and certain improvements which are necessary to ensure that the DSA can deliver on its stated objectives in an environment of increased legal certainty. We describe these points below in more detail but in terms of basic principles we take the view that the DSA must at a minimum:
• Remain faithful to the liability privilege regime established under Articles 12-14 of the E - Commerce Directive (ECD) in line with the relevant jurisprudence of the European Court of Justice (ECJ) and prevent the creation of new safe harbours
• Establish meaningful positive obligations for all information society services, including by linking eligibility for liability privileges to compliance with due diligence requirements. While the imposition of specific asymmetric due diligence obligations on very large online platforms is proportionate, the DSA must also be comprehensive. In this regard, the due diligence obligations in Sections 2 and 3 of Chapter III should extend to all hosting services, including micro or small enterprises.
• Clarify that the scope of provision on voluntary proactive measures applies solely to activities taken to detect, identify and take action against illegal content without affecting the imputation of knowledge and the consequent obligations
• Operate in a manner that promotes effective enforcement online

Vivendi is committed to working with the EU co-legislator to find the right balance between the various objectives and at the same time fostering legal certainty a s well as strengthening the EU's internal market to the benefit of all stakeholders. Scope Vivendi supports continued application of the country of origin principle with the appropriate exclusions per the Annex (derogations from Article 3) of the ECD. This principle is a critical component of any internal market measure. At the same time, we are also supportive of the proposal to ensure that the DSA applies to services which target users in the EU regardless of where they are established. This approach is critical to attainment of the DSA 's goals including, the creation of a safe digital environment and ensuring a level playing field. We also welcome the DSA clarifications as to how it interacts with and leave s unaffected other important areas of EU law. It is crucial for legal certainty and preservation of the current liability regime that the DSA have no impact on the legi speciali listed in Article 1(5). Liability privileges The DSA would maintain the framework of liability privileges for intermediar ies, which meet the conditions for "mere conduit", "caching" or "hosting" services under the E-Commerce Directive (ECD), by reproducing the relevant provisions with minor changes and clarifications. Vivendi considers some improvements and further clarifications are necessary if the DSA is to fulfil its promise while remaining faithful to key principles of EU law as interpreted by the European Court of Justice (ECJ). Active versus neutral Under the ECD, the l iability privileges o nly extend to interm ediaries whose activity is of "a mere technical, automatic and passive nature". This core principle was confirmed and further clarified by the ECJ in the seminal L'Oréal v. eBay case. The concept of neutrality is partially reflected in Recital 18 of the DSA, which confirms intermediaries which provide the content themselves or have editorial responsibility over the content, do not qualify for the privilege. In our view, however, this example while correct may create some confusion because it is rather obvious. Services that provide content themselves or exercise editorial responsibility over the content are not intermediaries. The L'Oréal/eBay1 case, which refers to optimising the presentation or promotion of the content, provides for a clearer more useful example. In this context, we are aware that the Commission wants to ensure that certain functionalities, which "are absolutely necessary to navigate among an endless amount of content, should not be cons idered as 'smoking gun' for an 'active role'". As a result, we would propose making it clear that a provider, which optimises or promotes the content (automatically or not) in a way that goes beyond offering basic search and indexing functionalities that are absolutely necessary to navigate through the content, is not neutral. Such an approach would codify ECJ case law in a manner that creates the right balance between online accountability and legal certainty. Structurally-infringing/Rogue services do not qualify for liability privileges Further to the need to ensure that the concept of neutrality functions in a manner consistent with the goals of the DSA, Recital 20 offers additional guidance noting that an intermediary which: "deliberately collaborates with a recipient of the services in order to undertake illegal activities does not provide its service neutrally and should therefore not be able to benefit from the exemptions from liability".

1 L'Oréal SA and Others v eBay International AG and Others, Case C-324/19, ECLI:EU:C:2011:474

We are concerned however that the reference t o "deliberate collaboration" establishes an element which would be d ifficult to prove in practice and could thereby create a loophole for some rogue services. In order to close that loophole, Vivendi proposes an approach that would exclude intermediaries which "engage in, facilitate or induce illegal activities " from the liability privilege. Moreover, rather than simply amending the Recital, we believe that this issue should also be addressed in a substantive provision (Article 5a). Liability privileges dependent on compliance with due diligence obligations Vivendi takes the position that compliance with Chapter III on due diligence obligations should be a pre-condition of eligibility for the relevant liability privileges. This threshold obligation would help to ensure that the standards that intermediaries have to meet to qualify for liability exemptions play a meaningful role in helping to achieve the DSA's goal of establishing a high level of safety and trust in the online environment for all stakeholders. Such a threshold obligation would in effect create a further incentive for compliance with the due diligence obligations and serve as a deterrent for intermediaries which might otherwise decide not to comply (e.g., because they consider administrative fines are a cost of doing business). The effect would be that failure to comply with due diligence obligations means that intermediaries are exposed to potential liability arising from illegal content or activity on their networks or platforms. The Commission did consider such an option but decided against it (Impact Assessment, Part 2, Section 3.4, pages 165-166). It argued that such approach would "incentivise" but not "require" compliance with the due diligence rules. However, that is not correct. The DSA could provide that compliance with the due diligence obligations is mandatory in addition to being a condition of eligibility for the liability exemptions. The idea is that there is no need to choose between the two approaches -- in fact they are complementary. The Commission also took the view that this approach would make regulatory supervision more burdensome, but this argument is also misplaced. The DSCs would not be required to assess whether intermediaries qualify for the li ability exemptions - that is a matter for the courts on a case-by-case basis (which the Commission acknowledges). Article 5(3) should apply to all hosting services In a justified departure from the terms of Article 14 of the ECD, Article 5(3) of the DSA proposal would disapply the hosting privilege for online marketplaces that present an item or enable a transaction "in a way that would lead an average and reasonably well-informed consumer to believe that the marketplace is providing it itself ". Such an approach is consistent with the concept of neutrality. As such there i s no justification for disapplying the privilege only for marketplaces, the same principle should apply to all hosting providers covered by Article 5. In fact, the existence of this explicit carveout for marketplaces is discriminatory and could potentially be misinterpreted. Article 5 (3) should extend to all hosting services when their users believe the information is provided by the hosting service itself. Bad Samaritans Article 6 would establish a so-called "Good Samaritan" clause which is inspired by US law (§230 of the Communications Decency Act ). It would provide tha t intermediaries are not disqualified from the privileges liability in Articles 3, 4 and 5 of the DSA solely because they carry out voluntary own - initiative investigations or other activities aimed at detecting, identifying and removing, or disabling of access to, illegal content or to comply with the law. Our concern here is that the DSA must operate to ensure that bad samaritans do not benefit from liability privileges. In this regard, Vivendi considers that this clarification is unnecessary since it quite clearly follows from the ECD as well as the ECJ case law which the Commission confirmed in similar terms in its

Communication on Tackling Illegal Content of November 2018, by noting that taking "proactive measures does not automatically lead to the online platform losing the benefit of the liability exemption". We are not aware of any intermediary ever having been held liable for removing illegal content. The current legal framework actually requires that intermediaries diligently address illegal content as a condition for benefitting from the liability privileg es. This requirement has been confirmed by the ECJ2 which held that hosting liability privileges are unavailable where an intermediary fails to act, despite being aware of facts or circumstances on the basis of which a diligent economic operator should have identified the illegality in question and disabled access to it. The loss of the liability privilege is linked to promoting illegal content - not to disabling access to it - which in any event is an obligation once awareness or knowledge is obtained. Finally, we note that the terms and conditions of most intermediaries reserve ample powers for them to address illegal content on their platforms or networks. As a result, we take the position that Article 6 must be clarified by stipulating that it only concerns activities solely taken to detect, identify and take action against illegal content. At the same time, Article 6 must not operate in a manner that prevents the imputation of actual knowledge in order to ensure expeditious removal of or disabling of access to the illegal content. No general monitoring obligation Article 7 basically copies over the prohibition on imposing a general obligation to monitor on intermediaries from Article 15 of the ECD. While Recital 28 clarifies that this prohibition does not concern monitoring obligations in a specific case, Vivendi takes the view that this provision should be amended to clarify further that providers can be required to undertake proactive measures to identify and remove illegal content or prevent its reappearance. The DSA Explanatory Memorandum provides explicit reference to the Facebook case (C-18/18) but this language should be inserted in Recital 28. Cross border orders Rather than creating a substantive new cause of action, Articles 8 and 9 would harmonise certain procedural aspects of orders to act against a specific item of illegal content and orders to provide a specific item of information respectively based on current EU or national law. According to Recital 29, the context is cross-border situations. However, these provisions are crafted in board terms, which seem to cover all orders, regardless of their territorial scope. Recital 33 further clarifies that such orders will not operate as a restriction on intermediaries' freedom to provide services across borders and therefore do not necessitate a country of origin derogation under Article 3 (4) of the ECD. To ensure consistency with the intent of these provisions as well as confirm that important remedies under national law are not undermined, Articles 8 and 9 should be explicitly limited to cross-border orders. The proposal to harmonise cross-border orders to provide a specific item of information also creates an opportunity to clarify the scope of available information. Vivendi considers that such information should include email addresses, telephone numbers, IP addresses and other necessary contact details in order to ensure meaningful compliance with EU and national law. Such an approach is consistent with the need to address some of the legislative gaps recently identified by the ECJ in the Constantin Film case (C-264/19). Subsidiarity/Action against intermediary vs individual end-user Recital 26 contains language which suggests that victims of illegal activity online should take action against individuals (end-users) rather than intermediaries. However, in most cases - particularly given that end-users are difficult to identify and many infringing services operate offshore - intermediaries

2 L'Oréal/eBay, see above

services are best placed to address illegal content in an effective manner which limits need for involving end-users. This language should be deleted and replaced with reference to the concept that intermediaries are often best placed to deal illegality on their platforms or networks. Due diligence obligations Notice & Action Mechanisms (NAMs) Article 14 is designed to harmonise NAMs "so as to provide for the timely, diligent and objective processing of notices on the basis of rules that are uniform, transparent and clear and that provide for robust safeguards to protect the rights and legitimate interests of all affected parties" (Recital 41). Vivendi is, however, concerned that on one hand the proposal creates burdensome hurdles to effective action while on the other hand it is missing out on important opportunities. If this provision is to improve the efficiency of notice sending with a view toward achieving effective and swift removal of illegal content and ongoing protection of users, it requires modification to ensure the following:
• A clear obligation to act by removing or disabl ing access to the notified information expeditiously
• A clear stay-down obligation to prevent the reappearance of notified illegal information - the alternative is a useless mechanism that serves no real purpose
• Reasonable requirements for what should constitute a sufficiently precise and adequately substantiated notice. The requirement that notices should contain "the exact URL" to identify illegal information is unworkable, particularly with regard to apps and other services that do not depend on URLs. The standard should be that the notice must include sufficient information to permit action.

These proposals are designed to ensure that NAMs advance the goals of the DSA. Know Your Business Customer (KYBC) provision Article 22 on "traceability of traders" would introduce an obligation for online platforms which allow "consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders" to know the identities of traders using their services to promote messages or offer products or services to EU consumers. As a result, the DSA's provision for KYBC is unfortunately limited to online marketplaces. The situation is further exacerbated by the fact that micro and small enterprises are exempt from compliance. Thus, only larger online marketplaces are subject to the proposed Regulation. This extremely limited approach to a major problem is very disappointing. It means that the DSA lacks the tools necessary to enhance the safety and trust of digital service s. The Commission's proposal omits an essential tool for combatting illegal activities online. It merely carries over a problem that was already apparent due to the fact that Article 5 of the ECD is toothless and basically unenforceable. In order to operate online, a business requires a domain name, it needs to be hosted and it will invariably rely on advertisement or payment services. These intermediary services, having a direct relationship with the business, are therefore best placed to ensure that only businesses that are willing to comply with the existing identification rules should have access to their services. The logic of such an approach is already apparent in the financial services sector in the form of Anti-Money Laundering instruments. Indeed, KYBC under the DSA could rely heavily on existing structures such as registers which are publicly accessible, including through national company registers, European Business Register (EBR) and Ultimate Beneficial Owners register (UBO register). In recognition of the need to respect the fundamental right of privacy, KYBC should be limited to business customers only. As a result, individual consumers are not covered but they will benefit from a safer and more predictable online environment.

Vivendi therefore takes the view that:
• Article 2 should be amended to include a definition of "business customers" which clearly distinguishes between commercial operators and private customers (who would be out of scope) and establishes safeguards to ensure full compliance with GDPR while limiting any extra unnecessary bureaucratic burdens.
• At the same time, Vivendi proposes that Article 22 be moved to Chapter III Section 1 with the effect that it extends to all providers of intermediary services, including providers of infrastructure services.
• Alternatively, a new KYB C Article could be elaborated and include more details on the verification procedure. Trusted Flaggers Article 19 would introduce a legal requirement for online platforms to establish so-called trusted flagger provisions which ensures that "notices submitted by trusted flaggers are processed and decided upon with priority and without delay". Article 19 would also create a key role for t he Digital Services Coordinator (DSC) of the Member State of establishment of the entity seeking status of trusted flagger. DSCs are charged with awarding such status to a n entity where it meets three conditions, including that it represents collective interests. Recital 46 provides an important clarification that online platforms are in no way precluded from giving similar "trusted flagger" treatment to notices submitted by entities or individuals that have not been awarded trusted flagger status by the DSCs. At the very least, this guidance must stay in place. Vivendi is supportive of the establishment of trusted flagger mechanism. We note that many platforms already operate similar systems and indeed certain companies in our group are already considered "trusted flaggers". We are however concerned about two key aspects of this proposal. First, we can see no reason for limiting the scope of Article 19 to "online platforms" only - we believe it should apply to all hosting services (e.g., cyberlockers). Second, we believe it is vital that the criterion that trusted flaggers need to represent collective interests is removed. The focus should be ensuring that trusted flaggers have the necessary know-how and experience. Entities merit the priority handling o f their notices where their notices are likely to be accurate because they have demonstrated expertise and a high rate of accuracy when flagging content. Such entities which may not be part of trade associations or collective bodies should not be excluded. Repeat Infringers Article 20 mandates an important provision for ensuring online safety and tackling illegal content by introducing a repeat infringer mechanism. However, the scope of this provision is very limited. Vivendi proposes that the r epeat infringer provision be moved to Chapter II to ensure that it applies to all hosting services (e.g. cyberlockers). Moreover, Article 20 should also permit the termination o f the provision of services in egregious cases - for example in cases of repeated suspension. Intermediaries should also take steps to limit abusive practices by establishing mechanisms to prevent re-registration by suspended or terminated individuals that frequently provide manifestly illegal content. Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) Vivendi welcomes the asymmetric and proportionate approach of ensuring increased online accountability for VLOPs. The sheer scale of such platforms means that they pose additional risks and wield tremendous power. At the same time, they are well placed to mitigate those risks and play a meaningful role in creating a safer internet. As noted above, we take the view th at intermediaries should be deemed ineligible for the liability privileges in the DSA where they fail to adhere to their

due diligence obligations - this is especially important in the case of VLOPs. We also applaud the establishment of clear criteria to foster legal certainty but at the same time, we note the need for some flexibility which may be addressed through delegated acts (for example with regard to borderline cases). The obligation of VLOPs to conduct risk assessments (Article 26) which are specific to their services is a requisite tool for ensuring that the goals of the DSA are realised. However, we would like to point out that this obligation should not entail the exercise of any oversight role in respect of content distributed online by service providers who take full editorial responsibility for their content and as a result operate according to strict EU or national content regulations while respecting important journalistic and editorial principles. In order to function in manner that contributes to a safer online environment, the scope of Articles 26 and 27 must be broad enough to address the harm that can be caused by the risks detailed in the DSA. Vivendi also supports effective measures to enhance the accountability and transparency for VLOPs (Articles 28-33), particularly in view of the dual role they play as distributors and publishers. We believe however that these obligations need to be reinforced in several respects. Given the rapid and constant evolution of algorithms, the control and supervision mechanism must function effectively as close to real-time as possible. We consider that Article 28(4) needs to be tightened up to ensure that VLOPs are not in a position to ignore operational recommendations platforms too easily. As regards advertising, the DSA provides a useful first step by establishing an obligation to compile and make publicly available repositories through APIs. However, the reporting on th e information required under Article 30(2) needs to be undertaken with the appropriate regulatory or independent oversight. Finally, t he transparency measures should extend to the key criteria for aggregation, selection and presentation of content as well as functionalities of the algorithms in real time. Vivendi - Feedback on the Digital Services Act - deepening the internal market and clarifying responsibilities for digital services

Introduction Vivendi is a European company based in France. Vivendi is one of the few companies to be at the crossroads of several cultural and creative industries: music, cinema, television, communications, books, video games and live performances. Promoting creation in all its diversity and revealing talent are at the heart of Vivendi's strategy. All businesses contribute to this objective, in particular Universal Music Group, Canal+ Group, Editis and Gameloft. The distribution platforms (Dailymotion and myCanal), the agreements signed with numerous telco operators and content aggregators ensure a large distribution of content and talent. Havas Group possesses a unique creative exp ertise to make a meaningful difference to brands, businesses and people. In addition, through Vivendi Village, Vivendi develops complementary activities in live performance, ticketing and franchise developments. Overall, Vivendi group has more than 40,000 employees in 82 countries, including 12,420 in Europe. In 2020, the Group invested 4 Bn Eur in content. This position paper sets out Vivendi's initial views on the Proposal for a Regulation on a Single Market for Digital Services (the Digital Services Act or DSA). Vivendi supports the objective of strengthen ing the existing EU legal framework through clearer, more stringent and harmonised rules on the liability of intermediary service providers in order to ensure online accountability while protecting fundamental rights, promoting innovation and ensuring online safety. We are also supportive of the overall structure which aims to: (i) clarify the conditional liability framework for intermediary services providers; (ii) introduce proportionate due diligence obligations; and, (iii) establish rules on the implementation and enforcement of the DSA. However, our support is conditioned upon the introduction of a number of clarifications and certain improvements which are necessary to ensure that the DSA can deliver on its stated objectives in an environment of increased legal certainty.

However, our support is conditioned upon the introduction of a number of clarifications and certain improvements which are necessary to ensure that the DSA can deliver on its stated objectives in an environment of increased legal certainty. We describe these points below in more detail but in terms of basic principles we take the view that the DSA must at a minimum:
• Remain faithful to the liability privilege regime established under Articles 12-14 of the E - Commerce Directive (ECD) in line with the relevant jurisprudence of the European Court of Justice (ECJ) and prevent the creation of new safe harbours
• Establish meaningful positive obligations for all information society services, including by linking eligibility for liability privileges to compliance with due diligence requirements. While the imposition of specific asymmetric due diligence obligations on very large online platforms is proportionate, the DSA must also be comprehensive. In this regard, the due diligence obligations in Sections 2 and 3 of Chapter III should extend to all hosting services, including micro or small enterprises. • Clarify that the scope of provision on voluntary proactive measures applies solely to activities taken to detect, identify and take action against illegal content without affecting the imputation of knowledge and the consequent obligations
• Operate in a manner that promotes effective enforcement online

Vivendi is committed to working with the EU co-legislator to find the right balance between the various objectives and at the same time fostering legal certainty a s well as strengthening the EU's internal market to the benefit of all stakeholders. Scope Vivendi supports continued application of the country of origin principle with the appropriate exclusions per the Annex (derogations from Article 3) of the ECD. This principle is a critical component of any internal market measure. At the same time, we are also supportive of the proposal to ensure that the DSA applies to services which target users in the EU regardless of where they are established. This approach is critical to attainment of the DSA 's goals including, the creation of a safe digital environment and ensuring a level playing field. We also welcome the DSA clarifications as to how it interacts with and leave s unaffected other important areas of EU law. It is crucial for legal certainty and preservation of the current liability regime that the DSA have no impact on the legi speciali listed in Article 1(5).

We also welcome the DSA clarifications as to how it interacts with and leave s unaffected other important areas of EU law. It is crucial for legal certainty and preservation of the current liability regime that the DSA have no impact on the legi speciali listed in Article 1(5). Liability privileges The DSA would maintain the framework of liability privileges for intermediar ies, which meet the conditions for "mere conduit", "caching" or "hosting" services under the E-Commerce Directive (ECD), by reproducing the relevant provisions with minor changes and clarifications. Vivendi considers some improvements and further clarifications are necessary if the DSA is to fulfil its promise while remaining faithful to key principles of EU law as interpreted by the European Court of Justice (ECJ). Active versus neutral Under the ECD, the l iability privileges o nly extend to interm ediaries whose activity is of "a mere technical, automatic and passive nature". This core principle was confirmed and further clarified by the ECJ in the seminal L'Oréal v. eBay case. The concept of neutrality is partially reflected in Recital 18 of the DSA, which confirms intermediaries which provide the content themselves or have editorial responsibility over the content, do not qualify for the privilege. In our view, however, this example while correct may create some confusion because it is rather obvious. Services that provide content themselves or exercise editorial responsibility over the content are not intermediaries. The L'Oréal/eBay1 case, which refers to optimising the presentation or promotion of the content, provides for a clearer more useful example. In this context, we are aware that the Commission wants to ensure that certain functionalities, which "are absolutely necessary to navigate among an endless amount of content, should not be cons idered as 'smoking gun' for an 'active role'". As a result, we would propose making it clear that a provider, which optimises or promotes the content (automatically or not) in a way that goes beyond offering basic search and indexing functionalities that are absolutely necessary to navigate through the content, is not neutral. Such an approach would codify ECJ case law in a manner that creates the right balance between online accountability and legal certainty.

Such an approach would codify ECJ case law in a manner that creates the right balance between online accountability and legal certainty. Structurally-infringing/Rogue services do not qualify for liability privileges Further to the need to ensure that the concept of neutrality functions in a manner consistent with the goals of the DSA, Recital 20 offers additional guidance noting that an intermediary which: "deliberately collaborates with a recipient of the services in order to undertake illegal activities does not provide its service neutrally and should therefore not be able to benefit from the exemptions from liability". 1 L'Oréal SA and Others v eBay International AG and Others, Case C-324/19, ECLI:EU:C:2011:474

We are concerned however that the reference t o "deliberate collaboration" establishes an element which would be d ifficult to prove in practice and could thereby create a loophole for some rogue services. In order to close that loophole, Vivendi proposes an approach that would exclude intermediaries which "engage in, facilitate or induce illegal activities " from the liability privilege. Moreover, rather than simply amending the Recital, we believe that this issue should also be addressed in a substantive provision (Article 5a). Liability privileges dependent on compliance with due diligence obligations Vivendi takes the position that compliance with Chapter III on due diligence obligations should be a pre-condition of eligibility for the relevant liability privileges. This threshold obligation would help to ensure that the standards that intermediaries have to meet to qualify for liability exemptions play a meaningful role in helping to achieve the DSA's goal of establishing a high level of safety and trust in the online environment for all stakeholders. Such a threshold obligation would in effect create a further incentive for compliance with the due diligence obligations and serve as a deterrent for intermediaries which might otherwise decide not to comply (e.g., because they consider administrative fines are a cost of doing business). The effect would be that failure to comply with due diligence obligations means that intermediaries are exposed to potential liability arising from illegal content or activity on their networks or platforms. The Commission did consider such an option but decided against it (Impact Assessment, Part 2, Section 3.4, pages 165-166). It argued that such approach would "incentivise" but not "require" compliance with the due diligence rules. However, that is not correct.

The Commission did consider such an option but decided against it (Impact Assessment, Part 2, Section 3.4, pages 165-166). It argued that such approach would "incentivise" but not "require" compliance with the due diligence rules. However, that is not correct. The DSA could provide that compliance with the due diligence obligations is mandatory in addition to being a condition of eligibility for the liability exemptions. The idea is that there is no need to choose between the two approaches -- in fact they are complementary. The Commission also took the view that this approach would make regulatory supervision more burdensome, but this argument is also misplaced. The DSCs would not be required to assess whether intermediaries qualify for the li ability exemptions - that is a matter for the courts on a case-by-case basis (which the Commission acknowledges). Article 5(3) should apply to all hosting services In a justified departure from the terms of Article 14 of the ECD, Article 5(3) of the DSA proposal would disapply the hosting privilege for online marketplaces that present an item or enable a transaction "in a way that would lead an average and reasonably well-informed consumer to believe that the marketplace is providing it itself ". Such an approach is consistent with the concept of neutrality. As such there i s no justification for disapplying the privilege only for marketplaces, the same principle should apply to all hosting providers covered by Article 5. In fact, the existence of this explicit carveout for marketplaces is discriminatory and could potentially be misinterpreted. Article 5 (3) should extend to all hosting services when their users believe the information is provided by the hosting service itself. Bad Samaritans Article 6 would establish a so-called "Good Samaritan" clause which is inspired by US law (§230 of the Communications Decency Act ). It would provide tha t intermediaries are not disqualified from the privileges liability in Articles 3, 4 and 5 of the DSA solely because they carry out voluntary own - initiative investigations or other activities aimed at detecting, identifying and removing, or disabling of access to, illegal content or to comply with the law. Our concern here is that the DSA must operate to ensure that bad samaritans do not benefit from liability privileges.

Our concern here is that the DSA must operate to ensure that bad samaritans do not benefit from liability privileges. In this regard, Vivendi considers that this clarification is unnecessary since it quite clearly follows from the ECD as well as the ECJ case law which the Commission confirmed in similar terms in its

Communication on Tackling Illegal Content of November 2018, by noting that taking "proactive measures does not automatically lead to the online platform losing the benefit of the liability exemption". We are not aware of any intermediary ever having been held liable for removing illegal content. The current legal framework actually requires that intermediaries diligently address illegal content as a condition for benefitting from the liability privileg es. This requirement has been confirmed by the ECJ2 which held that hosting liability privileges are unavailable where an intermediary fails to act, despite being aware of facts or circumstances on the basis of which a diligent economic operator should have identified the illegality in question and disabled access to it. The loss of the liability privilege is linked to promoting illegal content - not to disabling access to it - which in any event is an obligation once awareness or knowledge is obtained. Finally, we note that the terms and conditions of most intermediaries reserve ample powers for them to address illegal content on their platforms or networks. As a result, we take the position that Article 6 must be clarified by stipulating that it only concerns activities solely taken to detect, identify and take action against illegal content. At the same time, Article 6 must not operate in a manner that prevents the imputation of actual knowledge in order to ensure expeditious removal of or disabling of access to the illegal content. No general monitoring obligation Article 7 basically copies over the prohibition on imposing a general obligation to monitor on intermediaries from Article 15 of the ECD. While Recital 28 clarifies that this prohibition does not concern monitoring obligations in a specific case, Vivendi takes the view that this provision should be amended to clarify further that providers can be required to undertake proactive measures to identify and remove illegal content or prevent its reappearance. The DSA Explanatory Memorandum provides explicit reference to the Facebook case (C-18/18) but this language should be inserted in Recital 28.

The DSA Explanatory Memorandum provides explicit reference to the Facebook case (C-18/18) but this language should be inserted in Recital 28. Cross border orders Rather than creating a substantive new cause of action, Articles 8 and 9 would harmonise certain procedural aspects of orders to act against a specific item of illegal content and orders to provide a specific item of information respectively based on current EU or national law. According to Recital 29, the context is cross-border situations. However, these provisions are crafted in board terms, which seem to cover all orders, regardless of their territorial scope. Recital 33 further clarifies that such orders will not operate as a restriction on intermediaries' freedom to provide services across borders and therefore do not necessitate a country of origin derogation under Article 3 (4) of the ECD. To ensure consistency with the intent of these provisions as well as confirm that important remedies under national law are not undermined, Articles 8 and 9 should be explicitly limited to cross-border orders. The proposal to harmonise cross-border orders to provide a specific item of information also creates an opportunity to clarify the scope of available information. Vivendi considers that such information should include email addresses, telephone numbers, IP addresses and other necessary contact details in order to ensure meaningful compliance with EU and national law. Such an approach is consistent with the need to address some of the legislative gaps recently identified by the ECJ in the Constantin Film case (C-264/19). Subsidiarity/Action against intermediary vs individual end-user Recital 26 contains language which suggests that victims of illegal activity online should take action against individuals (end-users) rather than intermediaries. However, in most cases - particularly given that end-users are difficult to identify and many infringing services operate offshore - intermediaries

2 L'Oréal/eBay, see above

services are best placed to address illegal content in an effective manner which limits need for involving end-users. This language should be deleted and replaced with reference to the concept that intermediaries are often best placed to deal illegality on their platforms or networks.

This language should be deleted and replaced with reference to the concept that intermediaries are often best placed to deal illegality on their platforms or networks. Due diligence obligations Notice & Action Mechanisms (NAMs) Article 14 is designed to harmonise NAMs "so as to provide for the timely, diligent and objective processing of notices on the basis of rules that are uniform, transparent and clear and that provide for robust safeguards to protect the rights and legitimate interests of all affected parties" (Recital 41). Vivendi is, however, concerned that on one hand the proposal creates burdensome hurdles to effective action while on the other hand it is missing out on important opportunities. If this provision is to improve the efficiency of notice sending with a view toward achieving effective and swift removal of illegal content and ongoing protection of users, it requires modification to ensure the following:
• A clear obligation to act by removing or disabl ing access to the notified information expeditiously
• A clear stay-down obligation to prevent the reappearance of notified illegal information - the alternative is a useless mechanism that serves no real purpose
• Reasonable requirements for what should constitute a sufficiently precise and adequately substantiated notice. The requirement that notices should contain "the exact URL" to identify illegal information is unworkable, particularly with regard to apps and other services that do not depend on URLs. The standard should be that the notice must include sufficient information to permit action. These proposals are designed to ensure that NAMs advance the goals of the DSA. Know Your Business Customer (KYBC) provision Article 22 on "traceability of traders" would introduce an obligation for online platforms which allow "consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders" to know the identities of traders using their services to promote messages or offer products or services to EU consumers. As a result, the DSA's provision for KYBC is unfortunately limited to online marketplaces. The situation is further exacerbated by the fact that micro and small enterprises are exempt from compliance. Thus, only larger online marketplaces are subject to the proposed Regulation. This extremely limited approach to a major problem is very disappointing. It means that the DSA lacks the tools necessary to enhance the safety and trust of digital service s. The Commission's proposal omits an essential tool for combatting illegal activities online.

This extremely limited approach to a major problem is very disappointing. It means that the DSA lacks the tools necessary to enhance the safety and trust of digital service s. The Commission's proposal omits an essential tool for combatting illegal activities online. It merely carries over a problem that was already apparent due to the fact that Article 5 of the ECD is toothless and basically unenforceable. In order to operate online, a business requires a domain name, it needs to be hosted and it will invariably rely on advertisement or payment services. These intermediary services, having a direct relationship with the business, are therefore best placed to ensure that only businesses that are willing to comply with the existing identification rules should have access to their services. The logic of such an approach is already apparent in the financial services sector in the form of Anti-Money Laundering instruments. Indeed, KYBC under the DSA could rely heavily on existing structures such as registers which are publicly accessible, including through national company registers, European Business Register (EBR) and Ultimate Beneficial Owners register (UBO register). In recognition of the need to respect the fundamental right of privacy, KYBC should be limited to business customers only. As a result, individual consumers are not covered but they will benefit from a safer and more predictable online environment. Vivendi therefore takes the view that:
• Article 2 should be amended to include a definition of "business customers" which clearly distinguishes between commercial operators and private customers (who would be out of scope) and establishes safeguards to ensure full compliance with GDPR while limiting any extra unnecessary bureaucratic burdens. • At the same time, Vivendi proposes that Article 22 be moved to Chapter III Section 1 with the effect that it extends to all providers of intermediary services, including providers of infrastructure services. • Alternatively, a new KYB C Article could be elaborated and include more details on the verification procedure. Trusted Flaggers Article 19 would introduce a legal requirement for online platforms to establish so-called trusted flagger provisions which ensures that "notices submitted by trusted flaggers are processed and decided upon with priority and without delay". Article 19 would also create a key role for t he Digital Services Coordinator (DSC) of the Member State of establishment of the entity seeking status of trusted flagger.

Article 19 would also create a key role for t he Digital Services Coordinator (DSC) of the Member State of establishment of the entity seeking status of trusted flagger. DSCs are charged with awarding such status to a n entity where it meets three conditions, including that it represents collective interests. Recital 46 provides an important clarification that online platforms are in no way precluded from giving similar "trusted flagger" treatment to notices submitted by entities or individuals that have not been awarded trusted flagger status by the DSCs. At the very least, this guidance must stay in place. Vivendi is supportive of the establishment of trusted flagger mechanism. We note that many platforms already operate similar systems and indeed certain companies in our group are already considered "trusted flaggers". We are however concerned about two key aspects of this proposal. First, we can see no reason for limiting the scope of Article 19 to "online platforms" only - we believe it should apply to all hosting services (e.g., cyberlockers). Second, we believe it is vital that the criterion that trusted flaggers need to represent collective interests is removed. The focus should be ensuring that trusted flaggers have the necessary know-how and experience. Entities merit the priority handling o f their notices where their notices are likely to be accurate because they have demonstrated expertise and a high rate of accuracy when flagging content. Such entities which may not be part of trade associations or collective bodies should not be excluded. Repeat Infringers Article 20 mandates an important provision for ensuring online safety and tackling illegal content by introducing a repeat infringer mechanism. However, the scope of this provision is very limited. Vivendi proposes that the r epeat infringer provision be moved to Chapter II to ensure that it applies to all hosting services (e.g. cyberlockers). Moreover, Article 20 should also permit the termination o f the provision of services in egregious cases - for example in cases of repeated suspension. Intermediaries should also take steps to limit abusive practices by establishing mechanisms to prevent re-registration by suspended or terminated individuals that frequently provide manifestly illegal content. Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) Vivendi welcomes the asymmetric and proportionate approach of ensuring increased online accountability for VLOPs. The sheer scale of such platforms means that they pose additional risks and wield tremendous power.

The sheer scale of such platforms means that they pose additional risks and wield tremendous power. At the same time, they are well placed to mitigate those risks and play a meaningful role in creating a safer internet. As noted above, we take the view th at intermediaries should be deemed ineligible for the liability privileges in the DSA where they fail to adhere to their

due diligence obligations - this is especially important in the case of VLOPs. We also applaud the establishment of clear criteria to foster legal certainty but at the same time, we note the need for some flexibility which may be addressed through delegated acts (for example with regard to borderline cases). Confindustria Radio Televisions sends a contribution with its own observations on the issue of the liability of intermediaries in the proposed regulation of the Digital Services Act

Legge sui servizi digitali Approfondire il mercato e chiarire le responsabilità per i servizi digitali

Position Paper CRTV 31 marzo 2021

The fears expressed concern, in particular, the issue of responsibility of online platforms on the contents conveyed and the enforcement tools, which should inspire the new "horizontal and coordinated" approach of the EU Commission. Instead, we welcome the provisions aimed at introducing general transparency obligations in the online advertising market with an incremental approach and more specific constraints for very large platforms.

1. Exemption from liability for intermediaries

Chapter II of the proposal reveals a vision of the responsibility of intermediaries that does not seem adequate to the current times. This is demonstrated by the fact that the categories like"mere conduit", hosting, caching are proposed again, despite seem unsuitable to describe the phenomena of th e network in the face of the technological and economic evolution of the sector. To better describe this aspect, it should be noted that one of the requirements for the limitations from liability is that of not "selecting" the contents or recipients. However, many large platforms, while not "selecting" the recipients of the material or the material itself, promote in various ways the contents that they believe to prevail, and use profiling tools to associate certain advertisements with certain categories of users. In these cases it's clear that these operators play an active role of these categories of operators. Even for cloud services, it cannot fail to be noted that content sharing systems create large digital spaces in which materials of all kinds are pl aced, without any control, especially if protected by copyright. Affirming a total impartiality of intermediaries does not appear, in this sense, correct or useful for creating a healthy digital environment. It should be noted that some platforms have made substantial income from the sale and distribution of content and goods on their services. Their liability has been confirmed by EUCJ, in cause C - 324/09 (L'Oréal vs eBay): "Where the operator of the online marketplace has not played an active role within the meaning of the preceding paragraph and the service provided falls, as a consequence, within the scope of Article 14(1) of Directive 2000/31, the operator none the less cannot, in a case which may result in an order to pay damages, rely on the exemption from liability provided for in that provision if it was aware of facts or circumstances on the basis of which a diligent economic operator should have realised that the offers for sale in question were unlawful and, in the event of it being so aware, failed to act expeditiously in accordance with Article 14(1)(b) of Directive 2000/31".

The safe harbor regime has to be reserved to the hosting provider which merely stores third party content. The DSA should better reflect this by explicitly referring to the passive nature of the services rather than to its neutral role in Recital 18. Every "active" service that intervenes on third party information and makes the information part of its business model - and not the mere technical service as the host - must be deemed liable for the content it hosts. Providers that build their business models on content uploaded by their users, must have an increased level of responsibility and upgraded duties of care that mere neutral and providers of technical services shouldn't face. If an intermediary plays an "indispensable role" or "essential role" in promoting the content he is no longer a purely passive intermediary and therefor can't benefit from the limitation of liability regime. That said, rather than recalling definitions and meanings that appear outdated, it would be necessary to evaluate the conduct of the platforms: they should be able to enjoy exemption from liability only when they apply safe and effective technological solutions, in full respect of the entrepreneurial autonomy of the parties, in order to possibly trace the contents and identify ownership and rights on them, control their dissemination, obtain their permanent removal (take down and stay down) in case of violation of the license. To this end, it is necessary to evaluate a series of solutions, including to "mark" the protected contents, so that, if one of these contents is placed on the network, it is the responsibility of the platform, without undue delay, to ensure that it is no longer available or that the uploader has the right to keep it online. In summary, it seems that the limitation in question should be granted only to those who have: acted promptly, after receiving a sufficiently motivated report from the holders of the rights, to disable access or remove the works or other materials subject to reporting from their websites; prevented future uploading of the reported protected material or equivalent material (see CJUE C-18/18, judgment of 3.10.19, Eva Glawischnig - Piesczek v. Facebook Ireland Limited).

2. Obligation of supervision.

Equally inadequate is the emphasis with which the prohibition of generalized surveillance is sanctioned (Article 7). It is necessary to remember, in this regard, that Article 15 of the E-commerce Directive prohibits the imposition of generalized controls. It is certainly necessary to ensure that the operational solutions do

not constitute a preventive filter or give rise to an obligation of continuous surveillance for the platforms, but an obligation of ex ant e intervention must also be envisaged, linked to the availability of the information by the same platforms necessary and relevant to prevent unauthorized content from being made available to the public. Having said this, it is necessary to reiterate the po ssibility of surveillance obligations in specific cases, already provided for by the E-Commerce Directive (Recital
47) and confirmed by the CJEU in the aforementioned case C-18/18. In this context, the principle of professional diligence therefore assumes a central value. Over the years, it has been declined by jurisprudence, also in the European context, in a broad and detailed way.

3. Content removal orders (Article 8) and notification and action mechanism (Article 14)

It should also be noted that it is i nappropriate to impose particularly detailed content on orders (even if issued by judicial authorities) and notifications relating to the removal of content. This especially with regard to the provision for which the order or notification in question shoul d also indicate the URL of the prohibited content, which doesn't reflect the eCommerce Directive provisions. CRTV has reiterated in several places that the obligation for the reporting party to indicate the URL of the prohibited content represents an obstacle to effective control of illegal content. Considered that is very easy to upload again a content deleted, the only possible signal is the one that identifies the characteristics of the content. This is especially true for copyrighted works. The foregoing applies, in the same way, to judicial or administrative orders for the removal of contents.

4. Obligations of transparency and communication

The rules on online platforms and large platforms, in particular those relating to transparency in advertising, should be appreciated. Currently, the possibility of profiled marketing, outside the stringent rules that apply to the audiovisual sector, represents an extremely relevant competitive element. In addition, there is hardly ever an attention to the origin and content of advertising messages in large platforms. The transparency and communication obligations provided for in art. 30 may constitute, in perspective, the tool for the implementation of a level playing field, with a view to greater atten tion to legality, fundamental rights and correctness of information.

5. Traceability of commercial operators

The scope of application of the traceability obligation provided for in Article 22 is too limited. To improve its effectiveness, not only commercial operators who want to conclude distance contracts with consumers should be included, but all information society service providers who provide services that can contribute, in any way, to the realization of an offense. This is relevant both as regards th e unauthorized distribution of content protected by copyright, and for the dissemination of disinformation through the acquisition of advertising spaces offered by the platform.

Confindustria Radio Televisions sends a contribution with its own observations on the issue of the liability of intermediaries in the proposed regulation of the Digital Services Act

Legge sui servizi digitali Approfondire il mercato e chiarire le responsabilità per i servizi digitali

Position Paper CRTV 31 marzo 2021

The fears expressed concern, in particular, the issue of responsibility of online platforms on the contents conveyed and the enforcement tools, which should inspire the new "horizontal and coordinated" approach of the EU Commission. Instead, we welcome the provisions aimed at introducing general transparency obligations in the online advertising market with an incremental approach and more specific constraints for very large platforms. 1. Exemption from liability for intermediaries

Chapter II of the proposal reveals a vision of the responsibility of intermediaries that does not seem adequate to the current times. This is demonstrated by the fact that the categories like"mere conduit", hosting, caching are proposed again, despite seem unsuitable to describe the phenomena of th e network in the face of the technological and economic evolution of the sector. To better describe this aspect, it should be noted that one of the requirements for the limitations from liability is that of not "selecting" the contents or recipients. However, many large platforms, while not "selecting" the recipients of the material or the material itself, promote in various ways the contents that they believe to prevail, and use profiling tools to associate certain advertisements with certain categories of users. In these cases it's clear that these operators play an active role of these categories of operators. Even for cloud services, it cannot fail to be noted that content sharing systems create large digital spaces in which materials of all kinds are pl aced, without any control, especially if protected by copyright. Affirming a total impartiality of intermediaries does not appear, in this sense, correct or useful for creating a healthy digital environment. It should be noted that some platforms have made substantial income from the sale and distribution of content and goods on their services.

Affirming a total impartiality of intermediaries does not appear, in this sense, correct or useful for creating a healthy digital environment. It should be noted that some platforms have made substantial income from the sale and distribution of content and goods on their services. Their liability has been confirmed by EUCJ, in cause C - 324/09 (L'Oréal vs eBay): "Where the operator of the online marketplace has not played an active role within the meaning of the preceding paragraph and the service provided falls, as a consequence, within the scope of Article 14(1) of Directive 2000/31, the operator none the less cannot, in a case which may result in an order to pay damages, rely on the exemption from liability provided for in that provision if it was aware of facts or circumstances on the basis of which a diligent economic operator should have realised that the offers for sale in question were unlawful and, in the event of it being so aware, failed to act expeditiously in accordance with Article 14(1)(b) of Directive 2000/31". The safe harbor regime has to be reserved to the hosting provider which merely stores third party content. The DSA should better reflect this by explicitly referring to the passive nature of the services rather than to its neutral role in Recital 18. Every "active" service that intervenes on third party information and makes the information part of its business model - and not the mere technical service as the host - must be deemed liable for the content it hosts. Providers that build their business models on content uploaded by their users, must have an increased level of responsibility and upgraded duties of care that mere neutral and providers of technical services shouldn't face. If an intermediary plays an "indispensable role" or "essential role" in promoting the content he is no longer a purely passive intermediary and therefor can't benefit from the limitation of liability regime.

If an intermediary plays an "indispensable role" or "essential role" in promoting the content he is no longer a purely passive intermediary and therefor can't benefit from the limitation of liability regime. That said, rather than recalling definitions and meanings that appear outdated, it would be necessary to evaluate the conduct of the platforms: they should be able to enjoy exemption from liability only when they apply safe and effective technological solutions, in full respect of the entrepreneurial autonomy of the parties, in order to possibly trace the contents and identify ownership and rights on them, control their dissemination, obtain their permanent removal (take down and stay down) in case of violation of the license. To this end, it is necessary to evaluate a series of solutions, including to "mark" the protected contents, so that, if one of these contents is placed on the network, it is the responsibility of the platform, without undue delay, to ensure that it is no longer available or that the uploader has the right to keep it online. In summary, it seems that the limitation in question should be granted only to those who have: acted promptly, after receiving a sufficiently motivated report from the holders of the rights, to disable access or remove the works or other materials subject to reporting from their websites; prevented future uploading of the reported protected material or equivalent material (see CJUE C-18/18, judgment of 3.10.19, Eva Glawischnig - Piesczek v. Facebook Ireland Limited). 2. Obligation of supervision. Equally inadequate is the emphasis with which the prohibition of generalized surveillance is sanctioned (Article 7). It is necessary to remember, in this regard, that Article 15 of the E-commerce Directive prohibits the imposition of generalized controls. It is certainly necessary to ensure that the operational solutions do

not constitute a preventive filter or give rise to an obligation of continuous surveillance for the platforms, but an obligation of ex ant e intervention must also be envisaged, linked to the availability of the information by the same platforms necessary and relevant to prevent unauthorized content from being made available to the public. Having said this, it is necessary to reiterate the po ssibility of surveillance obligations in specific cases, already provided for by the E-Commerce Directive (Recital
47) and confirmed by the CJEU in the aforementioned case C-18/18.

Having said this, it is necessary to reiterate the po ssibility of surveillance obligations in specific cases, already provided for by the E-Commerce Directive (Recital
47) and confirmed by the CJEU in the aforementioned case C-18/18. In this context, the principle of professional diligence therefore assumes a central value. Over the years, it has been declined by jurisprudence, also in the European context, in a broad and detailed way. 3. Content removal orders (Article 8) and notification and action mechanism (Article 14)

It should also be noted that it is i nappropriate to impose particularly detailed content on orders (even if issued by judicial authorities) and notifications relating to the removal of content. This especially with regard to the provision for which the order or notification in question shoul d also indicate the URL of the prohibited content, which doesn't reflect the eCommerce Directive provisions. CRTV has reiterated in several places that the obligation for the reporting party to indicate the URL of the prohibited content represents an obstacle to effective control of illegal content. Considered that is very easy to upload again a content deleted, the only possible signal is the one that identifies the characteristics of the content. This is especially true for copyrighted works. The foregoing applies, in the same way, to judicial or administrative orders for the removal of contents. 4. Obligations of transparency and communication

The rules on online platforms and large platforms, in particular those relating to transparency in advertising, should be appreciated. Currently, the possibility of profiled marketing, outside the stringent rules that apply to the audiovisual sector, represents an extremely relevant competitive element. In addition, there is hardly ever an attention to the origin and content of advertising messages in large platforms. The transparency and communication obligations provided for in art. 30 may constitute, in perspective, the tool for the implementation of a level playing field, with a view to greater atten tion to legality, fundamental rights and correctness of information. 5. Traceability of commercial operators

The scope of application of the traceability obligation provided for in Article 22 is too limited. To improve its effectiveness, not only commercial operators who want to conclude distance contracts with consumers should be included, but all information society service providers who provide services that can contribute, in any way, to the realization of an offense.

To improve its effectiveness, not only commercial operators who want to conclude distance contracts with consumers should be included, but all information society service providers who provide services that can contribute, in any way, to the realization of an offense. EUROPEAN SOFTWARE DEVELOPERS AND USERS RELY ON OPEN SOURCE SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT PLATFORMS AND CODE REPOSITORIES TO INNOVATE AND COMPETE GLOBALLY

Brussels, 31 March 2021

Further to our one-pager on Digital Services Act (8/9/20), OpenForum Europe (OFE) wishes to submit more detailed comments as an active advocate of technological openness and our long-standing collaboration with the Open Source software (OSS) community. OFE welcomes the Commission’s proposal to strengthen protection of consumers’ exposure to harmful and illegal content whilst bolstering Europe’s internet economy.

The OSS community relies on online platforms to build and ship software. European companies in all sectors, such as pharmaceuticals, telecoms, banking and manufacturing, rely heavily on OSS development platforms and code repositories to innovate and compete globally. 

OSS development is at the heart of Europe's digitisation efforts and objective to ensure genuine IT choice and sovereignty across a wide range of key technologies and solutions such as Federated Cloud, HPC, edge computing and so forth. The economic impact of OSS on the EU economy is estimated to be between EUR 65 and EUR 95 billion in 2018. EU countries and EU located companies made significant investments into OSS of Euro 1 billion in 2018, the product of which is available for reuse by the private and public sector and would require 16,000 full time developers to provide the same volume of code. The ecosystem consists of European developers from the public sector, industry, universities and SMEs tackling challenges which no single company or organisation can solve on its own. 

Due to the integral nature of online platforms to the functioning of the OSS ecosystem, OFE has provided input to earlier legislative dossiers potentially affecting these platforms, in particular the Copyright Directive of 2019. It is important to underscore that many platforms have a more specific user-base or purpose, and thus have a lower risk profile than general purpose platforms. For example, platforms on which software developers rely are often at much lower risk, if not legally irrelevant, to many concerns that policymakers are seeking to address related to online content. It is thus vital that measures taken to address activity conducted by a platform’s users be tailored to the relevant risk so that the rules achieve their intended outcomes without unintended consequences. 

With this in mind, and in order to safeguard this mode of innovation, on which the European Digital transformation relies, we have a few areas where we would like to see clarifications being added throughout the co-legislative process. Please see our article-specific feedback attached as a file.

EUROPEAN SOFTWARE DEVELOPERS AND USERS RELY ON OPEN SOURCE SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT PLATFORMS AND CODE REPOSITORIES TO INNOVATE AND COMPETE GLOBALLY Brussels, 31 March 2021 Further to our one-pager on Digital Services Act (8/9/20), OpenForum Europe (OFE) wishes to submit more detailed comments as an active advocate of technological openness and our long-standing collaboration with the Open Source software (OSS) community. OFE welcomes the Commission's proposal to strengthen protection of consumers' exposure to harmful and illegal content whilst bolstering Europe's internet economy. The OSS community relies on online platforms to build and ship software. European companies in all sectors, such as pharmaceuticals, telecoms, banking and manufacturing, rely heavily on OSS development platforms and code repositories to innovate and compete globally. OSS development is at the heart of Europe's digitisation efforts and objective to ensure genuine IT choice and sovereignty across a wide range of key technologies and solutions such as Federated Cloud, HPC, edge computing and so forth. The economic impact of OSS on the EU economy is estimated to be between EUR 65 and EUR 95 billion in 2018. EU countries and EU located companies made significant investments into OSS of Euro 1 billion in 2018, the product of which is available for reuse by the private and public sector and would require 16,000 full time developers to provide the same volume of code. The ecosystem consists of European developers from the public sector, industry, universities and SMEs tackling challenges which no single company or organisation can solve on its own. Due to the integral nature of online platforms to the functioning of the OSS ecosystem, OFE has provided input to earlier legislative dossiers potentially affecting these platforms, in particular the Copyright Directive of 2019. It is important to underscore that many platforms have a more specific user-base or purpose, and thus have a lower risk profile than general purpose platforms. For example, platforms on which software developers rely are often at much lower risk, if not legally irrelevant, to many concerns that policymakers are seeking to address related to online content. It is thus vital that measures taken to address activity conducted by a platform's users be tailored to the relevant risk so that the rules achieve their intended outcomes without unintended consequences. With this in mind, we welcome that for the Digital Services Act proposal, the European Commission has included Articles 5 (hosting defence), 6 (allowing voluntary moderation) and 7 (prohibiting general monitoring). In order to safeguard this mode of innovation, on which the European Digital transformation relies, we have a few areas where we would like to see clarifications being added throughout the co-legislative process.

Article 5(b) As drafted, this article would require hosting services, "upon obtaining such knowledge or awareness, [to] act[s] expeditiously to remove or to disable access to the illegal content," while Article 14 requires online platforms to act on notice of "illegal content." However, Article 2(g) defines "illegal content" in a way that runs counter to the harmonization desired by a Digital Single Market approach: It would require platforms to know the law of each Member State: as "any information, which, in itself or by its reference to an activity, including the sale of products or provision of services is not in compliance with Union law or the law of a Member State, irrespective of the precise subject matter or nature of that law." Without clear definitions of specific kinds of illegal content, it will often be difficult for a platform to be able to act expeditiously, without needing to err on the side of removing lawful content. Article 8 Regarding government takedowns, we believe a possible improvement would be good to allow/require platforms to give advance notice and a chance to dispute to affected users, rather than a chance to redress after the takedown. This is a point of particular importance to OSS platforms, as takedowns can be very disruptive to real time collaborative content like that produced by software development processes. At the same time, we believe that notice to users should not be required for certain kinds of malicious activity (such as spam and malware) given the likelihood that those users will be able to more easily replicate the malicious activity if they are aware of the impending enforcement. Article 13 We believe that transparency reporting requirements should correlate with the risk profile of a platform for certain kinds of content and focus on content removals. Regarding Article 13(c), platform design and content display differs across platforms. Consider, for example, the complexity of how content might appear on a software development platform as opposed to a message-sharing app's feed. It can take a substantial amount of tracking/engineering work to reliably track and report on such a wide variety of measures. This can be disproportionately burdensome for smaller platforms. We suggest only requiring reporting on content removals, and to make the categorisation by reason something that's uniform/harmonised in a way that will be easier for platforms to report on. Moreover, as stated in Article 13(a), "the average time needed for taking those decisions" is not always a meaningful indicator. Particularly where context can be relevant to understanding why a platform might need more time for certain kinds of cases, including that it was waiting on a user to provide additional information necessary to review the claim. Articles 17 and 18 We believe that the internal complaint-handling system and the out of court dispute settlement could be disproportionately burdensome for some smaller platforms, such as OSS development platforms. We suggest focusing on the need to provide meaningful opportunity to dispute/appeal rather than the particular form it takes.

OSS platforms and the European digital economy European users leverage the highly innovative development model of Open Source Software as vital to the acceleration of European digitisation - benefiting from the open source freedoms (protected by OSI/FSF recognised licensing) and thereby avoid lock-in and secure genuine IT choice/sovereignty. It is not just of importance here and now. Our research shows that OSS has the potential of generating significant contributions to EU GDP. It is estimated that an increase of code contributions of 10% would generate around additional EUR 100 billion in EU GDP per year. Secondly, an increase of 10% would generate an additional 1,000 ICT start-ups per year in the EU. Considering the role of OSS development platforms, particular care needs to be given to the nature of these platforms when drafting the DSA. Should you wish to discuss our position and its implications, we would welcome the opportunity to meet with you or to answer questions by email. OpenForumEurope is a not-for-profit, independent European based think tank which focuses on openness within the IT sector. OFE draws its support from a broad range of stakeholders committed to openness: Among them leading global IT technology providers, European SMEs, user organisations, the openness academic community represented by the OpenForum Academy and the wider openness community. Tapping into this broad basis for support provides OFE with expertise across all major ICT topics, including applying its knowledge to the evolving technologies such as artificial intelligence,

blockchain, cloud computing and IoT. Views expressed by OFE do not necessarily reflect those held by all its supporters.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation is among the leading non-profit organizations defending civil liberties in the digital world. Founded in 1990, EFF champions user privacy, free expression, and innovation through impact litigation, policy analysis, grassroots activism, and technology development. Working with a unique team of technologists, activists and attorneys, we strive to ensure that rights and freedoms are enhanced and protected as our lives move increasingly online. 

We welcome the option to give feedback on the proposed Digital Services Act (DSA). Our principles and detailed positions on the Digital Services Act and the Digital Markets Act can be accessed at https://www.eff.org/issues/eu-policy-principles. Our focus is on four key areas: limited platform liability, interoperability mandates, procedural justice, and user control. For the purpose of this consultation, we would like to share our opinion on a number of key issues of the proposed DSA, on which we have elaborated in detail in the document attached to this submission.

We remain at your disposal for any questions you may have.
