full_text:
March 31, 2021

EFF Response to the EU Commission's Consultation on the Digital Services Act

The Electronic Frontier Foundation is among the leading non-profit organizations defending civil liberties in the digital world. Founded in 1990, EFF champions user privacy, free expression, and innovation through impact litigation, policy analysis, grassroots activism, and technology development. Our principles and detailed positions on the Digital Services Act and the Digital Markets Act can be accessed at https://www.eff.org/issues/eu-policy-principles.

For the purpose of this feedback, we will focus on a number of key issues:

System of limited liability and ban of general monitoring obligations

We welcome that the Commission kept the system of country of origin, limited liability and ban of general monitoring under the ECD intact. Without these principles, freedom to information would be impaired and platforms would be pushed to affirmatively monitor how users behave and would block and remove any content that is controversial. (https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2020/07/effs-eu-policyprinciples-platform-liability-and-monitoring).

Procedural justice

We also appreciate the numerous elements of procedural justice under the DSA, such as rules on how platforms must handle complaints submitted through their internal complaint-handling system. We very much welcome that the Commission has followed EFF's suggestion to introduce a right to reinstatement of content and accounts in case platforms make mistakes (Art 17(3)). The same holds true for putting limits on the scope of takedown orders issued by national judicial or administrative authorities. Without such a rule, it would be possible that one country's government dictates what residents of other countries can say, see, or share online (https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2020/07/our-eu-policy-principlesprocedural-justice). Regulation of process rather than speech Finally, the Commission was correct to focus on the regulation of process rather than speech. The DSA proposal would help users to better understand how content moderation decisions are made, and the role of algorithmic decision-making (Art 12). We are also glad to see that under the proposal users would have a right to learn about the main parameters used in recommender systems and a right to opt for a system that is not based on profiling (Art 29), though privacy by default protection is necessary. Finally, we support transparency reports about content moderation and options for vetted researchers and relevant regulators to take a closer look at how platforms determine users' online experience (Art 33). https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2020/08/our-eu-policy-principles-user-controls However, improvements are necessary, as detailed below: Interoperability: the EC missed the mark The Commission missed the mark on giving users more freedom and control over their Internet experience. Interoperability obligations are only addressed in the proposal for a Digital Markets Act -

and there insufficiently. If the EU wants to end the online dominance of a few powerful platforms, we need rules that enable users to communicate with friends across platform boundaries. Interoperability in ancillary services such as payment processing is nice to have, but not good enough. https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2020/06/our-eu-policy-principles-interoperability Article 14(3) will lead to overblocking In the current form, the DSA could push platforms into a position of quasi-law enforcers, turning the bill into a censorship machine. The notice and action mechanism (Article 14) provides that properly substantiated notices automatically give rise to actual knowledge of the notified content. As host providers only benefit from limited liability for third party content when they expeditiously remove content they know to be illegal, platforms will have no other choice than to blocking content to try to avoid the liability threat. Attaching actual knowledge to every substantiated notice will undermine, rather than foster, freedom of expression and inevitably lead to overblocking of highly contextual content. Platforms as "law-enforcers"

A censorship-push through a badly designed notice and action system may be accelerated by other provisions that could, in its current design, encourage more private censorship and the application of filter systems. We welcome the clarification that providers can undertake voluntary own-initiative investigations and actions for legal compliance without being stripped of the exemptions from liability for third-party content (Art 6 - "Good Samaritan"). We also welcome that those actions comprise measures taken by platforms to implement the legal requirements for terms of service enforcement. However, as the DSA Proposal has not abandoned the nebulous distinction between passive and active host providers for liability exemptions to ap ply, taking voluntary actions in good faith neither guarantees nor precludes that platforms enjoy immunity for content that users upload and share online. The lack of legal certainty is exacerbated by the vague scope of such privileged voluntary measures: Recital 25 explains that online platforms must act in good faith and in a diligent manner, without explaining the standard for such diligence. https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2021/03/twitter-trump-andtough-decisions-eu-freedom-expression-and-digital-services-act

There are other open questions and risks of inappropriate removals of user content:

For example, Art 12 provides that providers of intermediary services have to include information about content restrictions and are required to act in a "diligent, objective, and proportionate manner when enforcing their own terms and conditions." However, the yardstick for such a proportionality test is not clear, and its practicality will be put to the test in situations where platforms face an abundance of substantiated user notifications or in situations where platforms encounter a frequent display of manifestly illegal content and thus are compelled to suspend user accounts (Art 20). Finally, there are situations where the type of content requires platforms to alert law enforcement authorities (Art 21) or where platforms face pressure from public authorities - independency-guarantees are missing - to remove content (Art 8).

Risk assessments and mitigation measures

These examples show that it's not necessarily a single provision that is problematic, but the interplay of several provisions that pose a risk that platforms will not be able to "hold opinions and to receive and impart information and ideas without interference by public authority and regardless of frontiers." Such interplay can be best demonstrated by Art 26 and 27, which impose due diligence duties for very large platforms to address systematic risks, including freedom of expression (which we appreciate).

Platforms are required to mitigate risks that occur as a result of their terms of service enforcement, user notifications, and measures allowing platforms to identify potential illegal content. Combined with the provisions on sanctions, such a model would create a strong incentive to proactively avoid the occurrence of risks, using measures that cannot be mandated by the letter of the law (such as automated systems), but are the most cost-effective way to comply with the obligations under the DSA. Safeguards that avoid the intrusion of privacy or the use of upload filters are missing entirely, and it is unlikely that the co-regulatory approach in the form of EU Commission "guidelines" on how to mitigate systemic risks on online platforms (Article 27(3)) will give enough orientation to platforms for when to act and when not to act.

International impact

The more platforms are pushed into an active role to check, censor, and report what users post online, the greater the need for ex ante safeguards and fundamental rights protections. We are concerned that the DSA proposal may follow the footsteps of recent disastrous internet bills, such as the French Avia Bill (declared unconstitutional), the Austrian draft law on hate speech (under Commission scrutiny), or elements of the German NetzDG (under constitutional scrutiny). These bills ignore fundamental rights in that they target services regardless of their place of establishment. They have spawned dozens of copycats throughout the world, including in countries with far fewer protections for speech, and human rights more generally. All of these bills require the appointment of a legal representative, who faces enforcement actions for non-compliance. The DSA proposal, too, comes with a wide territorial scope of application, as non-EU platforms that provide services to the EU must comply with the DSA and appoint a legal representative. We support effective oversight and enforcement measures. However, we are concerned about the fundamental rights impacts of these provisions, and the risk that platforms, in particular smaller ones, stop offering services to the EU when facing such requirements, which could ultimately undermine users' access to information.

EFF's perspective is informed by our decades of experience fighting for users' rights, and by our deep expertise in innovative but user-centric technology that works for people. Many thanks for taking our comments and recommendations into account for the ongoing legislative process. We remain at your disposal for any questions you may have. Best regards, Dr. Christoph Schmon International Policy Director christoph@eff.org

The Electronic Frontier Foundation is among the leading non-profit organizations defending civil liberties in the digital world. Founded in 1990, EFF champions user privacy, free expression, and innovation through impact litigation, policy analysis, grassroots activism, and technology development. Our principles and detailed positions on the Digital Services Act and the Digital Markets Act can be accessed at https://www.eff.org/issues/eu-policy-principles. We welcome that the Commission kept the system of country of origin, limited liability and ban of general monitoring under the ECD intact. Without these principles, freedom to information would be impaired and platforms would be pushed to affirmatively monitor how users behave and would block and remove any content that is controversial. (https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2020/07/effs-eu-policyprinciples-platform-liability-and-monitoring). Procedural justice

We also appreciate the numerous elements of procedural justice under the DSA, such as rules on how platforms must handle complaints submitted through their internal complaint-handling system. We very much welcome that the Commission has followed EFF's suggestion to introduce a right to reinstatement of content and accounts in case platforms make mistakes (Art 17(3)). The same holds true for putting limits on the scope of takedown orders issued by national judicial or administrative authorities. Without such a rule, it would be possible that one country's government dictates what residents of other countries can say, see, or share online (https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2020/07/our-eu-policy-principlesprocedural-justice). The Polish Filmmakers Association – Union of Audiovisual Authors and Producers (SFP-ZAPA) would like to thank the European Commission for organising consultations on the extremely important matter of the future of digital services. The legal regulation of intermediary services that offer products and services online and base their activities on using third party content is at the moment very selective and not adapted to the digital and technological reality, which is subject to constant change.

Such inadequate state of legislation principally comes from the fact that the last European Union's legal act covering this matter comprehensively was created in 2000. Although other regulations, for example on copyright, also covered the matter indirectly, legislative initiatives presented by the European Commission on 15 December 2020 provide the first occasion for a wider debate how to restructure the regulatory environment of digital platforms. It is no longer possible to perceive those entities as micro enterprises entering the market or start-ups discovering new space for development of their products. Today, the activities of the majority of large platforms definitely go beyond the area of passive provision of hosting services which means that also the legal framework needs an update. The most important element of the proposed Regulation should therefore be an express conclusion in Article 5 that it is possible to invoke the liability exemptions only when the activity of the platform is limited to the technical process of operating and giving access to a communication network and is of mere automatic and passive nature. In order to be able to release itself from liability for storing and making available content, the entity providing information society services may not have any control over such content. 

The next pillar for regulating the liability of online intermediaries the mechanism for removal of illegal content. Notice and action notification systems, although helpful, turn out to be insufficient in fighting infringements of rights. Most of the websites already today, in the event of receiving a notice from  rightholders, remove links to illegal content. The essence of the problem is, however, that after a short time successive links or accounts appear, and notices about the necessity of their removal must be sent again, which makes the entire process highly ineffective and costly. Those problems could be solved by adopting, at the European level, certain measures that make it impossible for users to repeatedly place illegal content – a take down and stay down mechanism. The fact that the Proposal decides to adopt only the notice and action system creates a huge disproportion between the situation of authors and other rightholders and the rights of  information society services whose business model is based on using third party creative output. 

Notwithstanding the above, we would like to emphasise that since the beginning of works on the Digital Services Act, SFP-ZAPA has supported the assumption followed by the European Commission when drafting commented provisions, i.e. rebalance the rights and responsibilities of users, rightholders, intermediary platforms, and public authorities in the online world. Unfortunately, the final effect of the Digital Services Act seems to favour the position of the platforms, ignoring the interests of other market participants, especially the creative sector.

Please find attached more w detailed comments on the DSA. At the same time, we note that we are willing to cooperate with the European Commission during further stages of works.

Stowarzyszenie Filmowców Polskich ZAPA - Związek Autorów i Producentów Audiowizualnych

Polish Filmmakers Association ZAPA - Union of Audiovisual Authors and Producers

Warsaw, 31 March 2021

Re: Proposal for a regulation on digital services COM (2020) 825 - Digital Services Act

Acting on behalf of the Polish Filmmakers Association - Union of Audiovisual Au thors and Producers (hereinafter as: SFP-ZAPA), we would like to thank the European Commision for organising consultations on the extremely important matter of the future of digital services. The legal regulation of intermediary services that offer products and services online a nd base their activities on using third party content is at the moment very selective and not adapted to the digital and technological reality, which is subject to constant change.

Such inadequate state of legislation principally comes from the fact that the last European Union's legal act covering this matter comprehensively was created in 2000. Although other regulations, for example on copyright, also covered the matter indirectly, legislative initiatives presented by the European Commission on 15 December 2020 provide the first occasion for a wider debate how to restructure the regulatory environment of digital platforms. It is no longer possible to perceive those entities as micro enterprises entering the market or start-ups discovering new space for development of their products. Today, the activities of the majority of large platforms definitely go beyond the area of passive provision of hosting services, for which the liability exemptions were formulated 20 years ago, which means that also the legal framework needs an update.

With the above in mind, please find below detailed comments on the Proposal for a regulation on digital services COM (2020) 825 (hereinafter as the "Regulation", "Digital Services Act").

1. Liability of providers of intermediary services

The principles of service provider's exemptions from liability have been transferred from the e-Commerce Directive. The procedure has been carried out nearly mechanically in spite of the fact that the regulatory environment created more than two decades ag o was to respond to completely different needs and problems than those we are facing today. Over the last years online platforms have dominated the market of media and content distribution, developing in most countries without any control and restrictions. They popularised their business models based on using - not always legally - third party content and avoided paying taxes in the full amount, without encountering any serious resistance from domestic authorities or EU institutions.

Over twenty years ago, when most entities operated by storing content in a technical, automatic and passive way, the problem was covered by the provisions very laconically. But even then it seemed obvious that the privilege of being exempted from liability may not apply to a ser vice provider playing an active role, promoting and organising content available for its users. It is

shown by the wording of Recital 42 of the e-Commerce Directive, in which the legislator seems to decide on that issue. This question has a fundamental significance for creating fair principles of functioning in the online reality. In the Regulation, it was explained laconically in the recitals, instead of resolving this issue unambiguously in the provisions.

The most important element of the proposed Regul ation should be an express conclusion in Article 5 that it is possible to invoke the liability exemptions only when the activity of the platform is limited to the technical process of operating and giving access to a communication network and is of mere au tomatic and passive nature. In order to be able to release itself from liability for storing and making available content, the entity providing information society services may not have any control over such content.

2. System of notifying right infringing content

The next pillar for regulating the liability of online intermediaries the mechanism for removal of illegal content. Notice and action notification systems, although helpful, turn out to be insufficient in fighting infringements of rights. Most of the websites already today, in the event of receiving a notice from rightholders, remove links to illegal content. The essence of the problem is, however, that after a short time successive links or accounts appear, and notices about the necessity of their removal must be sent again, which makes the entire process highly ineffective and costly. A holder of copyright or related rights, who does not have appropriate technical and organisational resources, is unable to monitor on an ongoing basis on h is own whether content is appearing on online platforms without his consent. By co-operating with specialised entities monitoring illegal content in the Internet, SFP-ZAPA tries to support rightholders in the fight with copyright infringements. But the scale of infringements occurring on online platforms is massive. The cost of contracting the monitoring activities to specialised firms most often exceeds the financial capabilities of authors and producers. But the biggest problem is that even the use of suc h services does not prevent infringements. We have to remember that notices on infringements must apply to specific works made available by specific users (or even specific files or links including or connecting to specific works). Hence control and notices may be only selective, and after the files or links covered by the notice have been removed, new files or links appear right away.

Those problems could be solved by adopting, at the European level, certain measures that make it impossible for users to re peatedly place illegal content - a take down and stay down mechanism. The application of the notice and stay down procedure would lead to a noticeable increase in fighting infringements of exclusive rights in the Internet and would constitute a step in th e direction of abolishing the current disproportion in the obligations connected with monitoring and fight against illegal content. Implementation of the notice and stay down mechanism would also have an impact on making the costs connected with such activity more rational. At the moment, the entire burden connected with the prevention of illegal distribution of content on online platforms rests on injured parties. In addition, appropriate legal regulations will also definitely contribute to popularisation of technologies that are to ensure that content already removed is not placed again. The fact that the Proposal decides to adopt only the notice and action system creates a huge disproportion between the situation of authors and other rightholders and the rights of information society services whose business model is based on using third party creative output.

The adoption of such an attitude is also contrary to the ruling of the Court of Justice of the European Union in Case C-18/18 Eva Glawischnig-Piesczek, wherein the CJEU found that the provisions of the e-Commerce Directive do not prevent a court of a Member State from ordering a host provider to remove any information stored by it whose content is identical or equivalent

to the content of the information which had previously been declared to be unlawful, or to block access to that information, irrespective of who had requested the storage of that information. In the statement of reasons, the Court explained that an injunction to block content must be able to extend to information the content of which, whilst essentially conveying the same message, is worded slightly differently, because of the words used or their combination, compared with the information whose content was declared to be illegal. Other wise, as emphasised by the CJEU, the effects of such an injunction could easily be circumvented by the storing of messages which are scarcely different from those which were previously declared to be illegal, which could result in the person concerned having to initiate multiple proceedings in order to bring an end to the conduct of which he is a victim. The quoted ruling of the CJEU in Case C-18/18 Eva Glawischnig-Piesczek should be a guidepost for legislators when designing mechanisms for notifying illegal content.

The positive element of the Digital Services Act is that it implements an institution of trusted flaggers, whose notices about the presence of illegal content will be treated with priority. But this solution will have a limited significance in practice, taking into account that the fundamental problem now is not the lack of response to notices on illegal content but the ineffective notification system, as discussed above. This issue is connected with ensuring independence for Digital Services Coordinators, whose powers will include, without limitation, the award of the status of trusted flaggers. Please note that the provisions regarding the manner of election of individual authorities referred to in the Regulation and their powers require a detailed analysis.

In the opinion of SFP-ZAPA, the Regulation should be changed to include the notice and stay down mechanism, which is the only one that can ensure effective removal of content infringing intellectual property rights in the Internet.

3. Voluntary mechanisms identifying illegal content

In the opinion of SFP-ZAPA, the law should encourage service providers to innovate as regards the creation of mechanisms for effective removal of illegal content, without increasing the risk of legal liability. Voluntary own-initiative investigations are generally perceived as a solution to this problem. However, a thorough analysis of Article 6 of the Regulation leads to a disturbing conclusion that the legal norm contained in that provision extends the liability exemptions as adopted in Article 3 to Artic le 5 of the Regulation. Having voluntary measures in place aimed at detecting illegal content means, in fact, having actual knowledge that rights are being infringed. Knowledge about the illegal nature of information should always lead to a loss of privilege, such as the exemption from liability. Adoption of the norm included in Article 6 makes invalid the premise specified in Article 5(1)(a), which means that in the new legal regime platforms will obtain legal legitimacy to base their activities on using r ight infringing content.

4. Orders issued by domestic court or administrative authorities

Substantial doubts are also raised by the provisions of Article 8 and Article 9, which relate to orders applying to illegal content or the provision of information about a recipient of service, issued by competent domestic court or administrative authorities. The new regulations will interfere with the domestic judicial or administrative systems and will result in slowdown of the proceedings. What is worth emphasising, the only reason for implementing those provisions seems to be the facilitation of activities carried on by foreign enterprises. We should note that national courts will have an obligation to prepare an order in a language freely selected by intermediaries and sent it to respective contact points. No additional explanation is needed in

order to understand how the very necessity to prepare court orders and statements of reasons thereof in a foreign language will prolong the proceedings. It is also obvious that the speed of proceedings in cases that involve removal of illegal content is a key element of their effectiveness. Also the content and form of court rulings and adminis trative decisions should be specified by provisions of the substantive law and procedures of individual countries, and not imposed by the platforms.

5. Relation between the Digital Services Act and the Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market

According to Article 1(5),the proposal is without prejudice to the rules laid down in legal acts enumerated in that provision, but only with respect to copyright and related rights there is a general reference to the Union law. The other acts have been na med directly. The structuring of proper relations between the provisions of the Regulation and other acts will be probably the biggest legislative challenge during works on the Digital Services Act. Because of a general reference mentioned above, a thorough analysis should be made to what extent the Regulation will be applicable to copyright and related rights. The rules of liability of providers of online content-sharing services for works placed by their users are specified in Directive 2019/790/EU on copyright and related rights in the Digital Single Market and amending Directives 96/9/EC and 2001/29/EC (hereinafter: the "DSM Directive"). It assumes that a provider of such services makes works available to the public or communicates them to the public within the meaning of Article 3 of Directive 2001/29/EC on copyright in the information society. These rules are completely different than those adopted in the Regulation. But they apply to a very small group of entities which comply with the criteria specified in Article 2(10) and Article 17 of the DSM Directive. It should be highlighted that the DSM Directive lays down also many exemptions from the rule obligating to acquire licences, for example for entities such as start-ups or encyclopaedias, and releases them from compliance with the provisions meeting certain conditions.

In the Explanatory Memorandum and in Recitals 9-11 of the Digital Services Act, the Commission indicates that EU legislation relating to specific sectors applies as lex specialis to the provisions of the Regulation, and emphasises that the Regulation should complement such legislation and be applicable in each situation not covered by the DSM Directive and to each situation for which exceptions are adopted. The provisions of the Regulati on should apply directly to issues not regulated in the abovementioned Directive but regulated in the Regulation. It is assumed that the norm which is more detailed and regulates a given matter in a narrower way should repeal the norm which regulates the same matter more generally or identifies its addressee in a broader way. The expression "should repeal" may not be understood in a literal way as annulling the lex generalis norm. The lex specialis provisions only excludes the application of the lex gene ralis norm when the two norms coincide. In that case, the norms relating to the scope of liability of service providers will coincide primarily when a provider of information society services stores and gives public access to a large amount of copyright - protected works or other protected subject matter uploaded by its users, which it organises and promotes for profit-making purposes.. When the entity does not fall into the definition of online content-sharing services provider, has been directly excluded fr om that definition or its obligations have been restricted in Article 17(6) of the DSM Directive, the provisions of the Regulation should be applicable directly. The same applies to a situation where service providers will be exempted from liability for pu blic sharing activities not subject to any authorisation because of meeting the due diligence condition.

It seems that the issues addressed above regarding the relation between the DSM Directive and the Proposal for a regulation are not regulated in a sufficiently clear way. This issue requires a detailed analysis in the course of works on the subject Proposal. In the long term, such general exemption will require constant monitoring in order to prevent a situation that some entities will not be subject to any regulation and will benefit from a gap in law in order to build business models based on infringements on rights.

Regardless of the foregoing, we should bear in mind that the DSM Directive stipulates expressly that when an online content-sharing service provider performs an act of making available to the public or an act of communication to the public under the conditions laid down in the Copyright Directive, the limitation of liability established in Article 14(1) of Directive 2000/31/EC shall not apply (Article 5 of the Regulation). In such situations, the mechanisms adopted towards online content-sharing service providers as specified in the DSM Directive will apply.

6. Definitions

6.1. Online platform

The definition of online platform adopted in Article 1(1)(h) leaves a big margin for interpretation. In many cases it is difficult to specify when the activity involving the storage and dissemination of content is really a minor and purely ancillary featur e of another service and, for objective and technical reasons, cannot be used without that other service. Some platforms may intentionally create services of that type in order to circumvent the law. And although the Regulation takes into account such a po ssibility, it may be very problematic to determine such fact in practice. Even more concerns are brought about by the clarification included in Recital 13 of the Regulation, indicating that the comments section in an online newspaper may have a function of ancillary service, where it is clear that it is ancillary to the main service represented by the publication of news under the editorial responsibility of the publisher. In our practice we came across a situation where online intermediaries used exactly that ancillary activity for mass infringements of rights. Numerous exemptions for small and medium enterprises may also constitute a problem in practice. Enterprises employing less than 50 persons with their annual turnover not exceeding EUR 10 million and those employing less than 10 persons with their annual turnover not exceeding EUR are not an exception among the Polish online platforms. The exemptions will apply to, among other things, the obligations of reporting, transparency or implementation for them of different rules of notifying illegal content by trusted flaggers. Small and medium platforms will be also exempted from putting in place measures preventing misuse, specified in Article 20 of the Regulation, ordering service providers to "suspend" us ers frequently providing illegal content. Numerous exemptions of that type may cause the domestic market of digital services to continue to be insufficiently regulated, in spite of having been granted numerous privileges.

6.2 Illegal content

The European Commission emphasises that the notion of "illegal content" should be understood broadly and that it covers also information relating to illegal content, products, services and actions. But it has not been decided univocally that if a hyperlink referring users to target rightinfringing information is placed on a given platform, this is also storage and dissemination of illegal content. This issue should be reflected in the provisions or at last as clarification of the definition from Article 2(g) in the recitals of the Regulation. It should be reminded that the problem of specifying legal nature of links has been considered in the doctrine for many years and covered numerous requests for preliminary ruling addressed by domestic courts to the Court

of Justice of the European Union. So the legislator should take advantage of the possibility of avoiding a situation in which interpretation doubts about the application of those provisions in practice will be appearing over the course of many years.

7. Jurisdiction

The rules adopted in the Regulation do not solve the problem with platforms from third countries which do not cooperate with rightholders and do not respond to requests for removing illegal content. According Article 40 of the Regulation, the Member State in which the main establishment of the online service provider is located is competent to examine and resolve about the issues regulated in Chapter III and IV. However, an online service provider which does not have an establishment in the Union but which offers its services in the Union is deemed, for the purposes of Chapter III and IV, to be under jurisdiction of the Member State where its legal representative resides or is established.

Adoption of the principle of country of origin in determining a court competent in matters connected with the performance of obligations of due diligence and the implementation and enforcement of provisions of the Regulation is another facilitation for online platforms. Interests of rightholders are disregarded, and often they will have to bring actions in a Member State other than their place of residence, which makes the regulation very difficult to apply in practice.

There is also no doubt that online platforms should be obliged to designate its legal representatives in every Member State, and not only in one of the sta tes in which a provider offers its services. Re: Proposal for a regulation on digital services COM (2020) 825 - Digital Services Act

Acting on behalf of the Polish Filmmakers Association - Union of Audiovisual Au thors and Producers (hereinafter as: SFP-ZAPA), we would like to thank the European Commision for organising consultations on the extremely important matter of the future of digital services. The legal regulation of intermediary services that offer products and services online a nd base their activities on using third party content is at the moment very selective and not adapted to the digital and technological reality, which is subject to constant change. Such inadequate state of legislation principally comes from the fact that the last European Union's legal act covering this matter comprehensively was created in 2000. Although other regulations, for example on copyright, also covered the matter indirectly, legislative initiatives presented by the European Commission on 15 December 2020 provide the first occasion for a wider debate how to restructure the regulatory environment of digital platforms. It is no longer possible to perceive those entities as micro enterprises entering the market or start-ups discovering new space for development of their products. Today, the activities of the majority of large platforms definitely go beyond the area of passive provision of hosting services, for which the liability exemptions were formulated 20 years ago, which means that also the legal framework needs an update. With the above in mind, please find below detailed comments on the Proposal for a regulation on digital services COM (2020) 825 (hereinafter as the "Regulation", "Digital Services Act"). 1. Liability of providers of intermediary services

The principles of service provider's exemptions from liability have been transferred from the e-Commerce Directive. The procedure has been carried out nearly mechanically in spite of the fact that the regulatory environment created more than two decades ag o was to respond to completely different needs and problems than those we are facing today. Over the last years online platforms have dominated the market of media and content distribution, developing in most countries without any control and restrictions. They popularised their business models based on using - not always legally - third party content and avoided paying taxes in the full amount, without encountering any serious resistance from domestic authorities or EU institutions. Over twenty years ago, when most entities operated by storing content in a technical, automatic and passive way, the problem was covered by the provisions very laconically. But even then it seemed obvious that the privilege of being exempted from liability may not apply to a ser vice provider playing an active role, promoting and organising content available for its users. It is

shown by the wording of Recital 42 of the e-Commerce Directive, in which the legislator seems to decide on that issue. This question has a fundamental significance for creating fair principles of functioning in the online reality. In the Regulation, it was explained laconically in the recitals, instead of resolving this issue unambiguously in the provisions.

This question has a fundamental significance for creating fair principles of functioning in the online reality. In the Regulation, it was explained laconically in the recitals, instead of resolving this issue unambiguously in the provisions. The most important element of the proposed Regul ation should be an express conclusion in Article 5 that it is possible to invoke the liability exemptions only when the activity of the platform is limited to the technical process of operating and giving access to a communication network and is of mere au tomatic and passive nature. In order to be able to release itself from liability for storing and making available content, the entity providing information society services may not have any control over such content. 2. System of notifying right infringing content

The next pillar for regulating the liability of online intermediaries the mechanism for removal of illegal content. Notice and action notification systems, although helpful, turn out to be insufficient in fighting infringements of rights. Most of the websites already today, in the event of receiving a notice from rightholders, remove links to illegal content. The essence of the problem is, however, that after a short time successive links or accounts appear, and notices about the necessity of their removal must be sent again, which makes the entire process highly ineffective and costly. A holder of copyright or related rights, who does not have appropriate technical and organisational resources, is unable to monitor on an ongoing basis on h is own whether content is appearing on online platforms without his consent. By co-operating with specialised entities monitoring illegal content in the Internet, SFP-ZAPA tries to support rightholders in the fight with copyright infringements. But the scale of infringements occurring on online platforms is massive. The cost of contracting the monitoring activities to specialised firms most often exceeds the financial capabilities of authors and producers. But the biggest problem is that even the use of suc h services does not prevent infringements. We have to remember that notices on infringements must apply to specific works made available by specific users (or even specific files or links including or connecting to specific works). Hence control and notices may be only selective, and after the files or links covered by the notice have been removed, new files or links appear right away.

Hence control and notices may be only selective, and after the files or links covered by the notice have been removed, new files or links appear right away. Those problems could be solved by adopting, at the European level, certain measures that make it impossible for users to re peatedly place illegal content - a take down and stay down mechanism. The application of the notice and stay down procedure would lead to a noticeable increase in fighting infringements of exclusive rights in the Internet and would constitute a step in th e direction of abolishing the current disproportion in the obligations connected with monitoring and fight against illegal content. Implementation of the notice and stay down mechanism would also have an impact on making the costs connected with such activity more rational. At the moment, the entire burden connected with the prevention of illegal distribution of content on online platforms rests on injured parties. In addition, appropriate legal regulations will also definitely contribute to popularisation of technologies that are to ensure that content already removed is not placed again. The fact that the Proposal decides to adopt only the notice and action system creates a huge disproportion between the situation of authors and other rightholders and the rights of information society services whose business model is based on using third party creative output. The adoption of such an attitude is also contrary to the ruling of the Court of Justice of the European Union in Case C-18/18 Eva Glawischnig-Piesczek, wherein the CJEU found that the provisions of the e-Commerce Directive do not prevent a court of a Member State from ordering a host provider to remove any information stored by it whose content is identical or equivalent

to the content of the information which had previously been declared to be unlawful, or to block access to that information, irrespective of who had requested the storage of that information. In the statement of reasons, the Court explained that an injunction to block content must be able to extend to information the content of which, whilst essentially conveying the same message, is worded slightly differently, because of the words used or their combination, compared with the information whose content was declared to be illegal.

In the statement of reasons, the Court explained that an injunction to block content must be able to extend to information the content of which, whilst essentially conveying the same message, is worded slightly differently, because of the words used or their combination, compared with the information whose content was declared to be illegal. Other wise, as emphasised by the CJEU, the effects of such an injunction could easily be circumvented by the storing of messages which are scarcely different from those which were previously declared to be illegal, which could result in the person concerned having to initiate multiple proceedings in order to bring an end to the conduct of which he is a victim. The quoted ruling of the CJEU in Case C-18/18 Eva Glawischnig-Piesczek should be a guidepost for legislators when designing mechanisms for notifying illegal content. The positive element of the Digital Services Act is that it implements an institution of trusted flaggers, whose notices about the presence of illegal content will be treated with priority. But this solution will have a limited significance in practice, taking into account that the fundamental problem now is not the lack of response to notices on illegal content but the ineffective notification system, as discussed above. This issue is connected with ensuring independence for Digital Services Coordinators, whose powers will include, without limitation, the award of the status of trusted flaggers. Please note that the provisions regarding the manner of election of individual authorities referred to in the Regulation and their powers require a detailed analysis. In the opinion of SFP-ZAPA, the Regulation should be changed to include the notice and stay down mechanism, which is the only one that can ensure effective removal of content infringing intellectual property rights in the Internet. 3. In the opinion of SFP-ZAPA, the law should encourage service providers to innovate as regards the creation of mechanisms for effective removal of illegal content, without increasing the risk of legal liability. Having voluntary measures in place aimed at detecting illegal content means, in fact, having actual knowledge that rights are being infringed. Knowledge about the illegal nature of information should always lead to a loss of privilege, such as the exemption from liability. Adoption of the norm included in Article 6 makes invalid the premise specified in Article 5(1)(a), which means that in the new legal regime platforms will obtain legal legitimacy to base their activities on using r ight infringing content. 4. Substantial doubts are also raised by the provisions of Article 8 and Article 9, which relate to orders applying to illegal content or the provision of information about a recipient of service, issued by competent domestic court or administrative authorities. The new regulations will interfere with the domestic judicial or administrative systems and will result in slowdown of the proceedings. What is worth emphasising, the only reason for implementing those provisions seems to be the facilitation of activities carried on by foreign enterprises. We should note that national courts will have an obligation to prepare an order in a language freely selected by intermediaries and sent it to respective contact points. No additional explanation is needed in

It is also obvious that the speed of proceedings in cases that involve removal of illegal content is a key element of their effectiveness. The structuring of proper relations between the provisions of the Regulation and other acts will be probably the biggest legislative challenge during works on the Digital Services Act. Because of a general reference mentioned above, a thorough analysis should be made to what extent the Regulation will be applicable to copyright and related rights. The rules of liability of providers of online content-sharing services for works placed by their users are specified in Directive 2019/790/EU on copyright and related rights in the Digital Single Market and amending Directives 96/9/EC and 2001/29/EC (hereinafter: the "DSM Directive"). It assumes that a provider of such services makes works available to the public or communicates them to the public within the meaning of Article 3 of Directive 2001/29/EC on copyright in the information society. These rules are completely different than those adopted in the Regulation. But they apply to a very small group of entities which comply with the criteria specified in Article 2(10) and Article 17 of the DSM Directive. It should be highlighted that the DSM Directive lays down also many exemptions from the rule obligating to acquire licences, for example for entities such as start-ups or encyclopaedias, and releases them from compliance with the provisions meeting certain conditions. In the Explanatory Memorandum and in Recitals 9-11 of the Digital Services Act, the Commission indicates that EU legislation relating to specific sectors applies as lex specialis to the provisions of the Regulation, and emphasises that the Regulation should complement such legislation and be applicable in each situation not covered by the DSM Directive and to each situation for which exceptions are adopted. The provisions of the Regulati on should apply directly to issues not regulated in the abovementioned Directive but regulated in the Regulation. It is assumed that the norm which is more detailed and regulates a given matter in a narrower way should repeal the norm which regulates the same matter more generally or identifies its addressee in a broader way. The expression "should repeal" may not be understood in a literal way as annulling the lex generalis norm. The lex specialis provisions only excludes the application of the lex gene ralis norm when the two norms coincide.

The expression "should repeal" may not be understood in a literal way as annulling the lex generalis norm. The lex specialis provisions only excludes the application of the lex gene ralis norm when the two norms coincide. In that case, the norms relating to the scope of liability of service providers will coincide primarily when a provider of information society services stores and gives public access to a large amount of copyright - protected works or other protected subject matter uploaded by its users, which it organises and promotes for profit-making purposes.. When the entity does not fall into the definition of online content-sharing services provider, has been directly excluded fr om that definition or its obligations have been restricted in Article 17(6) of the DSM Directive, the provisions of the Regulation should be applicable directly. The same applies to a situation where service providers will be exempted from liability for pu blic sharing activities not subject to any authorisation because of meeting the due diligence condition. It seems that the issues addressed above regarding the relation between the DSM Directive and the Proposal for a regulation are not regulated in a sufficiently clear way. This issue requires a detailed analysis in the course of works on the subject Proposal. Transparency of advertising
Online advertising drives excessive data collection, personal data abuse and intrusive targeting. In addition to the large-scale privacy breaches that continue to escape GDPR enforcement, this situation has led to the manipulation of democratic elections and the distortion of online public debate around the world. The DSA has a chance to set this right:
-	We welcome Articles 22, 24 and 30 on advertising transparency, advertising repositories and the traceability of traders, and believe these provisions should be maintained. This is in line with demands from a coalition of 31 CSOs calling for universal ad transparency.
-	In order to ensure meaningful transparency, the advertising repositories of Very Large Online Platforms should also include:
-	User access to their dynamic advertising profiles;
-	Audience reached;
-	Engagements with the ad;
-	GDPR basis for data processing and data source.

Assessing and mitigating systemic risks
In the face of the COVID-19 pandemic, platforms have shown their ability to counter the societal harms that their services amplify and accelerate, such as COVID-19 disinformation. Yet the storming of Capitol Hill has highlighted platforms’ inability or unwillingness to intervene without political pressure to do so. Platforms thus seem ill-equipped and unsuited to identify and mitigate systemic risks as identified in the Digital Services Act. 
While the principles of risk assessments (Article 26), risk mitigation (Article 27) and independent audits (Article 28) are appropriate, the Commission proposal needs to be refined in the following ways:
-	The risks detailed in Article 26 need to be more clearly phrased and defined. Broad terms like “civic discourse” and “intentional manipulation” of electoral processes risk being so vague that they will either not be applied, or implemented in a way that may harm freedom of expression and the press. 
-	Risk assessments and decisions on mitigation measures should be conducted through an inclusive, transparent and participatory process with participation from digital services coordinators, data protection authorities and media regulators, as well as civil society and rights groups, media associations and representatives of minority and disadvantaged groups. Decisions such as demoting particular kinds of content cannot continue to be taken without any oversight from free speech advocates. Such decisions need to undergo rigorous checks for their potential impact on people’s right to opinion formation, freedom of speech, freedom of the press and non-discrimination.
-	Codes of conduct that may trigger investigations into Very Large Online Platforms upon non-compliance are the right tool for defining systemic risks and stipulating the participatory process for risk assessments. 
-	Risk assessments reports and mitigation measures need to be made publicly available, at minimum in an edited form.
-	While audits are an excellent accountability mechanism, such audits should be conducted by a public oversight agency such as the European Board of Digital Services, rather than by private sector auditors. This is necessary to ensure consistent standards and methodologies for auditing over time and across platforms. Moreover, it would mitigate the risk of revolving doors between Very Large Online Platforms and the very few auditing firms who would be capable of auditing Very Large Online Platforms. 

“Gold standard”: While the DSA is EU legislation designed for the EU, similarly to the GDPR, a secondary aim of the legislation is to set a global “gold standard” for ensuring internet safety and accountability online. However, this global view does not take into account the global voices and experiences. This is despite the very real threat that “copycat” legislative measures may pose to the freedom of expression and other fundamental rights in countries. Legislators should be aware of this more global reach and responsibility.

STM welcomes the Commission’s proposal for a Regulation on a Single Market for Digital Services (Digital Services Act, DSA) and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (E-Commerce Directive, ECD). STM believes that the DSA provides a positive horizontal approach which seeks to provide clarity regarding the responsibilities of providers of intermediary services. It also looks to improve the functioning of the Digital Single Market and enhance legal certainty for providers of services, businesses, and consumers alike, while complementing relevant sector-specific Union law.

STM appreciates the opportunity to submit observations and comments on the Commission’s proposal on: (1) the liability mechanism for intermediary services including the liability exemptions, general monitoring prohibition and voluntary own initiative measures; (2) due diligence obligations for hosting services including the notice and action mechanism; (3) the due diligence obligations for online platforms including the exclusion of Micro or Small Enterprises (MSEs), trusted flaggers, notifications of serious offences and traceability of traders; and (4) enforcement.

STM position paper on the Digital Services Act GENERAL COMMENTS STM welcomes the Commission's proposal for a Regulation on a Single Market for Digital Services (Digital Services Act, DSA) and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (E-Commerce Directive, ECD). STM believes that the DSA provides a positive horizontal approach which seeks to provide clarity regarding the responsibilit ies of providers of intermediary services. It also looks to improve the functioning of the Digital Sin gle Market, and enhance legal certainty for providers of services, businesses, and consumers alike, while complementing relevant sector-specific Union law. STM appreciates the opportunity to submit observations and comments on the Commission's proposal on: (1) the liability mechanism for intermediary services including the liability exemptions, general monitoring prohibition and voluntary own initiative measures; (2) due diligence obligations for hosting services including the notice and action mechanism; (3) the due diligence obligations for online platforms including the exclusion of Micro or Small Enterprises (MSEs), trusted flaggers, notifications of serious offences and traceability of traders; and (4) enforcement. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
1. STM supports preserving and clarifying a tried and tested liability framework (Articles 3 - 9) STM welcomes the maintenance of the horizontal framework of conditional exemptions from liability for providers of intermediary services laid down in the ECD and would recommend some further clarifications to ensure that the appropriate safeguards and transparency is included, and to avoid any uncertainty and/or loopholes within the system.
• "Voluntary own initiative investigations": Exemptions from liability should only be afforded to providers of intermediary services when they take appropriate measures in order to detect, identify and remove, or disable access to, illegal content in a transparent manner, with appropriate oversight and safeguards, and in compliance with req uirements of EU Law including the DSA.

STM recommends streamlined due diligence obligations for providers of hosting services (Articles 10 - 15) STM appreciates the new mechanism clarifying the responsibilities for providers of digital services in ensuring that the online environment is fair, transparent, safe for consumers and businesses,

and that all rights are respected. To ensur e the new obligations are workable, we would suggest clarification of the following points.
• Notice and action mechanism: We welcome a harmonised mechanism for notice and action, which should be practical and not over-burdensome for either rightsholders or platforms. The information required for a notice to be sufficiently precise, adequately substantiated, and should be no more than the information necessary for an online platform to act.

3. STM proposes streamlined due diligence obligations for online platforms (Articles 16 - 24)
• Trusted Flaggers: The trusted flagger status is a welcome addition but should not be limited to representative organisations. This status should be available to both organisations and companies. a. Overall STM applauds the upholding of the country-of-origin principle in the Digital Services Act (DSA), which is a fundamental characteristic of the single market and which fosters legal certainty. We also acknowledge that a fall-back option is provided for Member States to e xercise jurisdiction where providers fail to appoint a legal representative in the EU. STM welcomes the approach of the Commission to centre the provisions in the DSA on illegal content, broadly defined as not in

Whilst recognising the impact o f harmful content on European consumers and businesses, STM believes that the provisions within the DSA should offer clear and harmonised solutions for digital services to tackle illegal rather than harmful content. Other instruments, such as the forthcoming European Democracy Action Plan, would be better vehicles to address harmful content, and can work alongside and complement the DSA.
b. Dissemination to the Public and Interpersonal Communication Services STM notes that Recital 14 holds that interpersonal communication services (ICSs) such as private messaging services would fall outside the scope of the DSA. We strongly recommend that ICSs should be eligible to be considered providers of intermediary services when their activities fit the definitional criteria. There are already instances of specialised private messaging groups where the dissemination of illegal content occurs on a wide scale, reaching hundreds of thousands of users. Furthermore, Recital 14 provides that the dissemination of information wit hin closed groups consisting of a finite number of pre-determined persons, and should not be considered as "dissemination to the public". In STM's view, the relevant criteria in determining dissemination to the public should be considered on the basis of giving access to content to a potentially unlimited number of recipients of a service, irrespective of whether these recipients actually access that content. The mere fact that the number of recipients is finite does not exclude the number from being very large, rapidly growing and potentially unlimited. The assessment of the public should be made on a case-by-case basis and reflect the specific circumstances of each case examined.

• STM requests that the concept of 'dissemination to the public' should not automatically exclude dissemination of information within closed groups merely becau se they consist of a finite number of pre-determined persons.
2. Liability
a. Liability exemptions mechanisms The proposal that the existing liability exemption regime of the E-Commerce Directive (ECD, Directive 2000/31/EC) is maintained is welcomed by STM, as it allows for flexibility and is still fit for purpose. It also provides legal certainty and clarifies when liability exemptions are available to providers of intermediary services, making sure that these are not exploited for illegal purposes. Recital 18 is a opportune addition to the active/passive distinction developed by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) clarifying which providers can benefit from the liability exemptions, and building on Recital 42 of the ECD. Recital 18 positively recognises that exemptions from liability should not apply when a provider of intermediary services plays an active role so as to give it knowledge of, or control over, that information. However, Recital 18 does not properly reflect the jurisprudence of t he Court as it narrows what jurisprudence considers being "active" by putting as a single example, "information that has been developed under the editorial

responsibility of that provider." While STM welcomes the intent of Recital 18, Recital 18 should be amended so as to reflect the L'Oréal vs eBay line of jurisprudence of the Court on what can give rise to activity as follows " Those exemptions should accordingly not be available in respect of liability relating to information provided not by the recipient of the service but by the provider of intermediary service itself, including where the information has been developed under the editorial responsibility of that provider including, but not limited to, when the provider of intermediary services optimises the presentation or promotes content." This will ensure the DSA is futureproof and business model neutral". The language of Recital 18 should not benefit providers of intermediary services whose activities are not purely of a technical nature. Recital 20 aims at closing off liability exemptions to those " that deliberately collaborates with a recipient of the services in order to undertake illegal activities ". STM supports the principle of explicitly excluding certain intermediary services from relying on li ability exemptions when such services undertake illegal activities but believes that the test used in the current language does not capture the full scope of services that should be covered by this provision. " Deliberately collaborates" is a very high threshold and extremely hard to prove. Rather, it should be clear that the liability exemptions cannot be claimed by services the main purpose of which is to engage in or to facilitate illegal activities. STM proposes to follow similar language to that already adopted in Recital 62 of the Copyright in the DSM Directive, which reads as follows: "[ ] the liability exemption mechanism provided for in this Directive should not apply to service providers the main purpose of which is to engage in or to facilitate copyright piracy."

• STM requests that the liability exemption mechanism provided for in the DSA does not apply to providers of intermediary services the main purpose of which is to engage in or to facilitate illegal activities, and that such provision is included in Chapter II of the DSA under Article 5a.
b. Voluntary own initiative investigations Article 6 and related Recital 25 should not be interpreted in any way that falls short of the safeguards and the high standards of transparency set by the DSA, nor should it lead to legal uncertainty. Under Article 6, the concept of " voluntary own-initiative investigations", "in good fai th and in a diligent manner" as specified by Recital 25 leaves substantial margin of discretion to providers to undertake voluntary measures that do not lead to the unavailability of the liability exemptions under Article 3, 4 and 5 of the DSA. Article 6 and Recital 25 leave undefined the types of voluntary measures that can be taken and does not set any specific boundaries. Although it is welcomed that Article 6 and Recital 25 provide that measures should be taken in good faith to comply with requirements of Union Law, including the obligations of the DSA. The current provisions leave too great a margin of discretion to providers to implement measures unilaterally, with little transparency, possibility for scrutiny, or follow-up on the effectiveness of those measures. STM believes that voluntary measures should only be undertaken by providers of intermediary services in order to comply with existing requirements of Union law and the obligations set forth in the DSA. In order to avoid loopholes and ensure effectiveness and enforceability of the provisions enshrined in the DSA, STM recommends amending Article 6 and accompanying Recital 25 to narrow

permissible voluntary own initiative measures for the detection, identification and action against illegal content to those measures solely necessary to ensure compliance with the requirements of Union law.
• Exemptions from liability should only be afforded to providers of intermediary services when they take measures in a transparent manner, with appropriate oversig ht and safeguards, to detect, identify and remove, or disable access to, illegal content in compliance with requirements of EU Law including the requirements of the DSA.
c. General Monitoring Prohibition Article 7 lays down a prohibition of general monitorin g or active fact-finding obligations for providers of intermediary services, which is a key principle that the DSA should uphold, consistently with the regime established by the ECD. STM welcomes the explicit mention that the prohibition does not affect mo nitoring that is concerning specific cases in Recital 28. Nonetheless, specific monitoring should be explicitly delineated in line with the jurisprudence of the CJEU as concerning content in identical and/or equivalent form to which was previously declared to be unlawful. Furthermore, STM notes that the DSA only maintains part of the former Article 15(2) of the ECD, which allowed Member States to establish obligations for providers to promptly inform the competent public authorities of alleged illegal activities undertaken. STM believes that the requirements under Article 9 for providers of intermediary services to provide information about individual recipients of their services when requested to do so by a national authority and under Article 21 for online platforms to notify authorities only of suspicions of serious criminal offences are of more limited application. The obligation to notify serious criminal offenses only applies to online platforms as part of their due diligence obligations and not to all providers of intermediary services. Thus, STM would recommend reintroducing the possibility for Member States to establish obligations for providers to promptly info rm the competent public authorities of alleged illegal activities undertaken and giving it prominence in a stand-alone provision within the liability chapter of the DSA which is applicable to all providers of intermediary services alike.
• STM welcomes the explicit mention that the prohibition does not affect monitoring concerning specific cases in Recital 28 and asks that specific monitoring be clearly delineated in line with the jurisprudence of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) as concerning content in identical and/or equivalent form to which was previously declared to be unlawful.
• STM requests the reintroduction for Member States to establish obligations for providers to promptly inform the competent public authorities of alleged illegal activities undertaken as a stand-alone provision within the liability chapter of the DSA which is applicable to all providers of intermediary services alike.
3. Due diligence obligations STM welcomes the approach of the DSA that provides for additional due diligence obligations, independent from the possibility to qualify or not for a claim to a liability exemption, as outlined in Chapter II. Those due diligence obligations will clarify the accountability of intermediary services. With regards to Chapter III, we acknowledge the asymmetrical system introduced and recommend further discussions on the categorisation of services and on the scope of applicability of obligations to ensure that no loopholes are left and that the principle of "What is illegal offline should be illegal online" is thoroughly respected and always true.

a. Due diligence obligations for hosting services
i. Notice and action mechanism Aa harmonised notice and action system as introduced under Article 14 is welcomed by STM. The information provided for a notice should be the information necessary for an online platform to act. The requirements under the notice and action mechanism should be practical and not over - burdensome. On notices more specifically, STM requests that the language regarding " the exact URL " under Article 14(2)(b) be removed to broaden and simplify the applicability of this provision. STM believes it would best read as " a clear indication of the electronic location of that information". The requirement of location of the content in the notice should encompass other means besides the "exact" URL to specifically address the recurrence of identical or equivalent content. This is because requiring a URL is neither future proof, technologically neutral nor even in some cases - for example with apps - even relevant. Further, STM welcomes the addition in Article 14(3) clarifying that notices that include the elements listed shall be considered to give rise to actual knowledge or awareness for the purpose of Article 5 in respect to the specific item of content noticed (Hosting).
• STM requests that the notice requirements concerning the location of the content be simple and technologically neutral. ii. Notice and permanent take down mechanism Once content has been identified as illegal and either removed or the access has been disabled, the issue of the reposting of illegal content should be addressed through a permanent take-down principle, to be inserted as part of the notice and action proce dure. In today's digital world, consumers and rightsholders alike are confronted with repeated infringements and/or the reappearance of infringing content in identical or equivalent form elsewhere. Thus, not only a notice and take down, but a notice and permanent take down mechanism would be in line with the objectives of the DSA for a safe, predictable and trustworthy online environment for all - and following the principle that "what is illegal offline is illegal online". Furthermore, this would also be consistent with existing law in Europe (e.g., Directive (EU) 2019/790). A notice and permanent take down could help ensure that any illegal content, including but not limited to terrorist content, sexual abuse material or copyright-protected content, unsafe products, or counterfeit goods, does not resurface easily. A notice-and-permanent-take-down principle can be both effective and also respecting of EU fundamental rights such as the freedom of expression online. This will be the case if the permanent take down is envisioned as concerning specific content including content that is identical or equivalent to that which was previously declared unlawful. Such a mechanism would prevent any further infringement of the same type and often by the same infrin ger. This would be targeted, proportionate and specific to already identified material rather than a wholly new set of content. Because of the close proximity with the content identified as illegal in the first place, this mechanism would not infringe any fundamental rights. Furthermore, additional safeguards that refer to the internal-complaint handling system provided for under Article 17 can be explicitly made part of Article 14.
• STM requests that a notice and permanent take down mechanism be added to Article 14.

c. Due diligence obligations for online platforms
i. Trusted Flaggers Mechanism STM welcomes the introduction of the concept of a trusted flagger in Article 19 and is eager to play active role in this going forward. Nonetheless, th is mechanism should not be limited to representative organisations, and should be available to both organisations and companies. Moreover, some online platforms that would fall under the scope of the DSA have already put in place specific programmes akin to the trusted flagger mechanisms, in which many prominent organisations or companies partake. The DSA is an unprecedented opportunity to make such innovative practices the norm by recognising these successful practices between private entities and online pla tforms. It should th erefore be sufficient to notify the Digital Services Coordinator (DSC) when a well-functioning, mutually agreed, customary practice exists between a private entity and an online platform as regards to trusted flagging.
• STM requests that both the representative organisations and companies be able to apply for the trusted flagger status, and that their ongoing collaboration with online platforms not be invalidated by the new system. ii. Measures and protection against misuse Article 20 provides for measures and protection against misuses. STM welcomes the possibility of online platforms to suspend repeat infringers and/or entities that abuse the notice and action system. Nonetheless, repeated infringements should be evaluated for illegal content as defined by the DSA and not "manifestly illegal content", which would artificially narrow the category of illegal content to be taken into account and create legal uncertainty. Furthermore, STM believes that layperson test ing as outlined under Recital 47 to determine whether the content is manifestly illegal is not appropriate in this context. This excludes the necessity of addressing and remove all types of repeat infringements and restricts legitimate action to only manifestly illegal content in the eye of a layperson without any substantive analysis. Finally, the provision does not include any clear transparency obligations nor the possibility to contest the decision taken by the platform, in contrast with Recital 46. STM supports the redre ss in Recital 46 but notes that instead of being available to all potentially injured parties such rightsholders; it is limited to recipients of services only.
• STM requests that the word "manifestly" is deleted on the basis that if the content is illegal, it is illegal. There is no qualitative measurement needed.
• STM requests that repeated infringements are considered under the mechanism at Article 20 as involving the provision of illegal content and asks the deletion of the layperson test under Recital 47 as inappropriate to determine whether the content is illegal.

Notification of criminal offences STM welcomes the obligation to notify serious criminal offences under Article 21 as part of the due diligence obligations applicable to online platforms.
