proposal requires online platforms to only notify authorities of serious criminal offences involving a threat to the life or safety of persons that has taken place, is taking place or is likely to take place. Serious crimes in most jurisdictions only cover a restricted set of crimes attached to the persons, but rarely cover significant financial/commercial harm including Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) crimes. In order to achieve a safe, predictable and trustworthy online environment, authorities should be notified of other damaging criminal offences, in particular of suspicions of criminal offences related to, but not limited to, counterfeited and pirate content. Most criminal offences carried out online are significant an d often cause substantial commercial/financial harm to the affected parties. Such crimes are not victimless.
• STM suggests that Article 21 be extended to the notification of a wider range of significant and damaging criminal offences - in particular commercial/financial crimes. iv. Traceability of traders The requirements around the traceability of traders under Article 22 (the so-called Know Your Business Customer, KYBC principle) are extremely welcome. They are helpful to establishing a safe, predictable, and trustworthy online environment for all and should be extended beyond their current scope. STM believes that the requirements outlined at Article 22, that are currently limited to online marketplaces and traders, should be extended to providers of hosting services and their business users, including small and micro enterprises. The se also should be strengthened to ensure that they are effective, draw from the experience caused by the inability to enforce the related provisions of the ECD and are derived from the already well-functioning framework existing in the financial sector. A provider of intermediary services should request trustworthy and accurate information from their business customers (that can be derived from publicly available sources) and verify the information to effectively know the business customer. A meaningful mechanism for enforcement should be established to ensure that businesses cannot wilfully bypass their obligations and are required to provide validated documents, data, or information such as corporate registration or other sufficient proof of identity. Service Providers should be able to disclose business customer information to third parties when required and in accordance with national law. This would help ensure that EU consumers have as little exposure as possible to illegal content, services, and products. STM notes that the obligation under Article 22 would only require providers to verify the identity of their business customers, not of all their user base. To further protect individual users, we suggest including a definition of "business customers" in Article 2 to clarify that not all users are covered. A distinction between commercial operators and private customers (who would be out of scope) should thus be added. This distinction is essential to ensure full compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, Regulation (EU) 2016/679) as the scope of "business users" would be limited.
• STM requests that the KYBC principle be extended to providers of inter mediary services, in proper enforcement. In particular, online platforms should request their business users provide trustworthy and accurate information and verify the information provided to know the identify their business user. Providers should only disclose business user information to third parties where required.

v. Exclusion of Micro or Small Enterprises Article 16 specifies that the obligations at Section 3 are not applicable to micro or small enterprises (MSEs). Whilst acknowledging the need to not impose too high a burden on MSEs and to give them the possibility to scale up, companies should build their business on legal and fair foundations from the start, not only when they reach a certain threshold. Indeed, abiding to certain lawful obligations is a fundamental part of doing business and should be asked of all intermediary services, including new players. For the DSA to achieve the objective of ensuring a safe, trustworthy, and fair environment for all the parties involved, building a business online should not be done at the expense of EU citizens, who, for the most part, will not be able to determine whether a given platform is a MSE when interacting with them.. STM agrees that it is disproportionate to expect all online platforms to have the same level of sophistication for the application of the provisions. Thus, their size, audience and turnover should be taken into account when adhering to due diligence obligations. At the very least, the obligation to establish an internal complaint-handling system noted under Article 17 should be required of MSEs. They should not offer lower standards and a weaker redress mechanism to consumers, who, in turn, might not have adequate information about the size of the provider they are using to determine whether this important right is available to them. MSEs should also be required to notify suspicions of criminal offences as established by Article 21, especially in light of the obligation already on them to have a notice and action system in place. Because notices give rise to awareness under Article 14 for the purpose of Article 5 (Hosting), MSEs would already be aware of suspicions of criminal offences, and would be in a good position, once such awareness has been acquired, to notify the competent authorities. This is even more important because, as previously noted, the proposed Chapter II on liability does not include a n obligation to notify competent authorities of suspected illegal activities. Similarly, a set of basic verification obligations such as verifying publicly available information about their business users should apply to MSEs. Exempting them from the prov isions at Article 22 would create possible loopholes where MSEs could deal with business users they do not verify which could exploit them for illegal activities and lead to an uncontrolled spread of illegal content on their services while bigger intermediaries would need to comply with such obligation.
• STM requests that basic obligations under Articles 17, 21 and 22 are required of micro and small enterprises (MSEs), too. STM is grateful for the commitment of the Commission to support and promote the development and implementation of voluntary industry standards under Article 34, including the quick and effective submission of notices through APIs. STM is extremely active and involved in this field and will continue working towards an efficient, trustworthy, and safe digital scholarly communication infrastructure.
4. Digital Services Coordinator STM welcomes the powers attributed to DSCs in Article 41, in particular the investigating powers as well as enforcement powers such as ordering the cessation of infringements, imposing interim measures to avoid serious harm and fines as well as adopting interim measures to avoid risk of serious harm. However, STM notes that Article 43 does not explicitly provide for the right of individuals or representative organisations to lodge a complaint to DSCs. This possibility is only addressed at

Recital 81. Furthermore, the opportunity for affected parties to be heard provided for under Article 41 and Recital 82 should also be included in Article 43.
• STM requests that Article 43 provide that individuals or representative organisations be able to lodge any complaint related to compliance with the DSA with the DSC in the territory where they received the service, without prejudice to this Regulation's rules on jurisdiction. CONCLUSION STM would welcome the opportunity to work with the European Commission and the co-legislators for a swift adoption of the new rules, aiming at an effective functioning of the internal market based on a clear, tried, and tested liability regime and streamlined due diligence obligations. About STM At STM we support our members in their mission to advance research worldwide. Our over 140 members based in over 20 countries around the world collectively publish 66% of all journal articles and tens of thousands of monographs and reference works. As academic and professional publishers, learned societies, university presses, start-ups, and established players we work together to serve society by developing standards and technology to ensure research is of high quality, trustworthy and easy to access. We promo te the contribution that publishers make to innovation, openness and the sharing of knowledge and embrace change to support the growth and sustainability of the research ecosystem. As a common good, we provide data and analysis for all involved in the global activity of research. Recital 18 positively recognises that exemptions from liability should not apply when a provider of intermediary services plays an active role so as to give it knowledge of, or control over, that information. However, Recital 18 does not properly reflect the jurisprudence of t he Court as it narrows what jurisprudence considers being "active" by putting as a single example, "information that has been developed under the editorial

responsibility of that provider." While STM welcomes the intent of Recital 18, Recital 18 should be amended so as to reflect the L'Oréal vs eBay line of jurisprudence of the Court on what can give rise to activity as follows " Those exemptions should accordingly not be available in respect of liability relating to information provided not by the recipient of the service but by the provider of intermediary service itself, including where the information has been developed under the editorial responsibility of that provider including, but not limited to, when the provider of intermediary services optimises the presentation or promotes content." This will ensure the DSA is futureproof and business model neutral". The language of Recital 18 should not benefit providers of intermediary services whose activities are not purely of a technical nature. Recital 20 aims at closing off liability exemptions to those " that deliberately collaborates with a recipient of the services in order to undertake illegal activities ". STM supports the principle of explicitly excluding certain intermediary services from relying on li ability exemptions when such services undertake illegal activities but believes that the test used in the current language does not capture the full scope of services that should be covered by this provision. " Deliberately collaborates" is a very high threshold and extremely hard to prove. Rather, it should be clear that the liability exemptions cannot be claimed by services the main purpose of which is to engage in or to facilitate illegal activities.

" Deliberately collaborates" is a very high threshold and extremely hard to prove. Rather, it should be clear that the liability exemptions cannot be claimed by services the main purpose of which is to engage in or to facilitate illegal activities. STM proposes to follow similar language to that already adopted in Recital 62 of the Copyright in the DSM Directive, which reads as follows: "[ ] the liability exemption mechanism provided for in this Directive should not apply to service providers the main purpose of which is to engage in or to facilitate copyright piracy."
• STM requests that providers of intermediary services not benefit from a liability exemption when they play an active role of such kind as to give them knowledge or control over the content, including but not limited to when the provider optimises the presentation or promotes the content. • STM requests that the liability exemption mechanism provided for in the DSA does not apply to providers of intermediary services the main purpose of which is to engage in or to facilitate illegal activities, and that such provision is included in Chapter II of the DSA under Article 5a. b. Voluntary own initiative investigations Article 6 and related Recital 25 should not be interpreted in any way that falls short of the safeguards and the high standards of transparency set by the DSA, nor should it lead to legal uncertainty. Under Article 6, the concept of " voluntary own-initiative investigations", "in good fai th and in a diligent manner" as specified by Recital 25 leaves substantial margin of discretion to providers to undertake voluntary measures that do not lead to the unavailability of the liability exemptions under Article 3, 4 and 5 of the DSA. Article 6 and Recital 25 leave undefined the types of voluntary measures that can be taken and does not set any specific boundaries. Although it is welcomed that Article 6 and Recital 25 provide that measures should be taken in good faith to comply with requirements of Union Law, including the obligations of the DSA. The current provisions leave too great a margin of discretion to providers to implement measures unilaterally, with little transparency, possibility for scrutiny, or follow-up on the effectiveness of those measures.

The current provisions leave too great a margin of discretion to providers to implement measures unilaterally, with little transparency, possibility for scrutiny, or follow-up on the effectiveness of those measures. STM believes that voluntary measures should only be undertaken by providers of intermediary services in order to comply with existing requirements of Union law and the obligations set forth in the DSA. In order to avoid loopholes and ensure effectiveness and enforceability of the provisions enshrined in the DSA, STM recommends amending Article 6 and accompanying Recital 25 to narrow

permissible voluntary own initiative measures for the detection, identification and action against illegal content to those measures solely necessary to ensure compliance with the requirements of Union law. • Exemptions from liability should only be afforded to providers of intermediary services when they take measures in a transparent manner, with appropriate oversig ht and safeguards, to detect, identify and remove, or disable access to, illegal content in compliance with requirements of EU Law including the requirements of the DSA. c. General Monitoring Prohibition Article 7 lays down a prohibition of general monitorin g or active fact-finding obligations for providers of intermediary services, which is a key principle that the DSA should uphold, consistently with the regime established by the ECD. STM welcomes the explicit mention that the prohibition does not affect mo nitoring that is concerning specific cases in Recital 28. Nonetheless, specific monitoring should be explicitly delineated in line with the jurisprudence of the CJEU as concerning content in identical and/or equivalent form to which was previously declared to be unlawful. Furthermore, STM notes that the DSA only maintains part of the former Article 15(2) of the ECD, which allowed Member States to establish obligations for providers to promptly inform the competent public authorities of alleged illegal activities undertaken. STM believes that the requirements under Article 9 for providers of intermediary services to provide information about individual recipients of their services when requested to do so by a national authority and under Article 21 for online platforms to notify authorities only of suspicions of serious criminal offences are of more limited application. The obligation to notify serious criminal offenses only applies to online platforms as part of their due diligence obligations and not to all providers of intermediary services.

The obligation to notify serious criminal offenses only applies to online platforms as part of their due diligence obligations and not to all providers of intermediary services. Thus, STM would recommend reintroducing the possibility for Member States to establish obligations for providers to promptly info rm the competent public authorities of alleged illegal activities undertaken and giving it prominence in a stand-alone provision within the liability chapter of the DSA which is applicable to all providers of intermediary services alike. • STM welcomes the explicit mention that the prohibition does not affect monitoring concerning specific cases in Recital 28 and asks that specific monitoring be clearly delineated in line with the jurisprudence of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) as concerning content in identical and/or equivalent form to which was previously declared to be unlawful. • STM requests the reintroduction for Member States to establish obligations for providers to promptly inform the competent public authorities of alleged illegal activities undertaken as a stand-alone provision within the liability chapter of the DSA which is applicable to all providers of intermediary services alike. 3. Due diligence obligations STM welcomes the approach of the DSA that provides for additional due diligence obligations, independent from the possibility to qualify or not for a claim to a liability exemption, as outlined in Chapter II. Those due diligence obligations will clarify the accountability of intermediary services. With regards to Chapter III, we acknowledge the asymmetrical system introduced and recommend further discussions on the categorisation of services and on the scope of applicability of obligations to ensure that no loopholes are left and that the principle of "What is illegal offline should be illegal online" is thoroughly respected and always true. a. Due diligence obligations for hosting services
i. Notice and action mechanism Aa harmonised notice and action system as introduced under Article 14 is welcomed by STM. The information provided for a notice should be the information necessary for an online platform to act. The requirements under the notice and action mechanism should be practical and not over - burdensome. On notices more specifically, STM requests that the language regarding " the exact URL " under Article 14(2)(b) be removed to broaden and simplify the applicability of this provision. STM believes it would best read as " a clear indication of the electronic location of that information".

On notices more specifically, STM requests that the language regarding " the exact URL " under Article 14(2)(b) be removed to broaden and simplify the applicability of this provision. STM believes it would best read as " a clear indication of the electronic location of that information". The requirement of location of the content in the notice should encompass other means besides the "exact" URL to specifically address the recurrence of identical or equivalent content. This is because requiring a URL is neither future proof, technologically neutral nor even in some cases - for example with apps - even relevant. Further, STM welcomes the addition in Article 14(3) clarifying that notices that include the elements listed shall be considered to give rise to actual knowledge or awareness for the purpose of Article 5 in respect to the specific item of content noticed (Hosting). • STM requests that the notice requirements concerning the location of the content be simple and technologically neutral. ii. Notice and permanent take down mechanism Once content has been identified as illegal and either removed or the access has been disabled, the issue of the reposting of illegal content should be addressed through a permanent take-down principle, to be inserted as part of the notice and action proce dure. In today's digital world, consumers and rightsholders alike are confronted with repeated infringements and/or the reappearance of infringing content in identical or equivalent form elsewhere. Thus, not only a notice and take down, but a notice and permanent take down mechanism would be in line with the objectives of the DSA for a safe, predictable and trustworthy online environment for all - and following the principle that "what is illegal offline is illegal online". Furthermore, this would also be consistent with existing law in Europe (e.g., Directive (EU) 2019/790). A notice and permanent take down could help ensure that any illegal content, including but not limited to terrorist content, sexual abuse material or copyright-protected content, unsafe products, or counterfeit goods, does not resurface easily. A notice-and-permanent-take-down principle can be both effective and also respecting of EU fundamental rights such as the freedom of expression online. This will be the case if the permanent take down is envisioned as concerning specific content including content that is identical or equivalent to that which was previously declared unlawful.

This will be the case if the permanent take down is envisioned as concerning specific content including content that is identical or equivalent to that which was previously declared unlawful. Such a mechanism would prevent any further infringement of the same type and often by the same infrin ger. This would be targeted, proportionate and specific to already identified material rather than a wholly new set of content. Because of the close proximity with the content identified as illegal in the first place, this mechanism would not infringe any fundamental rights. Furthermore, additional safeguards that refer to the internal-complaint handling system provided for under Article 17 can be explicitly made part of Article 14. • STM requests that a notice and permanent take down mechanism be added to Article 14. c. Due diligence obligations for online platforms
i. Trusted Flaggers Mechanism STM welcomes the introduction of the concept of a trusted flagger in Article 19 and is eager to play active role in this going forward. Nonetheless, th is mechanism should not be limited to representative organisations, and should be available to both organisations and companies. Moreover, some online platforms that would fall under the scope of the DSA have already put in place specific programmes akin to the trusted flagger mechanisms, in which many prominent organisations or companies partake. The DSA is an unprecedented opportunity to make such innovative practices the norm by recognising these successful practices between private entities and online pla tforms. It should th erefore be sufficient to notify the Digital Services Coordinator (DSC) when a well-functioning, mutually agreed, customary practice exists between a private entity and an online platform as regards to trusted flagging. • STM requests that both the representative organisations and companies be able to apply for the trusted flagger status, and that their ongoing collaboration with online platforms not be invalidated by the new system. ii. Measures and protection against misuse Article 20 provides for measures and protection against misuses. STM welcomes the possibility of online platforms to suspend repeat infringers and/or entities that abuse the notice and action system. Nonetheless, repeated infringements should be evaluated for illegal content as defined by the DSA and not "manifestly illegal content", which would artificially narrow the category of illegal content to be taken into account and create legal uncertainty.

Nonetheless, repeated infringements should be evaluated for illegal content as defined by the DSA and not "manifestly illegal content", which would artificially narrow the category of illegal content to be taken into account and create legal uncertainty. Furthermore, STM believes that layperson test ing as outlined under Recital 47 to determine whether the content is manifestly illegal is not appropriate in this context. This excludes the necessity of addressing and remove all types of repeat infringements and restricts legitimate action to only manifestly illegal content in the eye of a layperson without any substantive analysis. Finally, the provision does not include any clear transparency obligations nor the possibility to contest the decision taken by the platform, in contrast with Recital 46. STM supports the redre ss in Recital 46 but notes that instead of being available to all potentially injured parties such rightsholders; it is limited to recipients of services only. • STM requests that the word "manifestly" is deleted on the basis that if the content is illegal, it is illegal. There is no qualitative measurement needed. • STM requests that repeated infringements are considered under the mechanism at Article 20 as involving the provision of illegal content and asks the deletion of the layperson test under Recital 47 as inappropriate to determine whether the content is illegal. • STM requests that clear transparency and redress mechanisms be offered to representative groups and individuals such as rightsholders. iii. Notification of criminal offences STM welcomes the obligation to notify serious criminal offences under Article 21 as part of the due diligence obligations applicable to online platforms. STM believes that the scope of damaging criminal offences subject to the notification requirement shou ld be broadened. The Commission

proposal requires online platforms to only notify authorities of serious criminal offences involving a threat to the life or safety of persons that has taken place, is taking place or is likely to take place. Serious crimes in most jurisdictions only cover a restricted set of crimes attached to the persons, but rarely cover significant financial/commercial harm including Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) crimes. In order to achieve a safe, predictable and trustworthy online environment, authorities should be notified of other damaging criminal offences, in particular of suspicions of criminal offences related to, but not limited to, counterfeited and pirate content.

In order to achieve a safe, predictable and trustworthy online environment, authorities should be notified of other damaging criminal offences, in particular of suspicions of criminal offences related to, but not limited to, counterfeited and pirate content. Most criminal offences carried out online are significant an d often cause substantial commercial/financial harm to the affected parties. Such crimes are not victimless. • STM suggests that Article 21 be extended to the notification of a wider range of significant and damaging criminal offences - in particular commercial/financial crimes. iv. Traceability of traders The requirements around the traceability of traders under Article 22 (the so-called Know Your Business Customer, KYBC principle) are extremely welcome. They are helpful to establishing a safe, predictable, and trustworthy online environment for all and should be extended beyond their current scope. STM believes that the requirements outlined at Article 22, that are currently limited to online marketplaces and traders, should be extended to providers of hosting services and their business users, including small and micro enterprises. The se also should be strengthened to ensure that they are effective, draw from the experience caused by the inability to enforce the related provisions of the ECD and are derived from the already well-functioning framework existing in the financial sector. A provider of intermediary services should request trustworthy and accurate information from their business customers (that can be derived from publicly available sources) and verify the information to effectively know the business customer. A meaningful mechanism for enforcement should be established to ensure that businesses cannot wilfully bypass their obligations and are required to provide validated documents, data, or information such as corporate registration or other sufficient proof of identity. Service Providers should be able to disclose business customer information to third parties when required and in accordance with national law. This would help ensure that EU consumers have as little exposure as possible to illegal content, services, and products. STM notes that the obligation under Article 22 would only require providers to verify the identity of their business customers, not of all their user base. To further protect individual users, we suggest including a definition of "business customers" in Article 2 to clarify that not all users are covered. A distinction between commercial operators and private customers (who would be out of scope) should thus be added.

To further protect individual users, we suggest including a definition of "business customers" in Article 2 to clarify that not all users are covered. A distinction between commercial operators and private customers (who would be out of scope) should thus be added. This distinction is essential to ensure full compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, Regulation (EU) 2016/679) as the scope of "business users" would be limited. • STM requests that the KYBC principle be extended to providers of inter mediary services, in proper enforcement. In particular, online platforms should request their business users provide trustworthy and accurate information and verify the information provided to know the identify their business user. Providers should only disclose business user information to third parties where required. v. Exclusion of Micro or Small Enterprises Article 16 specifies that the obligations at Section 3 are not applicable to micro or small enterprises (MSEs). Whilst acknowledging the need to not impose too high a burden on MSEs and to give them the possibility to scale up, companies should build their business on legal and fair foundations from the start, not only when they reach a certain threshold. Indeed, abiding to certain lawful obligations is a fundamental part of doing business and should be asked of all intermediary services, including new players. For the DSA to achieve the objective of ensuring a safe, trustworthy, and fair environment for all the parties involved, building a business online should not be done at the expense of EU citizens, who, for the most part, will not be able to determine whether a given platform is a MSE when interacting with them.. STM agrees that it is disproportionate to expect all online platforms to have the same level of sophistication for the application of the provisions. Thus, their size, audience and turnover should be taken into account when adhering to due diligence obligations. At the very least, the obligation to establish an internal complaint-handling system noted under Article 17 should be required of MSEs. They should not offer lower standards and a weaker redress mechanism to consumers, who, in turn, might not have adequate information about the size of the provider they are using to determine whether this important right is available to them.

They should not offer lower standards and a weaker redress mechanism to consumers, who, in turn, might not have adequate information about the size of the provider they are using to determine whether this important right is available to them. MSEs should also be required to notify suspicions of criminal offences as established by Article 21, especially in light of the obligation already on them to have a notice and action system in place. Because notices give rise to awareness under Article 14 for the purpose of Article 5 (Hosting), MSEs would already be aware of suspicions of criminal offences, and would be in a good position, once such awareness has been acquired, to notify the competent authorities. This is even more important because, as previously noted, the proposed Chapter II on liability does not include a n obligation to notify competent authorities of suspected illegal activities. Similarly, a set of basic verification obligations such as verifying publicly available information about their business users should apply to MSEs. Exempting them from the prov isions at Article 22 would create possible loopholes where MSEs could deal with business users they do not verify which could exploit them for illegal activities and lead to an uncontrolled spread of illegal content on their services while bigger intermediaries would need to comply with such obligation. • STM requests that basic obligations under Articles 17, 21 and 22 are required of micro and small enterprises (MSEs), too. STM is grateful for the commitment of the Commission to support and promote the development and implementation of voluntary industry standards under Article 34, including the quick and effective submission of notices through APIs. STM is extremely active and involved in this field and will continue working towards an efficient, trustworthy, and safe digital scholarly communication infrastructure. 4. Digital Services Coordinator STM welcomes the powers attributed to DSCs in Article 41, in particular the investigating powers as well as enforcement powers such as ordering the cessation of infringements, imposing interim measures to avoid serious harm and fines as well as adopting interim measures to avoid risk of serious harm. However, STM notes that Article 43 does not explicitly provide for the right of individuals or representative organisations to lodge a complaint to DSCs. This possibility is only addressed at

Recital 81.

However, STM notes that Article 43 does not explicitly provide for the right of individuals or representative organisations to lodge a complaint to DSCs. This possibility is only addressed at

Recital 81. Furthermore, the opportunity for affected parties to be heard provided for under Article 41 and Recital 82 should also be included in Article 43. • STM requests that Article 43 provide that individuals or representative organisations be able to lodge any complaint related to compliance with the DSA with the DSC in the territory where they received the service, without prejudice to this Regulation's rules on jurisdiction. CONCLUSION STM would welcome the opportunity to work with the European Commission and the co-legislators for a swift adoption of the new rules, aiming at an effective functioning of the internal market based on a clear, tried, and tested liability regime and streamlined due diligence obligations. About STM At STM we support our members in their mission to advance research worldwide. Our over 140 members based in over 20 countries around the world collectively publish 66% of all journal articles and tens of thousands of monographs and reference works. As academic and professional publishers, learned societies, university presses, start-ups, and established players we work together to serve society by developing standards and technology to ensure research is of high quality, trustworthy and easy to access. We promo te the contribution that publishers make to innovation, openness and the sharing of knowledge and embrace change to support the growth and sustainability of the research ecosystem. As a common good, we provide data and analysis for all involved in the global activity of research. POSITION STATEMENT

Proposal for a Regulation on a Single Market for Digital Services

Background

On 15 December 2020 the European Commission published its long-awaited package to update the rules governing digital services in the EU. The Digital Services Act (DSA) and Digital Markets Act (DMA) are intended to ensure that all users have access to a wide and innovative range of products and services online, and receive a high standard of protection while doing so. The DSA will amend the e-Commerce Directive, introducing new obligations around the transparency, liability and competitiveness of digital services.

General considerations

The Federation of Small Businesses (FSB) welcomes efforts to make the digital single market a reality and to ensure a fair, stable trading environment. Completion of the digital single market will help accelerate digital growth and further enable cross-border trade between Member States and globally.

The digital transition has fundamentally altered the way small and medium-sized businesses operate. Small and medium-sized businesses make use of digital technology to reduce costs, grow their business and serve a wider customer base, from basic changes such as setting up their own online shops and using social media to more complex innovations harnessing cloud computing.

In particular, online platforms offer unrivalled opportunities for small businesses to expand their reach, access or test products in new markets at reduced risk and cost. According to In summary

➢ FSB welcomes the intention to complete the digital single market and establish a fair, stable regulatory environment that facilitates cross-border trade. Further action is needed to redress the balance between online platforms and small business users. ➢ FSB is concerned about the potential consequences of overregulation or unintended bureaucratic burdens that would hinder the ability of small firms to participate in digital trade. ➢ FSB welcomes requirements around notice and action measures, but cautions that processes must be carefully constructed to minimise the potential for the removal of compliant content or products. This should include ensuring human oversight of automated tools. ➢ FSB supports the exclusion of online platforms that are micr o or small enterprises, which have fewer resources and are less able to absorb the costs of new regulatory requirements. ➢ Internal complaint-handling systems must be transparent and produce timely and objective results. Safeguards should be in place to protect small businesses from potential retaliatory measures taken by online platforms. ➢ Traceability obligations should not have the effect of discouraging smal l businesses from trading online. Article 22 should therefore take a more proportionate approach to onboarding requirements. ➢ FSB supports the obligation to inform users of the parameters used in recommender systems. ➢ FSB strongly supports the facilitation of codes of conduct to ensure the proper application of the Digital Services Act, the development of which should include the voice of small businesses.

FSB's 2019 Digital Trade Survey, approximately one in five small exporters use online platforms to export and import. 1 Services offered by online platforms are extremely valuable to small firms that lack the resources or economies of scale available to larger firms, but the position of online platforms as intermediators of business customer relationships creates an unequal balance of power and can result in unfair and potentially anti-competitive trading practices.

FSB therefore supports the intention of the DSA to establish a single horizontal regulatory framework, building on the foundation of Regulation 2019/1150 (the 'P2B Regulation') to redress the balance between online platforms and small business users.

Further consideration will need to be given however to a number of issues within the scope of the DSA in order to minimise the potential of unintended bureaucratic burdens or costs that would hinder the ability of small firms to participate in digital trade.

Specific comments

• Article 8: Orders to act against illegal content

Infringements of intellectual property rights can be extremely damaging and costly for small firms. One in ten small businesses that participate in digital trade see IP infringement as a major concern.2 FSB therefore welcomes the requirement set out in Article 8 for service providers to respond without undue delay to orders from national judicial or administrative authorities to remove illegal content, and for a clear statement of reasons to be provided explaining the decision (see also Article 15).

However, small businesses have reported instances of compliant content or i tems being removed from online platforms, resulting in lengthy and costly redress processes to reinstate the item. The DSA contains welcome clarification that service providers must allow decisions removing or disabling content to be contested quickly and provide information about available redress mechanisms. FSB nonetheless cautions that the processes used to carry out the identification and removal of illegal content must be carefully constructed and proportionate in order to minimise the potential for the removal of compliant content or products either by accident or by design. The definition and scope of 'illegal cont ent' must furthermore be consistently applied across the EU at domestic level.

• Article 14: Notice and action mechanisms

As noted above, FSB welcomes the use of clear and robust processes to identify illegal or non-compliant content as a means of safeguarding users and protecting businesses from intellectual property infringements and other harmful business practices. However, these mechanisms must be carefully designed to minimise the potential for compliant content or products to be wrongfully removed.

This is particularly pertinent in the case of the use of automated tools to identify and remove content. As a study from the European Parliament Policy Department for Economic, Scientific and Quality of Life Policies points out, there are limits to the accuracy of automated tools.3 Safeguards should therefore be in place to improve the effectiveness

1 Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), Destination Digital, 2019, p16-17 2 Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), Spotlight on Innovation: How Government Can Unlock Small Business Productivity, July 2018, p12 3 European Parliament Policy Department for Economic, Scientific and Quality of Life Policies, Online Platforms' Moderation of Illegal Content Online (2020), p45

of notice and action mechanisms, including human agency and oversight, in line with the requirements for trustworthy AI set out in the 2019 Commission Communication. 4

• Article 16: Exclusion for micro and small enterprises

FSB supports the exemption for online platforms that are micro or small enterprises from the requirements set out in Section 3 of the DSA. Small businesses have fewer resources to adapt and are less able to absorb the costs and administrative burdens related to new regulatory requirements.

• Article 17: Internal complaint-handling system

FSB supports the introduction of an obligation to provide online platform users with access to an effective internal system for complaint handling. A successful complaint-handling system must be transparent and produce timely and objective results. Safeguards must be in place to protect the interests of small businesses, which can sometimes be reluctant to raise complain ts against online platforms due to fear of direct or indirect retaliatory measures and the potential loss of a substantial income stream.

In light of the above comments related to Article 14, FSB welcomes the requirement that decisions to remove or dis able access to information, or suspend provision of a service, should not be taken solely on the basis of automated means (Article 17(5)).

• Article 22: Traceability of traders

FSB welcomes the Commission's intentions to boost consumer trust in business integrity. There are concerns however from the small business community that the traceability of traders requirements as currently worded may impose significant administrative burdens on small businesses and may have unintended consequences for the digital single market. Lengthy and cumbersome onboarding processes may at best lead to an increase in platform fees payable by small businesses (as a result of platforms' increased administrative costs) and at worst discourage small businesses from using online platforms, impacting on the effectiveness and flexibility of the digital single market and ultimately undermining the aims of the DSA.

Traceability requirements must strike a balance between boosting transparency and accountability, to tackle practices such as free-riding, and creating a chilling effect on e - commerce by having the effect of discouraging legitimate small businesses from trading online. The burdens imposed by Article 22 must be proportionate to enable small businesses to continue to take advantage of the digital single market.

FSB further suggests that a tiered approach to onboarding requirements could be considered to minimise the impact of traceability obligations such as through a requirement to provide essential information only while onboarding, followed by more detailed supplementary information within a specified timeframe. This could differ according to the sector or products concerned through a risk-based approach. Businesses must also be given adequate time to comply with requirements, taking into account the limited resources available to small firms.

4 Commission Communication COM(2019)168, Building Trust in Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence (2019), p4

• Article 29: Recommender systems

Transparency and clarity regarding the parameters used for determining recommendations and rankings, as well as the reasons for their relative importance, is extremely valuable to small businesses. These disclosure requirements enable small businesses to make an informed choice wh en selecting a provider of an online intermediary service but do not require providers to disclose proprietary information, thereby striking the right balance. FSB therefore supports the obligation to inform users of the parameters used in recommender systems.

• Article 35: Codes of conduct

FSB strongly supports the facilitation of codes of conduct to ensure the proper application of the DSA. The Commission must regularly monitor and review these codes of conduct to ensure that they are robust and contribute to the achievement of their objectives. The Commission must also ensure that all relevant voices are heard in the development of these codes, including representative organisations of small businesses

One in ten small businesses that participate in digital trade see IP infringement as a major concern.2 FSB therefore welcomes the requirement set out in Article 8 for service providers to respond without undue delay to orders from national judicial or administrative authorities to remove illegal content, and for a clear statement of reasons to be provided explaining the decision (see also Article 15). However, small businesses have reported instances of compliant content or i tems being removed from online platforms, resulting in lengthy and costly redress processes to reinstate the item. The DSA contains welcome clarification that service providers must allow decisions removing or disabling content to be contested quickly and provide information about available redress mechanisms.

The DSA contains welcome clarification that service providers must allow decisions removing or disabling content to be contested quickly and provide information about available redress mechanisms. FSB nonetheless cautions that the processes used to carry out the identification and removal of illegal content must be carefully constructed and proportionate in order to minimise the potential for the removal of compliant content or products either by accident or by design. The definition and scope of 'illegal cont ent' must furthermore be consistently applied across the EU at domestic level. • Article 14: Notice and action mechanisms

As noted above, FSB welcomes the use of clear and robust processes to identify illegal or non-compliant content as a means of safeguarding users and protecting businesses from intellectual property infringements and other harmful business practices. However, these mechanisms must be carefully designed to minimise the potential for compliant content or products to be wrongfully removed. This is particularly pertinent in the case of the use of automated tools to identify and remove content. As a study from the European Parliament Policy Department for Economic, Scientific and Quality of Life Policies points out, there are limits to the accuracy of automated tools.3 Safeguards should therefore be in place to improve the effectiveness

1 Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), Destination Digital, 2019, p16-17 2 Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), Spotlight on Innovation: How Government Can Unlock Small Business Productivity, July 2018, p12 3 European Parliament Policy Department for Economic, Scientific and Quality of Life Policies, Online Platforms' Moderation of Illegal Content Online (2020), p45

FSB supports the introduction of an obligation to provide online platform users with access to an effective internal system for complaint handling. A successful complaint-handling system must be transparent and produce timely and objective results.

• Article 17: Internal complaint-handling system

FSB supports the introduction of an obligation to provide online platform users with access to an effective internal system for complaint handling. A successful complaint-handling system must be transparent and produce timely and objective results. Safeguards must be in place to protect the interests of small businesses, which can sometimes be reluctant to raise complain ts against online platforms due to fear of direct or indirect retaliatory measures and the potential loss of a substantial income stream. Lengthy and cumbersome onboarding processes may at best lead to an increase in platform fees payable by small businesses (as a result of platforms' increased administrative costs) and at worst discourage small businesses from using online platforms, impacting on the effectiveness and flexibility of the digital single market and ultimately undermining the aims of the DSA. • Article 29: Recommender systems

Transparency and clarity regarding the parameters used for determining recommendations and rankings, as well as the reasons for their relative importance, is extremely valuable to small businesses. These disclosure requirements enable small businesses to make an informed choice wh en selecting a provider of an online intermediary service but do not require providers to disclose proprietary information, thereby striking the right balance. FSB therefore supports the obligation to inform users of the parameters used in recommender systems. • Article 35: Codes of conduct

FSB strongly supports the facilitation of codes of conduct to ensure the proper application of the DSA. The Commission must regularly monitor and review these codes of conduct to ensure that they are robust and contribute to the achievement of their objectives. The Commission must also ensure that all relevant voices are heard in the development of these codes, including representative organisations of small businesses

Dear Madam/Sir,

Please find attached Etsy's feedback on the Digital Services Act (DSA) proposal. We remain at your disposal should you have any questions.

Kind regards,

Laura Blanco

DSA Proposal: Etsy's Feedback 31 March 2021 ABOUT ETSY Etsy is a global marketplace for unique and creative goods. Our mission is to keep commerce human, and we're committed to using the power of business to strengthen communities and empower people. Our marketplace provides a platform to enable a global community of sellers to market and sell their goods to buyers around the world, who come to Etsy to be inspired and delighted by items that are crafted and curated by creative entrepreneurs. As of 31 December 2020, Etsy marketplaces hosted 4.4 million sellers and over 81.9 million active buyers, operating in nearly every country in the world. Across our major European markets (the UK, France, and Germany), 86-88% of our sellers are women, 80-92% of sellers are businesses of one, and nearly all run their creative businesses out of their homes. For 29-43%, their creative business is their full-time occupation. For the rest, their creative business supplements other types of jobs and income. In many ways, Etsy provides a low-cost means to experiment with creative entrepreneurship. For 33-52%, Etsy was the first place they sold their goods. INTRODUCTION Etsy believes that marketplaces have a responsibility to help protect consumers. As a business, it's in our best interest to offer consumers a trusted place to find their favourite independent shops. That's why we continue to invest in the people and technology that underpin our marketplace trust and integrity functions, and move quickly to identify and remove potentially harmful content. Notwithstanding our commitment to promoting safety online and our support for the intended goal of the Digital Services Act (DSA), we believe that any new obligations placed on marketplaces should be proportionate to their capabilities, knowledge, and the role they play in the market. Etsy's marketplace does not take possession, inspect, design, set prices or distribute products, and our customers understand they are purchasing goods directly from individual sellers who market their goods and their businesses on our platforms. 2019 Global Seller Census https://www.etsy.com/press

Our main priority is to support a new legal framework which allows for a more consistent and effective implementation of EU law throughout the Single Market, while avoiding imposing inconsistent or confusing compliance burdens on small businesses, in particular microbusinesses. To this end, we submit the following comments, recommendations, and questions for clarification. OUR INITIAL FEEDBACK TO THE DSA PROPOSAL
1) E-Commerce Directive & intermediary liability: Intermediary liability protections enable platforms like Etsy to operate at scale and offer opportunities to entrepreneurs around the globe. Without such protections, Etsy could be forced to screen every item before allowing it on our site, a resource-intensive activity that would be nearly impossible to automate in many circumstances, given the diversity of products, shops and seller locations on Etsy. It's important to note that most of the +85M items for sale on Etsy are handmade or vintage items, not mass market goods. Moving to a curated business model would necessarily curtail the opportunities we currently provide to over four million microbusinesses, including many across the European Union, most of whom are women. Additional liabilities on a marketplace like ours would also reduce our ability to offer services in multiple markets, undermining the goals of the Digital Single Market: for example, systematically reviewing handmade products that Etsy does not possess or control would not be feasible in a global context. DSA comments: We welcome the fact that the DSA proposal maintains key principles of the e-Commerce Directive, including the limited liability framework, prohibition of general monitoring obligations, and country of origin principle. We nonetheless see areas for improvement and/or clarification in regards to the proposed: ● notice and action mechanism and its connection to "actual knowledge" of illegal content ( Article 14.3 ): according to Article 14, platforms should enable the submission of notices by individuals or entities that fulfil a list of criteria listed in paragraph two. One of the criteria to submit a 'sufficiently precise and adequately substantiated notice' consists of providing ' an explanation of the reasons why the individual or entity considers the information in question to be illegal content '. We are concerned that an individual could submit a notice fulfilling all the criteria (ticking all the right boxes) believing the listing to be 'illegal', while the platform may ultimately believe it does not have sufficient information to make the determination of illegality. From our experience, amongst other examples, individuals sometimes flag that an item is allegedly stolen goods; regional-specific offensive/illegal content; competes with their own products, or mature content, which may be 'offensive' to the person flagging the item but in itself not a proxy for policy violations. Draft Article 14.3 is therefore of great concern as it seems to suggest that a notice that fulfils all the criteria will be deemed valid (even before a legality determination) and will automatically lead to the platform having 'actual knowledge' of illegality and hence liability irrespective of the alleged validity. This

provision would only create an incentive for users to improperly flag content, and for platforms to over-remove potentially legal items to avoid a liability risk, and therefore platforms should, at a minimum, have the ability to challenge the validity of the notice. ● limitation to the intermediary liability exemption ( Article 5.3 ): the provision seems to imply that the limited liability framework does not apply for marketplaces and e-commerce platforms if the platform presents an item or enables the transaction in a way that it's not clear to the average consumer whether the item is sold by the platform or a third-party seller. On Etsy's marketplace, products are only available via a shop's own listings, and not via common product listings with availability across multiple shops. On Etsy, buyers understand they are always purchasing goods directly from individual sellers who market their goods and their businesses on our platforms. We prominently feature the seller's shop right on the listing page. As this approach is already a requirement under the Better enforcement and modernisation Directive (EU) 2019/2161 (Omnibus Directive), we think Article 5(3) of the DSA requires clarification on how this parallel liability regime interacts with this and other sectoral (consumer protection) legislation and whether this provision is primarily aimed at hybrid marketplaces that mix first and third party offerings? If so, the legislation should be more clear on this point.
2) Notice and action: Notice and action provides a reliable and tested horizontal approach to moderate all kinds of third-party illegal content. Unfortunately, the e-Commerce Directive has not been implemented consistently across EU Member States, with only some adopting formal notice-and-takedown systems. An efficient and harmonised notice and action regime will allow platforms to combat illegal content at scale, without inappropriately taking on police or judicial functions. DSA comments: We welcome the DSA's intention to harmonise notice and action rules across the EU. However, a framework that has the intention to harmonise and lead to more efficiency in content moderation practices should be flexible enough not to overburden platforms, in particular small and medium-sized platforms, and account for the different ways of operation that are best suited for certain business models and size. In particular we see points for improvement and/or clarification in regards to the proposed: ● Framework to notices from individuals (Article 14.5): this provision aims to oblige the provider to respond 'without undue delay' to notices from individuals and entities informing them of our decision vis-a-vis their notice. While notices from individuals can be helpful and appropriate inputs to platform moderation procedures, it's important to understand that they can also be inaccurate and subject to abuse. For example, large rights holders may submit overly broad takedown requests, demanding legitimate goods be removed from our platform, or submit three notices in rapid succession in an attempt to get a seller permanently banned before the seller can practically respond. Platforms

are also seeing an increase in false or improper notices, either from shops seeking to harm competitors during peak season, malicious conduct, or mere disagreement regarding lawful content. Given our experience with the prevalence of competing sellers on a platform, those engaging in fraud, and simple mistakes by members of the public, we strongly urge policymakers to incorporate flexibility into the requirement to respond 'without undue delay' to account for the time and resource-intensive process required for a platform like ours to make a determination on each and every notice from an individual. We also receive notices alleging IP infringement that clearly contain invalid email addresses. In this respect, we believe we could potentially cut down on such abusive notices if a requirement to submit a notice from an individual under Article 14(2) would include a "verified" or "valid" email address. ● Requirement to provide a Statement of Reasons (Article 15): Following the experience and reasoning discussed above regarding notices by individuals, the requirement to "inform the recipient, at the latest at the time of the removal or disabling the access, of the decision and provide clear and specific reasons'' would undermine the flexibility needed to account for certain situations where such disclosures could undermine investigations or user privacy. For example, there are certain types of content that Etsy may temporarily disable pending human review, and there are certain situations in which Etsy may suspend a seller's account without notifying the affected seller (e.g. where fraud or other criminal behavior is detected) Thus, the DSA should exempt platforms from the requirement to provide a Statement of Reasons "without undue delay" in certain circumstances. Moreover, Article 15.4 would require us to publish each and every decision and Statement of Reasons in a publicly available database. We believe that there is a need to balance transparency and information that is in the public interest (e.g. to demonstrate that tackling illegal activity is a focus for the platform, that appropriate resources are allocated, and what categories of violative content are prevalent on a given platform) with feasibility (e.g. there may be limitations on the type of data collection and analysis available to platforms, particularly smaller platforms). To account for the capacities of smaller platforms, we believe that reporting aggregate data annually (e.g. X listing removals for Y reasons, Z appeals) would be a more proportionate measure. Moreover, it's not clear who the intended audience of this database would be. If regulatory authorities would benefit most, then we recommend that this should not be a public database, but rather that platforms may provide such information upon request. ● Framework for working with trusted flaggers (Article 19): We strongly believe that third party experts and brands are best positioned to identify illegal content, and therefore welcome the DSA's draft Article 19 allowing for a notice and action process with identified trusted flaggers. We agree that content flagged by such trusted flaggers can be more easily escalated for review, but also that the status of trusted flagger should be revoked if too many decisions/flags are overturned or otherwise indicate abuse of the flagging system. We'd like to highlight the importance of ensuring that the eligibility

criteria for trusted flagger status should be awarded to competent and authoritative entities that reflect expertise in a specific type of digital content and services. The proposal says that trusted flaggers should represent 'collective interests', which seems to imply that individual brands cannot attain the status of trusted flaggers. When it comes to intellectual property specifically, from our experience in working with brands, we strongly believe that they're best placed to know about their own intellectual property infringements and Article 19 should account for that. The collective entity could perhaps play an important role in verifying brands as trusted flaggers and making that information available to the platform. At the same time, we believe that Article 19 lacks a counter-notice process to prevent abusing the system to suppress legitimate competition. The provision says that a trusted flagger status can be revoked following an investigation by the Digital Services Coordinator. We want to ensure that we don't block legitimate, legal items from being sold. This is especially important for a platform like Etsy, where our sellers are primarily women-led businesses of one working out of their homes, and who depend on their sales to earn income. Suspending their accounts, even temporarily, may have a significant impact. Thus, counter-notices are the most effective means an Etsy seller may have to protect her business. In these circumstances where further dialogue with the trusted flagger will be needed, a platform like ours will need a certain level of flexibility to act on these notices. 3) Due diligence obligations: Platforms like Etsy make it easier for Europeans to start microbusinesses and access the global market. We nonetheless recognise that they have not only created new economic and creative opportunities, but - like many intermediary platforms - bad actors find ways to disseminate content and goods that violate Etsy or regulatory policies, including potentially products that have not been certified by product or consumer protection regulators. Well-defined, proportionate and flexible due diligence rules for online platforms are therefore key to ensure a trusted place to shop and transact online. DSA comments: We welcome the DSA's graduated approach on the basis of those services' size and impact. We believe that any new due diligence obligations placed on marketplaces should be proportionate to key features of the services we offer, our capabilities, knowledge, and the role we play in the market. Ultimately, this will ensure the efficiency of the systems we put in place to meet the intended goals of these provisions. To this end, we see points for improvement and/or clarification in regards to the proposed: ● Traceability of traders obligation (Article 22): We deem it reasonable to impose a KYBC obligation on marketplaces for their sellers, and this is something Etsy already takes very seriously. However, we believe that this provision should take into account pre-existing EU legislation in relation to KYC/KYB obligations that are already imposed on online platform operators so that the various legislative frameworks are mutually consistent and do not create a situation where operators are subject to laws that conflict with each other. This will ensure the efficiency of our systems in implementing Article to meet

the intended goal of a higher consumer protection and product safety standards. Moreover, any new "KYBC" measure must be privacy-friendly, proportionate and supported by the right infrastructure in order to enable automatic and scalable verifications, while enabling the small and microbusinesses we host to thrive. To this end, we believe the text should be amended to: ○ Clarify concept of 'trader': The concept of 'trader' seems to be broadly defined under draft Article 2(e), ranging from anyone using a service for any professional purpose, to casual hobbyists who sell crafts, etc. Requiring such detailed information from private individuals would create disincentives or make it more difficult to sell handmade goods on digital platforms and deter the formation of creative businesses. This concept also adds to a growing number of varying definitions for professional sellers in tax, consumer protection, and other legislative regimes in the EU and its member states, as well as worldwide. For the majority of our sellers, Etsy was the first place they sold their goods. In that way our platform really functions as an on-ramp to entrepreneurship for women around the globe. Moreover, if a user signs up on our platform as a business or as an individual, we should be able to rely on the self-identification of the trader as such in the assessment of whether they should be in the KYBC scope as we cannot be expected to possess the information required to make that determination on our own (e.g. a person's sales volume outside of our platform) or to take on any direct liability connected to it beyond our services (e.g. tax-related). For this reason, we call for Article 2(e) to clarify and specify that a 'trader' should only constitute those individuals or legal entities that transact for professional purposes in line with existing concepts under EU law. Article 22 should also specify that platforms can rely on the self-identification of the users as a trader. ○ Align with existing data collection, verification and reporting requirements: Platforms already experience challenges managing multiple bespoke information requests from different jurisdictions for tax information about their users. The soon to be adopted DAC 7 Directive, is a positive step in that it aims to provide a streamlined mechanism to facilitate information sharing with, and between, tax authorities. However, meeting these requirements already requires significant legal and technical resources, an outcome that is challenging for our companies to manage and staff, never mind startups with much more limited resources and capacity. A completely different framework to collect and verify seller's data for the purpose of the DSA will put unnecessary and disproportionate strain on platforms like ours. From a business user perspective, having to provide similar data on multiple occasions during the customer experience is also likely to deter individuals from using the service, leading to decreased consumer choice. In order to make the DSA's Article 22 traceability requirement scaleable and workable for platforms, we request to align the collection, verification and

reporting requirements as much as possible to existing legislation (DAC 7 Directive). ○ Focus on high-volume traders: Reporting requirements should also be limited to platform sellers with revenues above a certain threshold, or at a minimum require a simplified KYBC procedure below a certain threshold (e.g. requiring less data collection, or at least no or limited verification). Absent such a threshold or simplified procedure, platforms would be forced to collect sensitive personal information at onboarding, a moment when our sellers may not trust our platform enough to share such personal information, and may be discouraged from opening a shop or transacting on our platforms at all. We strongly encourage such a threshold to include a combination of total revenues and number of transactions to ensure it does not capture casual, one time sellers. For example, the DAC 7 Directive referenced earlier provides for a 2000 EUR or 30 transactions in a year threshold. Article 22 should mandate traceability of high-volume sellers only or at a minimum require a simplified KYBC below a certain threshold. ○ Protect the privacy of sellers: Draft Article 22(6) includes a problematic disclosure requirement for a company such as Etsy, where the majority of our sellers are microbusinesses working out of their own homes, and thus their business address is also their home address. Mandating disclosure of such information would therefore undermine the ability of our platform to protect the personal data and privacy of our sellers. Furthermore, platforms often work with third party providers or even divide their services between different legal entities. In practice, this means that a payments service provider or entity which is already running KYC on the platform's users may not be authorized by applicable privacy rules to share this data or broader KYC results with the main marketplace service provider. Article 22 should create a legal obligation for this information to be shared by third parties that the main provider is working with, where it can help said provider to comply with the DSA's KYBC obligations. Article 22(6) should therefore exclude mandating disclosures of certain data points (e.g. address) in certain circumstances (such as when the trader is an individual) or at least require to disclose the geographical address in line with the Omnibus Directive. A provision should also be added to allow KYC relevant data and results to be shared from payments entities and third parties working with the main service provider to comply more efficiently with the DSA. ○ Include flexibility in verification methods: draft Article 22(b) requires all traders to provide a "copy of identification document" to the platform. In order to enable automatic and scalable verifications, platforms need to be supported by the right infrastructure. For example, not all marketplaces have the means or expertise to unilaterally verify PDF documents. Based on our anti-money

laundering experience, it's also important to consider that documents are actually easier to falsify (especially scan copies) than online database records. Document collection is most often a means of last resort, only where we're unable to verify the identity of our sellers by other means. Nonetheless, this process of screening sellers against publicly available databases for KYB/C purposes can also be costly and operationally burdensome. For all these reasons, and taking into account the diversity in seller typology between different marketplaces, we believe that the best result will be achieved by empowering platforms with a certain risk-and capacity-based characteristics flexibility in data verification methods (e.g. manual verification, private databases). Article 22 should therefore allow for more flexibility in verifying our seller's identity beyond checking against a "copy of identification document". ○ Avoid or limit disclosing contact information of economic operators: draft Article 22 requires platforms to collect, verify and disclose "the name, address, telephone number and electronic mail address of the economic operator, within the meaning of Article 3(13) and Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020" (Market Surveillance Regulation). As of July 2021, our non-EU toy sellers will be required to appoint an EU economic operator which, in itself, is an extremely challenging compliance burden for microbusinesses to manage. The microbusinesses who sell on Etsy do not have the resources to find, appoint, or pay a representative based in the EU to manage their compliance obligations. When faced with this requirement, we believe that most will choose to no longer sell goods into the EU, reducing choice for EU consumers. The Etsy community, including non-EU sellers, fully supports efforts to ensure that consumer protections function in the global marketplace. However, such an obligation is simply not designed with home-based microbusinesses in mind, including the longstanding community of individual toymakers, and the proposal to require a platform to collect, verify and disclose the contact details of the economic operators under the DSA would unnecessarily erect burdens to entrepreneurship and selling cross-border. We would, for example, have to request such information at onboarding from individuals who are looking to start a business and open a shop on Etsy for the very first time, with the likelihood of discouraging them from doing so altogether. Enabling Etsy sellers to comply with EU legislation in a simplified manner will help these small businesses grow - all of which is more important than ever given the global pandemic, and the role that these microbusiness can serve to help rebuild local economies. In view of helping small businesses thrive, Article 22 should therefore not mandate the collection, verification and disclosure of the contact details of economic operators within the meaning of Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020. ● Transparency Reporting obligations for online platforms (Articles and 23): We believe that publicly reporting on our enforcement efforts builds trust in our marketplace and demonstrates our commitment to transparency and accountability. This is reflected in our

annual Transparency Report. Etsy endeavors to balance transparency with the need to prevent bad actors from "gaming" detective controls. Providing specific details regarding automated control parameters may enable bad actors to evade detection. As previously stated, more specifically, we believe there is a need to balance transparency and information that is in the public interest with feasibility, particularly for smaller platforms. Small and medium-sized platforms like ours may also be limited in the frequency that they can feasibly publish such information. We are therefore concerned that: ○ the prescriptive nature of requirements under draft Articles and will not lead to a meaningful level of transparency that as intended by the DSA, and may in fact risk ill-intentioned users circumventing legitimate content moderation measures. While transparency around outcomes and actions is incredibly useful, we would caution against encouraging public transparency of enforcement methods as suggested by draft Article 23(1)(c), as bad actors iterate their own actions in response to enforcement efforts, and keeping these strategies confidential improves their effectiveness. Moreover, tools that may be effective for non-digital and non-standardised (handmade, artistic) products, are not necessarily effective for other products. ○ Draft Articles and also fail to clarify who the intended audience for these obligations are (e.g. users, regulatory authorities, researchers). In our experience, users experience more meaningful transparency through the messages a platform uses to communicate its decisions and functions, rather than having access to compiled figures and data with no context. Users will benefit most if they are able to understand the reasons for removal decisions, for example, or the factors weighed to determine search ranking. Take down volumes and appeal rates are data points where regulators would benefit most, compared to users who benefit most from understanding the decisions we take and how our policies are enforced. To this end, the burden to report information regarding our policies and measures may be assuaged by narrowing the scope of reporting obligations. For example, certain information currently not published in our annual Transparency Report may be provided with smaller groups (e.g. regulators) for specific cases and under certain circumstances. ○ Moreover, on the basis of our experience and annual transparency reports, we generally caution against mandating frequent transparency reporting (e.g. more than once a year as suggested in draft Article 23) as this may require operational changes that may be too burdensome for smaller players. On Etsy, we experience a higher number of users around the holiday season (Q4) and this seasonal effect may be misconstrued if we were to publicly report more than once a year.

○ Lastly, according to draft Article 23(2) "online platforms shall publish, at least once every six months, information on the average monthly active recipients of the service in each Member State". Disclosing the average monthly active recipients in each Member State may harm competition and conflict with securities laws in various jurisdictions. Etsy, for example, currently only discloses such information in our core markets. Once again, we believe that the burden to report such information may be assuaged by narrowing down the scope of reporting obligations to provide such information to regulators only or at least as an aggregate number in the EU. Policymakers should consider which audience benefits most from such information in order to make this requirement the most relevant for both the platform and the intended audience. CONCLUSION Etsy is a trusted brand and we stand ready to work with lawmakers, trusted partners and authorities to ensure that shopping on online marketplaces is a safe experience for consumers. Let's protect consumers in a way that also enables small and microbusinesses to thrive For more information, please contact: Althea Erickson VP, Global Public Policy and Impact aerickson@etsy.com Laura Blanco EU Public Policy Manager lblanco@etsy.com
