We nonetheless see areas for improvement and/or clarification in regards to the proposed: ● notice and action mechanism and its connection to "actual knowledge" of illegal content ( Article 14.3 ): according to Article 14, platforms should enable the submission of notices by individuals or entities that fulfil a list of criteria listed in paragraph two. One of the criteria to submit a 'sufficiently precise and adequately substantiated notice' consists of providing ' an explanation of the reasons why the individual or entity considers the information in question to be illegal content '.

One of the criteria to submit a 'sufficiently precise and adequately substantiated notice' consists of providing ' an explanation of the reasons why the individual or entity considers the information in question to be illegal content '. We are concerned that an individual could submit a notice fulfilling all the criteria (ticking all the right boxes) believing the listing to be 'illegal', while the platform may ultimately believe it does not have sufficient information to make the determination of illegality. From our experience, amongst other examples, individuals sometimes flag that an item is allegedly stolen goods; regional-specific offensive/illegal content; competes with their own products, or mature content, which may be 'offensive' to the person flagging the item but in itself not a proxy for policy violations. Draft Article 14.3 is therefore of great concern as it seems to suggest that a notice that fulfils all the criteria will be deemed valid (even before a legality determination) and will automatically lead to the platform having 'actual knowledge' of illegality and hence liability irrespective of the alleged validity. This

provision would only create an incentive for users to improperly flag content, and for platforms to over-remove potentially legal items to avoid a liability risk, and therefore platforms should, at a minimum, have the ability to challenge the validity of the notice. ● limitation to the intermediary liability exemption ( Article 5.3 ): the provision seems to imply that the limited liability framework does not apply for marketplaces and e-commerce platforms if the platform presents an item or enables the transaction in a way that it's not clear to the average consumer whether the item is sold by the platform or a third-party seller. On Etsy's marketplace, products are only available via a shop's own listings, and not via common product listings with availability across multiple shops. On Etsy, buyers understand they are always purchasing goods directly from individual sellers who market their goods and their businesses on our platforms. We prominently feature the seller's shop right on the listing page. As this approach is already a requirement under the Better enforcement and modernisation Directive (EU) 2019/2161 (Omnibus Directive), we think Article 5(3) of the DSA requires clarification on how this parallel liability regime interacts with this and other sectoral (consumer protection) legislation and whether this provision is primarily aimed at hybrid marketplaces that mix first and third party offerings?

As this approach is already a requirement under the Better enforcement and modernisation Directive (EU) 2019/2161 (Omnibus Directive), we think Article 5(3) of the DSA requires clarification on how this parallel liability regime interacts with this and other sectoral (consumer protection) legislation and whether this provision is primarily aimed at hybrid marketplaces that mix first and third party offerings? If so, the legislation should be more clear on this point. 2) Notice and action: Notice and action provides a reliable and tested horizontal approach to moderate all kinds of third-party illegal content. Unfortunately, the e-Commerce Directive has not been implemented consistently across EU Member States, with only some adopting formal notice-and-takedown systems. An efficient and harmonised notice and action regime will allow platforms to combat illegal content at scale, without inappropriately taking on police or judicial functions. DSA comments: We welcome the DSA's intention to harmonise notice and action rules across the EU. However, a framework that has the intention to harmonise and lead to more efficiency in content moderation practices should be flexible enough not to overburden platforms, in particular small and medium-sized platforms, and account for the different ways of operation that are best suited for certain business models and size. In particular we see points for improvement and/or clarification in regards to the proposed: ● Framework to notices from individuals (Article 14.5): this provision aims to oblige the provider to respond 'without undue delay' to notices from individuals and entities informing them of our decision vis-a-vis their notice. While notices from individuals can be helpful and appropriate inputs to platform moderation procedures, it's important to understand that they can also be inaccurate and subject to abuse. For example, large rights holders may submit overly broad takedown requests, demanding legitimate goods be removed from our platform, or submit three notices in rapid succession in an attempt to get a seller permanently banned before the seller can practically respond. Platforms

are also seeing an increase in false or improper notices, either from shops seeking to harm competitors during peak season, malicious conduct, or mere disagreement regarding lawful content.

Platforms

are also seeing an increase in false or improper notices, either from shops seeking to harm competitors during peak season, malicious conduct, or mere disagreement regarding lawful content. Given our experience with the prevalence of competing sellers on a platform, those engaging in fraud, and simple mistakes by members of the public, we strongly urge policymakers to incorporate flexibility into the requirement to respond 'without undue delay' to account for the time and resource-intensive process required for a platform like ours to make a determination on each and every notice from an individual. We also receive notices alleging IP infringement that clearly contain invalid email addresses. In this respect, we believe we could potentially cut down on such abusive notices if a requirement to submit a notice from an individual under Article 14(2) would include a "verified" or "valid" email address. ● Requirement to provide a Statement of Reasons (Article 15): Following the experience and reasoning discussed above regarding notices by individuals, the requirement to "inform the recipient, at the latest at the time of the removal or disabling the access, of the decision and provide clear and specific reasons'' would undermine the flexibility needed to account for certain situations where such disclosures could undermine investigations or user privacy. For example, there are certain types of content that Etsy may temporarily disable pending human review, and there are certain situations in which Etsy may suspend a seller's account without notifying the affected seller (e.g. where fraud or other criminal behavior is detected) Thus, the DSA should exempt platforms from the requirement to provide a Statement of Reasons "without undue delay" in certain circumstances. Moreover, Article 15.4 would require us to publish each and every decision and Statement of Reasons in a publicly available database. We believe that there is a need to balance transparency and information that is in the public interest (e.g. to demonstrate that tackling illegal activity is a focus for the platform, that appropriate resources are allocated, and what categories of violative content are prevalent on a given platform) with feasibility (e.g. there may be limitations on the type of data collection and analysis available to platforms, particularly smaller platforms). To account for the capacities of smaller platforms, we believe that reporting aggregate data annually (e.g. X listing removals for Y reasons, Z appeals) would be a more proportionate measure.

To account for the capacities of smaller platforms, we believe that reporting aggregate data annually (e.g. X listing removals for Y reasons, Z appeals) would be a more proportionate measure. Moreover, it's not clear who the intended audience of this database would be. If regulatory authorities would benefit most, then we recommend that this should not be a public database, but rather that platforms may provide such information upon request. ● Framework for working with trusted flaggers (Article 19): We strongly believe that third party experts and brands are best positioned to identify illegal content, and therefore welcome the DSA's draft Article 19 allowing for a notice and action process with identified trusted flaggers. We agree that content flagged by such trusted flaggers can be more easily escalated for review, but also that the status of trusted flagger should be revoked if too many decisions/flags are overturned or otherwise indicate abuse of the flagging system. We'd like to highlight the importance of ensuring that the eligibility

criteria for trusted flagger status should be awarded to competent and authoritative entities that reflect expertise in a specific type of digital content and services. The proposal says that trusted flaggers should represent 'collective interests', which seems to imply that individual brands cannot attain the status of trusted flaggers. When it comes to intellectual property specifically, from our experience in working with brands, we strongly believe that they're best placed to know about their own intellectual property infringements and Article 19 should account for that. The collective entity could perhaps play an important role in verifying brands as trusted flaggers and making that information available to the platform. At the same time, we believe that Article 19 lacks a counter-notice process to prevent abusing the system to suppress legitimate competition. The provision says that a trusted flagger status can be revoked following an investigation by the Digital Services Coordinator. We want to ensure that we don't block legitimate, legal items from being sold. This is especially important for a platform like Etsy, where our sellers are primarily women-led businesses of one working out of their homes, and who depend on their sales to earn income. Suspending their accounts, even temporarily, may have a significant impact.

This is especially important for a platform like Etsy, where our sellers are primarily women-led businesses of one working out of their homes, and who depend on their sales to earn income. Suspending their accounts, even temporarily, may have a significant impact. Thus, counter-notices are the most effective means an Etsy seller may have to protect her business. In these circumstances where further dialogue with the trusted flagger will be needed, a platform like ours will need a certain level of flexibility to act on these notices. 3) Due diligence obligations: Platforms like Etsy make it easier for Europeans to start microbusinesses and access the global market. We nonetheless recognise that they have not only created new economic and creative opportunities, but - like many intermediary platforms - bad actors find ways to disseminate content and goods that violate Etsy or regulatory policies, including potentially products that have not been certified by product or consumer protection regulators. Well-defined, proportionate and flexible due diligence rules for online platforms are therefore key to ensure a trusted place to shop and transact online. DSA comments: We welcome the DSA's graduated approach on the basis of those services' size and impact. We believe that any new due diligence obligations placed on marketplaces should be proportionate to key features of the services we offer, our capabilities, knowledge, and the role we play in the market. Ultimately, this will ensure the efficiency of the systems we put in place to meet the intended goals of these provisions. To this end, we see points for improvement and/or clarification in regards to the proposed: ● Traceability of traders obligation (Article 22): We deem it reasonable to impose a KYBC obligation on marketplaces for their sellers, and this is something Etsy already takes very seriously. However, we believe that this provision should take into account pre-existing EU legislation in relation to KYC/KYB obligations that are already imposed on online platform operators so that the various legislative frameworks are mutually consistent and do not create a situation where operators are subject to laws that conflict with each other. This will ensure the efficiency of our systems in implementing Article to meet

the intended goal of a higher consumer protection and product safety standards.

This will ensure the efficiency of our systems in implementing Article to meet

the intended goal of a higher consumer protection and product safety standards. Moreover, any new "KYBC" measure must be privacy-friendly, proportionate and supported by the right infrastructure in order to enable automatic and scalable verifications, while enabling the small and microbusinesses we host to thrive. To this end, we believe the text should be amended to: ○ Clarify concept of 'trader': The concept of 'trader' seems to be broadly defined under draft Article 2(e), ranging from anyone using a service for any professional purpose, to casual hobbyists who sell crafts, etc. Requiring such detailed information from private individuals would create disincentives or make it more difficult to sell handmade goods on digital platforms and deter the formation of creative businesses. This concept also adds to a growing number of varying definitions for professional sellers in tax, consumer protection, and other legislative regimes in the EU and its member states, as well as worldwide. For the majority of our sellers, Etsy was the first place they sold their goods. In that way our platform really functions as an on-ramp to entrepreneurship for women around the globe. Moreover, if a user signs up on our platform as a business or as an individual, we should be able to rely on the self-identification of the trader as such in the assessment of whether they should be in the KYBC scope as we cannot be expected to possess the information required to make that determination on our own (e.g. a person's sales volume outside of our platform) or to take on any direct liability connected to it beyond our services (e.g. tax-related). For this reason, we call for Article 2(e) to clarify and specify that a 'trader' should only constitute those individuals or legal entities that transact for professional purposes in line with existing concepts under EU law. Article 22 should also specify that platforms can rely on the self-identification of the users as a trader. ○ Align with existing data collection, verification and reporting requirements: Platforms already experience challenges managing multiple bespoke information requests from different jurisdictions for tax information about their users. The soon to be adopted DAC 7 Directive, is a positive step in that it aims to provide a streamlined mechanism to facilitate information sharing with, and between, tax authorities.

The soon to be adopted DAC 7 Directive, is a positive step in that it aims to provide a streamlined mechanism to facilitate information sharing with, and between, tax authorities. However, meeting these requirements already requires significant legal and technical resources, an outcome that is challenging for our companies to manage and staff, never mind startups with much more limited resources and capacity. A completely different framework to collect and verify seller's data for the purpose of the DSA will put unnecessary and disproportionate strain on platforms like ours. From a business user perspective, having to provide similar data on multiple occasions during the customer experience is also likely to deter individuals from using the service, leading to decreased consumer choice. In order to make the DSA's Article 22 traceability requirement scaleable and workable for platforms, we request to align the collection, verification and

reporting requirements as much as possible to existing legislation (DAC 7 Directive). ○ Focus on high-volume traders: Reporting requirements should also be limited to platform sellers with revenues above a certain threshold, or at a minimum require a simplified KYBC procedure below a certain threshold (e.g. requiring less data collection, or at least no or limited verification). Absent such a threshold or simplified procedure, platforms would be forced to collect sensitive personal information at onboarding, a moment when our sellers may not trust our platform enough to share such personal information, and may be discouraged from opening a shop or transacting on our platforms at all. We strongly encourage such a threshold to include a combination of total revenues and number of transactions to ensure it does not capture casual, one time sellers. For example, the DAC 7 Directive referenced earlier provides for a 2000 EUR or 30 transactions in a year threshold. Article 22 should mandate traceability of high-volume sellers only or at a minimum require a simplified KYBC below a certain threshold. ○ Protect the privacy of sellers: Draft Article 22(6) includes a problematic disclosure requirement for a company such as Etsy, where the majority of our sellers are microbusinesses working out of their own homes, and thus their business address is also their home address. Mandating disclosure of such information would therefore undermine the ability of our platform to protect the personal data and privacy of our sellers.

Mandating disclosure of such information would therefore undermine the ability of our platform to protect the personal data and privacy of our sellers. Furthermore, platforms often work with third party providers or even divide their services between different legal entities. In practice, this means that a payments service provider or entity which is already running KYC on the platform's users may not be authorized by applicable privacy rules to share this data or broader KYC results with the main marketplace service provider. Article 22 should create a legal obligation for this information to be shared by third parties that the main provider is working with, where it can help said provider to comply with the DSA's KYBC obligations. Article 22(6) should therefore exclude mandating disclosures of certain data points (e.g. address) in certain circumstances (such as when the trader is an individual) or at least require to disclose the geographical address in line with the Omnibus Directive. A provision should also be added to allow KYC relevant data and results to be shared from payments entities and third parties working with the main service provider to comply more efficiently with the DSA. ○ Include flexibility in verification methods: draft Article 22(b) requires all traders to provide a "copy of identification document" to the platform. In order to enable automatic and scalable verifications, platforms need to be supported by the right infrastructure. For example, not all marketplaces have the means or expertise to unilaterally verify PDF documents. Based on our anti-money

laundering experience, it's also important to consider that documents are actually easier to falsify (especially scan copies) than online database records. Document collection is most often a means of last resort, only where we're unable to verify the identity of our sellers by other means. Nonetheless, this process of screening sellers against publicly available databases for KYB/C purposes can also be costly and operationally burdensome. For all these reasons, and taking into account the diversity in seller typology between different marketplaces, we believe that the best result will be achieved by empowering platforms with a certain risk-and capacity-based characteristics flexibility in data verification methods (e.g. manual verification, private databases). Article 22 should therefore allow for more flexibility in verifying our seller's identity beyond checking against a "copy of identification document".

manual verification, private databases). Article 22 should therefore allow for more flexibility in verifying our seller's identity beyond checking against a "copy of identification document". ○ Avoid or limit disclosing contact information of economic operators: draft Article 22 requires platforms to collect, verify and disclose "the name, address, telephone number and electronic mail address of the economic operator, within the meaning of Article 3(13) and Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020" (Market Surveillance Regulation). As of July 2021, our non-EU toy sellers will be required to appoint an EU economic operator which, in itself, is an extremely challenging compliance burden for microbusinesses to manage. The microbusinesses who sell on Etsy do not have the resources to find, appoint, or pay a representative based in the EU to manage their compliance obligations. When faced with this requirement, we believe that most will choose to no longer sell goods into the EU, reducing choice for EU consumers. The Etsy community, including non-EU sellers, fully supports efforts to ensure that consumer protections function in the global marketplace. However, such an obligation is simply not designed with home-based microbusinesses in mind, including the longstanding community of individual toymakers, and the proposal to require a platform to collect, verify and disclose the contact details of the economic operators under the DSA would unnecessarily erect burdens to entrepreneurship and selling cross-border. We would, for example, have to request such information at onboarding from individuals who are looking to start a business and open a shop on Etsy for the very first time, with the likelihood of discouraging them from doing so altogether. Enabling Etsy sellers to comply with EU legislation in a simplified manner will help these small businesses grow - all of which is more important than ever given the global pandemic, and the role that these microbusiness can serve to help rebuild local economies. In view of helping small businesses thrive, Article 22 should therefore not mandate the collection, verification and disclosure of the contact details of economic operators within the meaning of Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020. ● Transparency Reporting obligations for online platforms (Articles and 23): We believe that publicly reporting on our enforcement efforts builds trust in our marketplace and demonstrates our commitment to transparency and accountability. This is reflected in our

annual Transparency Report.

● Transparency Reporting obligations for online platforms (Articles and 23): We believe that publicly reporting on our enforcement efforts builds trust in our marketplace and demonstrates our commitment to transparency and accountability. This is reflected in our

annual Transparency Report. Etsy endeavors to balance transparency with the need to prevent bad actors from "gaming" detective controls. Providing specific details regarding automated control parameters may enable bad actors to evade detection. As previously stated, more specifically, we believe there is a need to balance transparency and information that is in the public interest with feasibility, particularly for smaller platforms. Small and medium-sized platforms like ours may also be limited in the frequency that they can feasibly publish such information. We are therefore concerned that: ○ the prescriptive nature of requirements under draft Articles and will not lead to a meaningful level of transparency that as intended by the DSA, and may in fact risk ill-intentioned users circumventing legitimate content moderation measures. While transparency around outcomes and actions is incredibly useful, we would caution against encouraging public transparency of enforcement methods as suggested by draft Article 23(1)(c), as bad actors iterate their own actions in response to enforcement efforts, and keeping these strategies confidential improves their effectiveness. Moreover, tools that may be effective for non-digital and non-standardised (handmade, artistic) products, are not necessarily effective for other products. ○ Draft Articles and also fail to clarify who the intended audience for these obligations are (e.g. users, regulatory authorities, researchers). In our experience, users experience more meaningful transparency through the messages a platform uses to communicate its decisions and functions, rather than having access to compiled figures and data with no context. Users will benefit most if they are able to understand the reasons for removal decisions, for example, or the factors weighed to determine search ranking. Take down volumes and appeal rates are data points where regulators would benefit most, compared to users who benefit most from understanding the decisions we take and how our policies are enforced. To this end, the burden to report information regarding our policies and measures may be assuaged by narrowing the scope of reporting obligations. For example, certain information currently not published in our annual Transparency Report may be provided with smaller groups (e.g. regulators) for specific cases and under certain circumstances.

To this end, the burden to report information regarding our policies and measures may be assuaged by narrowing the scope of reporting obligations. For example, certain information currently not published in our annual Transparency Report may be provided with smaller groups (e.g. regulators) for specific cases and under certain circumstances. ○ Moreover, on the basis of our experience and annual transparency reports, we generally caution against mandating frequent transparency reporting (e.g. more than once a year as suggested in draft Article 23) as this may require operational changes that may be too burdensome for smaller players. On Etsy, we experience a higher number of users around the holiday season (Q4) and this seasonal effect may be misconstrued if we were to publicly report more than once a year. ○ Lastly, according to draft Article 23(2) "online platforms shall publish, at least once every six months, information on the average monthly active recipients of the service in each Member State". Disclosing the average monthly active recipients in each Member State may harm competition and conflict with securities laws in various jurisdictions. Etsy, for example, currently only discloses such information in our core markets. Once again, we believe that the burden to report such information may be assuaged by narrowing down the scope of reporting obligations to provide such information to regulators only or at least as an aggregate number in the EU. Policymakers should consider which audience benefits most from such information in order to make this requirement the most relevant for both the platform and the intended audience. CONCLUSION Etsy is a trusted brand and we stand ready to work with lawmakers, trusted partners and authorities to ensure that shopping on online marketplaces is a safe experience for consumers. Let's protect consumers in a way that also enables small and microbusinesses to thrive For more information, please contact: Althea Erickson VP, Global Public Policy and Impact aerickson@etsy.com Laura Blanco EU Public Policy Manager lblanco@etsy.com

In allegato le valutazioni di Confcommercio - Imprese per l'Italia sul Digital Services Act

Contributo sulla proposta di regolamento Digital Service Act La proposta di regolamento COM (2020) 825 final, cosiddetto Digital Services Act (DSA) rappresenta un significativo passo in avanti nella direzione di contrastare in maniera omogenea alcune delle evidenti problematiche connesse al funzionamento e all'uso di servizi digitali consentendo a imprese, professionisti, acquirenti e utenti di trarre beneficio da un mercato digitale più equo e competitivo.

Commenti generali DSA Responsabilità dei prestatori di servizi intermediari Riferimenti DSA: articoli 3, 4, 5, 7 È condivisibile il principio che i prestatori di servizi intermediari, qualora non abbiano un ruolo attivo sui contenuti che trasmettono o memorizzano (selezione destinatario, modifica informazioni, ecc.), non siano considerati responsabili di tali informazioni, né sia loro imposto un obbligo generale di sorveglianza sulle informazioni, o di accertare attivamente fatti o circostanze che indichino la presenza di attività illegali. Vanno tuttavia attentamente valutati i limiti e le condizioni di tale assenza di responsabilità e di sorveglianza che deve necessariamente trovare riscontro in una effettiva disponibilità dell'intermediario online ad intervenire, in seguito a motivate segnalazioni, al fine di non ledere gli interessi degli utenti di tali servizi di intermediazione. In particolare gli operatori commerciali soffrono l'assenza di una seppur minima forma di filtro che consenta la veridicità dei contenuti online a tutela anche degli stessi utenti finali, tema evidente nel caso della ristorazione ma non limitato a tale comparto, sono infatti noti i casi di "commentifici" che vendono recensioni fasulle. E gli operatori commerciali segnalano inoltre la difficoltà di ottenere un intervento da parte dell'intermediario online laddove quanto comunicato dall'utente finale, nel recensire, risulti non tollerabile per l'essere palesemente errato. "Muro di gomma" è l'espressione con cui viene metaforicamente descritto il servizio di assistenza delle piattaforme per l'atteggiamento mostrato nei confronti delle richieste degli operatori commerciali di identificare l'autore di un contenuto falso o di rimuovere tale contenuto dalla piattaforma.

Si consideri poi che gli stessi intermediari online potrebbero persino trarre un beneficio dal non porre alcun tipo di freno alle recensioni più esagerate (e pertanto errate) in quanto queste, rese più notiziabili dall'esagerazione, ad esempio parlare di "bomba d'acqua" per descrivere un temporale, potrebbero tradursi in vantaggi in termini di visualizzazione e valorizzazione economica degli spazi pubblicitari. Ciò però avverrebbe a spese degli operatori commerciali, oltre che degli stessi utenti finali, in quanto l'informazione errata, per rimanere all'esempio merceologico citato, avrebbe pesanti e negative ripercussioni sulle prenotazioni presso le strutture ricettive. I condivisibili principi di non responsabilità e di assenza di un obbligo generale di sorveglianza per le informazioni trasmesse, previsti dagli articoli 3-5 e 7 del DSA, dovrebbero allora essere vincolati a una effettiva disponibilità dell'intermediario a intervenire ove riceva dall'operatore commerciale segnalazioni precise, motivate e ragionevoli su contenuti e attività illegali. Più in generale il principio di non responsabilità sulle informazioni trasmesse e memorizzate, e le condizioni alle quali è possibile continuare ad affermarlo, andrebbero valutati anche alla luce di una diffusa abitudine degli intermediari online a chiamarsi sempre e comunque fuori da ogni responsabilità, anche per le parti di attività in cui, invece, dovrebbe essere chiaro come il loro ruolo debba tradursi in più responsabilità.

Ordine di contrastare i contenuti illegali Riferimenti DSA: articoli 8 e 9 È di grande interesse quanto disposto dagli articoli 8 e 9 del DSA, è cioè imporre l'obbligo per i prestatori di servizi intermediari, in relazione agli ordini delle autorità amministrative nazionali, di contrastare i contenuti illegali e di fornire informazioni. Occorrerebbe tuttavia chiarire, nel caso dell'ordinamento italiano, quali autorità amministrative sarebbero competenti per il contrasto ai contenuti illegali e con quali tempi di intervento. Qualora nei fatti occorresse ricorrere in via prevalente alle autorità giudiziarie, la misura, per via dei lunghi tempi che sarebbero necessari, non risulterebbe coerente con la rapidità con cui i contenuti si diffondono in rete e possono drasticamente minare la reputazione di un operatore commerciale.

Notifica e segnalatori attendibili Riferimenti DSA: articoli 14 e 19

Prevedere meccanismi che consentano di notificare la presenza di contenuti illegali e l'obbligo di trattare con priorità le notifiche dei segnalatori attendibili (tra le condizioni il rappresentare interessi collettivi e l'essere indipendenti dalle piattaforme online) sono misure di grande rilevanza. Si sottolinea però l'esigenza di garantire semplicità della procedura di segnalazione, tempestività e diligenza dell'azione da parte dell'intermediario online anche laddove le segnalazioni provengano da utenti commerciali. Come si evince anche dalle motivazioni che accompagnano la proposta di regolamento, spesso emerge insoddisfazione in merito alla risposta degli operatori digitali alle segnalazioni di merci e servizi illegali o dannosi, ai meccanismi di comunicazione adottati e si indicano discrepanze tra politiche dichiarate dagli intermediari e azioni intraprese.

Motivazione e gestione dei reclami Riferimenti DSA: articoli 15 e 17 L'obbligo di fornire motivazione e di istituire un sistema di gestione dei reclami in merito alle decisioni adottate dalle piattaforme online su presunti contenuti illegali o incompatibili con le condizioni generali del servizio sono misure fondamentali per consentire agli operatori di individuare prontamente eventuali non conformità e attivare le più idonee misure correttive. Così come garantirebbero una maggiore tutela degli operatori commerciali nei confronti delle decisioni della piattaforma. Nella pratica, infatti, gli operatori intervistati1 segnalano come la sospensione degli account possa avvenire senza opportuno preavviso e adeguate motivazioni, rendendo difficile per le imprese l'individuazione delle più idonee azioni correttive (ad es. laddove la sospensione derivi dalla segnalazione di terzi, il non sapere da dove è originata la motivazione della sospensione può rappresentare un ostacolo alla sua soluzione). Si aggiunge la non sempre adeguata comunicazione da parte delle piattaforme delle eventuali modifiche ai propri termini e condizioni, o l'assenza di un dovuto preavviso, che possono portare gli utenti commerciali delle piattaforme online a scoprire di non essere conformi a un eventuale aggiornamento delle condizioni solo a valle di una sospensione dell'account. La sospensione dell'account, inoltre, la cui durata può essere anche molto estesa può comportare l'inibizione alla vendita dei prodotti, il congelamento dei fondi sull'account e, per chi utilizza i servizi logistici della piattaforma, vi è il blocco 1 Le problematiche segnalate dagli operatori fanno riferimento al rapporto con il marketplace Amazon ma alcune di esse, come il non fornire sempre adeguate motivazioni in merito a una non conformità, sono valide anche nel caso di altre piattaforme e laddove l'intermediazione riguardi la vendita di servizi.

della merce in magazzino (non può pertanto essere venduta altrove), nonostante la piattaforma continui a fatturare il costo dello spazio. Queste restrizioni, comprese le soglie di performance oltre le quali si cade in una non conformità (che non si adattano, con soglie percentuali più elevate, in considerazione di chi vende pochi quantitativi) e la mancata chiarezza di alcuni motivi causa di non conformità, assieme alle modalità e tempi per la gestione della problematica emersa, vengono reputate eccessive. E rischiano, in particolare l'inibizione all'attività di vendita, di portare al collasso le imprese che operano sul marketplace in quando queste, per rispettare gli stringenti criteri di performance imposti, si sono necessariamente dovute strutturare (personale, magazzino ), con un appesantimento della struttura dei costi non sostenibile in caso di stop prolungato. full_text:
IBM welcomes the opportunity to give feedback on the Commission's proposal for a Digital Services Act (DSA).

As a global Business-to-Business (B2B) technology company with a significant European footprint, IBM plays a key role in the digital transformation of Europe's industry, enabling our clients to benefit from the power of data.

IBM believes that digital services providers should be responsible for the societal impact of their platforms: this has become an even greater imperative at a time when the use of digital technologies has accelerated amidst the ongoing COVID-19 crisis and will be an essential part in the recovery of our society and economy.

Therefore, IBM welcomes the proposal for a DSA. We fully support the Commission's targeted approach requiring different rules for different categories of services to tackle illegal content online, particularly when content is disseminated to the public, something IBM has long called for.

We believe this proposal is an important starting point to build greater trust in technology and can offer an opportunity for Europe to champion online responsibility and accountability, while allowing digital businesses to continue to grow and innovate.

Please find attached our full contribution to this feedback process.

DIGITAL SERVICES ACT (DSA)

IBM'S POSITION PAPER MARCH 2021

IBM a multinational technology company serving clients in over 170 countries. With more than 100 years of commitment in Europe, IBM is one of the largest technology employers in the EU and has many cloud data centers, research labs, innovation spaces, centers of excellence, etc. spread across Europe. IBM scientists from 50+ nationalities work in Europe on cutting-edge research and IBM will build Europe's first quantum computer in Germany.

IBM's expertise is in the intersection of technology and business, providing artificial intelligence (AI) and cloud-based solutions that are changing the way the world works. Above all, guided by principles for trust and transparency and support for a more inclusive society, IBM is committed to being a responsible technology innovator and a force for good in the world. For more information, visit www.ibm.com.

INTRODUCTION As a global Business-to-Business (B2B) technology company with a significant European footprint, IBM plays a key role in the digital transformation of Europe's industry, enabling our clients to benefit from the power of data. Cloud technologies, AI, Blockchain, IoT, and data analytics will continue to be crucial to increase the resilience of key sectors in Europe's economies and build technological sovereignty. With greater digitization comes greater responsibility: IBM believes that the safety of users online is paramount and we have earned the trust of our clients by responsibly managing their most valuable data, committing to our Trust and Transparency principles, ensuring that we can protect client data and insights, and preventing illegal content from spreading across the Internet. Digital services providers should be responsible for the societal impact of their platforms: this has become an even greater imperative at a time when the use of digital technologies has accelerated amidst the ongoing COVID-19 crisis and will be an essential part in the recovery of our society and economy. Therefore, IBM welcomes the European Commission's proposal for a Digital Services Act (DSA). We are pleased the Commission adopted a "precision regulation" approach that is focused clearly on placing more responsibility on the relevant platforms to tackle illegal content online, something IBM has long called for. We believe this proposal is an important starting point to build greater trust in technology and can offer an opportunity for Europe to champion online responsibility and accountability, while allowing digital businesses to continue to grow and innovate.

IBM'S COMMENTS ON THE DIGITAL SERVICES ACT

1. Maintaining a differentiated scope and limited liability for hosting services:

Companies providing online services to individuals and whose content is being disseminated to the public should be responsible for the societal effects those services can have, including facilitating criminal and terrorist activity and impacts on children and on elections: therefore, we fully support the Commission's targeted approach, creating a new "online platform" category and requiring different rules for different categories of services:

• The term "digital services" broadly encompasses today a large number of companies, business models, or services, many of whom play little to no role in the proliferation of illegal content online. For example, the business model of "pure" B2B services providers set them apart from the large platforms operating in the

consumer space. They deliver services designed to increase the efficiency and agility of businesses and processes of their enterprise clients, They do not offer content sharing services for end-consumers or the general public, and therefore do not have the ability to control, edit or curate user-generated content that may appear online.

• This is why passive intermediaries such as mere conduit, caching or passive hosting services, particularly B2B services, should continue to benefit from intermediary liability exemptions, and should not be subject to the same enhanced content moderation obligations as online platforms and very large online platforms (VLOPs).

• We support maintaining such differentiation in the scope of the DSA, consistent with recent EU legislation such as the Terrorist Content Online Regulation: a one-size-fits-all approach that would impose the same rules on all digital services would create disproportionate burden for many businesses particularly in the B2B sector. Such an approach would limit the uptake of cloud and emerging technologies across businesses, particularly SMEs. This could limit innovation in the EU and damage the broader data economy, as well as Europe's technological sovereignty.

2. Focus on illegal content:

We also support the Commission's approach and believe that regulatory efforts should focus on acting against illegal content (Article 8). Indeed, we believe that harmful content should be tackled separately, such as through voluntary or co-regulatory approaches. In practice, IBM reserves the right to take measures against customers whose activities might not be illegal but may cause harm: our cloud services agreement1 sets out various restrictions on how our services may be used: "Cloud Services may not be used for unlawful, harmful, obscene, offensive, or fraudulent Content or activity. Examples of prohibited activities are advocating or causing harm, interfering with or violating the integrity or security of a network or system, evading filters, sending unsolicited, abusive, or deceptive messages, introducing viruses or harmful code, or violating third party rights".

This broad language gives us the flexibility, in appropriate circumstances, to request our clients, if we believe they have violated the terms of our agreement, to remove legal, yet harmful, content. We also reserve the right to suspend/terminate the services if the client fails to remove such content.

1 https://www.ibm.com/support/customer/csol/contractexplorer/cloud/csa/be-en/11

3. No general monitoring obligation:

We support the prohibition of a monitoring obligation (Article 7). This is particularly important for B2B service providers (e.g. Cloud service providers) like IBM, who generally have no contractual rights and no technical access to content that enterprise customers store or process on our services. Only the enterprise customers have absolute control and responsibility over their own content and the services they operate.

General monitoring of cloud content would be a complex undertaking, requiring us to reengineer our service offering, and would also pose significant privacy issues should we be required to monitor personal, financial and medical data of potentially millions of data subjects, as well as the content of corporations and governments. Such a monitoring obligation would disincentivize business customers from moving to the cloud.

4. Know your Business Customer (KYBC):

We support the Commission's approach, limiting KYBC obligations to online platforms that allow consumers to conclude distant contracts with traders (Article 22).

We would specifically caution policymakers against expanding the proposed scope of these KYBC provisions and requiring that such obligations should be horizontally implemented by all digital services beyond online platforms: the objective of KYBC obligations is first and foremost to ensure consumers are protected against dishonest businesses selling illegal products online, therefore such rules should first take into account the role of digital services that are an active party in the provision of a B2C goods or services.

However, the provision of core services to regulated sectors such as operators of essential services depends entirely on the ability to provide robust cloud solutions that are neither designed nor intended to/directed at consumers. Many times, enterprise cloud-based solutions are offered on a "Pay as You Go" principle, which has contributed to the success of the cloud, particularly among small businesses and developers, hence the need to safeguard the smoothness and speed of online business operations.

Many B2B cloud services already implement strong safeguards to prevent fraudulent businesses from using our cloud services (e.g., contractual obligations in our service contracts, security-based services against fraud). Additional and disproportionate KY BC requirements may not only raise privacy and/or business confidentiality concerns, but could discourage companies, particularly SMEs and start-ups, from moving to the cloud, if held up from accessing services pending clearance.

SPECIFIC ISSUES IN CONTENT MODERATION RELATING TO B2B CLOUD SERVICES AS THEY ARE PROVIDED TO BUSI NESS CLIENTS

Client data and the insights produced on IBM's Cloud or from IBM's AI are owned by IBM's clients. This is a core feature of our business model. As a provider of B2B cloud services, this is an essential difference between business models and services like ours, and consumer-oriented services such as social media platforms; video streaming services; or video, image, audio or file sharing services.

Because our clients' data belong to our clients, we cannot remove specific content on our customers' websites, do not deploy any tools to monitor our clients' content and do not have the ability to identify illegal content ourselves. Only our business customers have absolute control and responsibility over their own content and the services they operate.

Our limitations to tackle illegal content are both technical and contractual:

§ Technical: IBM does not have control over its clients' data. Additionally, clients may, and often do, choose to encrypt their data on our cloud infrastructure. We give our clients the ability to keep the encryption key and we do not have any access for security and privacy reasons.

§ Contractual: our cloud services agreement2 limits the potential scope of IBM's access to, or use of, the client's content. In practice, this is a very limited right to access, and we do not have the right to monitor or modify the content: o "Content Content consists of all data, software, and information that Client or its authorized users provides, authorizes access to, or inputs to IBM Cloud Services. o Client grants the rights and permissions to IBM, its affiliates, and contractors of either, to use, provide, store, and otherwise process Content solely for the purpose of providing the IBM Cloud Services. o Use of the IBM Cloud Services will not affect Client's ownership or license rights in Content. o IBM, its affiliates, and contractors of either, will access and use the Content solely for the purpose of providing and managing the IBM Cloud Service. o IBM will treat Content as confidential by only disclosing to IBM employees and contractors to the extent necessary to provide the IBM Cloud Services." Altering contracts to allow IBM access to content for monitoring purposes would be very likely to discourage businesses from moving to the cloud for security and privacy reasons.

2 https://www.ibm.com/support/customer/csol/contractexplorer/cloud/csa/be-en/11

As a responsible technology company, we do, however, have "notice and action" processes in place to tackle illegal usage of our services (as outlined in our Acceptable Use Policy3), which are as follows:

• If we are made aware of the presence of illegal content on a client website, our abuse department will first assess the validity of the complaint from the content that is on the public website (NB: as IBM does not have any control over its business customers' data, it can only "see" what is visible on the public Internet and can only identify and inform the customer with whom IBM has a contractual relationship, who may be the party responsible for managing this content).

• If the complaint is deemed valid, IBM will notify our customer asking the content to be removed expeditiously (or ask our customer to instruct their customer to remove it). If the customer fails to remove the content or to have it removed by the person/entity who uploaded it, according to the notified timeframe, IBM will suspend the service or block access to the server for that particular customer (NB: as IBM does not have the ability to remove the specific content directly, the only option is to shut down the server in its entirety).

Regarding the nature of the content itself, the vast majority of the complaints we receive involve content infringes a trademark or copyright (IP) of a third party. Most of the time (well over 90%) the actual publisher of the infringing content is not a direct customer of ours, but rather a customer of one of our customers 3 https://www.ibm.com/services/us/imc/html/aup1.html

Therefore, IBM welcomes the proposal for a DSA. We fully support the Commission's targeted approach requiring different rules for different categories of services to tackle illegal content online, particularly when content is disseminated to the public, something IBM has long called for. We believe this proposal is an important starting point to build greater trust in technology and can offer an opportunity for Europe to champion online responsibility and accountability, while allowing digital businesses to continue to grow and innovate. IBM'S POSITION PAPER MARCH 2021

IBM a multinational technology company serving clients in over 170 countries. With more than 100 years of commitment in Europe, IBM is one of the largest technology employers in the EU and has many cloud data centers, research labs, innovation spaces, centers of excellence, etc. spread across Europe. IBM scientists from 50+ nationalities work in Europe on cutting-edge research and IBM will build Europe's first quantum computer in Germany. IBM's expertise is in the intersection of technology and business, providing artificial intelligence (AI) and cloud-based solutions that are changing the way the world works. Above all, guided by principles for trust and transparency and support for a more inclusive society, IBM is committed to being a responsible technology innovator and a force for good in the world. For more information, visit www.ibm.com. INTRODUCTION As a global Business-to-Business (B2B) technology company with a significant European footprint, IBM plays a key role in the digital transformation of Europe's industry, enabling our clients to benefit from the power of data. Cloud technologies, AI, Blockchain, IoT, and data analytics will continue to be crucial to increase the resilience of key sectors in Europe's economies and build technological sovereignty.

Cloud technologies, AI, Blockchain, IoT, and data analytics will continue to be crucial to increase the resilience of key sectors in Europe's economies and build technological sovereignty. With greater digitization comes greater responsibility: IBM believes that the safety of users online is paramount and we have earned the trust of our clients by responsibly managing their most valuable data, committing to our Trust and Transparency principles, ensuring that we can protect client data and insights, and preventing illegal content from spreading across the Internet. Digital services providers should be responsible for the societal impact of their platforms: this has become an even greater imperative at a time when the use of digital technologies has accelerated amidst the ongoing COVID-19 crisis and will be an essential part in the recovery of our society and economy. Therefore, IBM welcomes the European Commission's proposal for a Digital Services Act (DSA). We are pleased the Commission adopted a "precision regulation" approach that is focused clearly on placing more responsibility on the relevant platforms to tackle illegal content online, something IBM has long called for. We believe this proposal is an important starting point to build greater trust in technology and can offer an opportunity for Europe to champion online responsibility and accountability, while allowing digital businesses to continue to grow and innovate. IBM'S COMMENTS ON THE DIGITAL SERVICES ACT

1. Maintaining a differentiated scope and limited liability for hosting services:

Companies providing online services to individuals and whose content is being disseminated to the public should be responsible for the societal effects those services can have, including facilitating criminal and terrorist activity and impacts on children and on elections: therefore, we fully support the Commission's targeted approach, creating a new "online platform" category and requiring different rules for different categories of services:

• The term "digital services" broadly encompasses today a large number of companies, business models, or services, many of whom play little to no role in the proliferation of illegal content online. For example, the business model of "pure" B2B services providers set them apart from the large platforms operating in the

consumer space.

For example, the business model of "pure" B2B services providers set them apart from the large platforms operating in the

consumer space. They deliver services designed to increase the efficiency and agility of businesses and processes of their enterprise clients, They do not offer content sharing services for end-consumers or the general public, and therefore do not have the ability to control, edit or curate user-generated content that may appear online. • This is why passive intermediaries such as mere conduit, caching or passive hosting services, particularly B2B services, should continue to benefit from intermediary liability exemptions, and should not be subject to the same enhanced content moderation obligations as online platforms and very large online platforms (VLOPs). • We support maintaining such differentiation in the scope of the DSA, consistent with recent EU legislation such as the Terrorist Content Online Regulation: a one-size-fits-all approach that would impose the same rules on all digital services would create disproportionate burden for many businesses particularly in the B2B sector. Such an approach would limit the uptake of cloud and emerging technologies across businesses, particularly SMEs. This could limit innovation in the EU and damage the broader data economy, as well as Europe's technological sovereignty. 2. Focus on illegal content:

We also support the Commission's approach and believe that regulatory efforts should focus on acting against illegal content (Article 8). Indeed, we believe that harmful content should be tackled separately, such as through voluntary or co-regulatory approaches. In practice, IBM reserves the right to take measures against customers whose activities might not be illegal but may cause harm: our cloud services agreement1 sets out various restrictions on how our services may be used: "Cloud Services may not be used for unlawful, harmful, obscene, offensive, or fraudulent Content or activity. Examples of prohibited activities are advocating or causing harm, interfering with or violating the integrity or security of a network or system, evading filters, sending unsolicited, abusive, or deceptive messages, introducing viruses or harmful code, or violating third party rights". This broad language gives us the flexibility, in appropriate circumstances, to request our clients, if we believe they have violated the terms of our agreement, to remove legal, yet harmful, content. We also reserve the right to suspend/terminate the services if the client fails to remove such content. 1 https://www.ibm.com/support/customer/csol/contractexplorer/cloud/csa/be-en/11

We also reserve the right to suspend/terminate the services if the client fails to remove such content. 1 https://www.ibm.com/support/customer/csol/contractexplorer/cloud/csa/be-en/11

3. No general monitoring obligation:

We support the prohibition of a monitoring obligation (Article 7). This is particularly important for B2B service providers (e.g. Cloud service providers) like IBM, who generally have no contractual rights and no technical access to content that enterprise customers store or process on our services. Only the enterprise customers have absolute control and responsibility over their own content and the services they operate. General monitoring of cloud content would be a complex undertaking, requiring us to reengineer our service offering, and would also pose significant privacy issues should we be required to monitor personal, financial and medical data of potentially millions of data subjects, as well as the content of corporations and governments. Such a monitoring obligation would disincentivize business customers from moving to the cloud. 4. Know your Business Customer (KYBC):

We support the Commission's approach, limiting KYBC obligations to online platforms that allow consumers to conclude distant contracts with traders (Article 22). We would specifically caution policymakers against expanding the proposed scope of these KYBC provisions and requiring that such obligations should be horizontally implemented by all digital services beyond online platforms: the objective of KYBC obligations is first and foremost to ensure consumers are protected against dishonest businesses selling illegal products online, therefore such rules should first take into account the role of digital services that are an active party in the provision of a B2C goods or services. However, the provision of core services to regulated sectors such as operators of essential services depends entirely on the ability to provide robust cloud solutions that are neither designed nor intended to/directed at consumers. Many times, enterprise cloud-based solutions are offered on a "Pay as You Go" principle, which has contributed to the success of the cloud, particularly among small businesses and developers, hence the need to safeguard the smoothness and speed of online business operations. Many B2B cloud services already implement strong safeguards to prevent fraudulent businesses from using our cloud services (e.g., contractual obligations in our service contracts, security-based services against fraud). Additional and disproportionate KY BC requirements may not only raise privacy and/or business confidentiality concerns, but could discourage companies, particularly SMEs and start-ups, from moving to the cloud, if held up from accessing services pending clearance.

SPECIFIC ISSUES IN CONTENT MODERATION RELATING TO B2B CLOUD SERVICES AS THEY ARE PROVIDED TO BUSI NESS CLIENTS

Client data and the insights produced on IBM's Cloud or from IBM's AI are owned by IBM's clients. This is a core feature of our business model. As a provider of B2B cloud services, this is an essential difference between business models and services like ours, and consumer-oriented services such as social media platforms; video streaming services; or video, image, audio or file sharing services. Because our clients' data belong to our clients, we cannot remove specific content on our customers' websites, do not deploy any tools to monitor our clients' content and do not have the ability to identify illegal content ourselves. Only our business customers have absolute control and responsibility over their own content and the services they operate. Our limitations to tackle illegal content are both technical and contractual:

§ Technical: IBM does not have control over its clients' data. Additionally, clients may, and often do, choose to encrypt their data on our cloud infrastructure. We give our clients the ability to keep the encryption key and we do not have any access for security and privacy reasons. § Contractual: our cloud services agreement2 limits the potential scope of IBM's access to, or use of, the client's content. In practice, this is a very limited right to access, and we do not have the right to monitor or modify the content: o "Content Content consists of all data, software, and information that Client or its authorized users provides, authorizes access to, or inputs to IBM Cloud Services. o Client grants the rights and permissions to IBM, its affiliates, and contractors of either, to use, provide, store, and otherwise process Content solely for the purpose of providing the IBM Cloud Services. o Use of the IBM Cloud Services will not affect Client's ownership or license rights in Content. o IBM, its affiliates, and contractors of either, will access and use the Content solely for the purpose of providing and managing the IBM Cloud Service.

o Use of the IBM Cloud Services will not affect Client's ownership or license rights in Content. o IBM, its affiliates, and contractors of either, will access and use the Content solely for the purpose of providing and managing the IBM Cloud Service. o IBM will treat Content as confidential by only disclosing to IBM employees and contractors to the extent necessary to provide the IBM Cloud Services." Altering contracts to allow IBM access to content for monitoring purposes would be very likely to discourage businesses from moving to the cloud for security and privacy reasons. 2 https://www.ibm.com/support/customer/csol/contractexplorer/cloud/csa/be-en/11

As a responsible technology company, we do, however, have "notice and action" processes in place to tackle illegal usage of our services (as outlined in our Acceptable Use Policy3), which are as follows:

• If we are made aware of the presence of illegal content on a client website, our abuse department will first assess the validity of the complaint from the content that is on the public website (NB: as IBM does not have any control over its business customers' data, it can only "see" what is visible on the public Internet and can only identify and inform the customer with whom IBM has a contractual relationship, who may be the party responsible for managing this content). • If the complaint is deemed valid, IBM will notify our customer asking the content to be removed expeditiously (or ask our customer to instruct their customer to remove it). If the customer fails to remove the content or to have it removed by the person/entity who uploaded it, according to the notified timeframe, IBM will suspend the service or block access to the server for that particular customer (NB: as IBM does not have the ability to remove the specific content directly, the only option is to shut down the server in its entirety). Regarding the nature of the content itself, the vast majority of the complaints we receive involve content infringes a trademark or copyright (IP) of a third party. Most of the time (well over 90%) the actual publisher of the infringing content is not a direct customer of ours, but rather a customer of one of our customers 3 https://www.ibm.com/services/us/imc/html/aup1.html

Der DFL Deutsche Fußball Liga e.V. ist der Zusammenschluss der 36 Profifußballclubs der Bundesliga und 2. Bundesliga. In seinem Auftrag organisiert die DFL Deutsche Fußball Liga GmbH die Ligawettbewerbe und vermarktet die Bundesliga und 2. Bundesliga. Hierzu zählt insbesondere die Vermarktung der audiovisuellen Medienrechte an den Spielen der zwei obersten Spielklassen des deutschen Fußballs.

Die DFL hat im September 2020 an der öffentlichen Konsultation zum Gesetzgebungspaket um das „Gesetz über digitale Dienste“ teilgenommen und dargelegt, wie die Finanzierung des Sports in hohem Maße von der Nutzung und dem Schutz seiner geistigen Eigentumsrechte gerade im Umfeld digitaler Dienste abhängt. In unserer Stellungnahme haben wir auf die Besonderheiten der Verwertung von Sportveranstaltungen und die erforderlichen Maßnahmen für eine effektivere Bekämpfung von illegalen Sport-Inhalten im Umfeld digitaler Dienste hingewiesen. Zu den Besonderheiten des Sports gehört insbesondere das Live-Element. Dementsprechend stellt sich die wirtschaftliche Verwertbarkeit einer Sportveranstaltung als ein Recht dar, das sich in Form einer zeitlich eng begrenzten Gelegenheit präsentiert. Live-Rechte und Near Live-Rechte bilden somit den Kern unserer Wertschöpfung und sind die existenzsichernde Einnahmequelle des Fußballs. Diese Rechte sind zunehmend bedroht durch die Existenz von rechtverletzenden Webseiten (Aggregatoren-Webseiten und Live-Streaming-Dienste) und die Anonymität der Betreiber solcher Dienste. 

Aufgrund des besonderen Charakters audiovisueller Sport-Inhalte ist die Durchsetzung eigener Rechte für Sportveranstalter in Echtzeit von existenzieller Bedeutung. Die bisherigen Regelungsvorschläge der Kommission vom 15.12.2020 für ein „Gesetz über digitale Dienste“ (DSA) berücksichtigen die Betroffenheit des Sports nur unzureichend. 

Aus Sicht der DFL sind folgende Anpassungen dringend erforderlich: 

(1) Ausweitung des Anwendungsbereichs von Art. 14: Um die Verbreitung illegaler Live-Inhalte wirksam und schnell zu unterbinden, bedarf es einer Verpflichtung zur Bereitstellung eines gesonderten Abhilfeverfahrens für live/near-live übertragene Sport-Inhalte in Echtzeit (spätestens 30 Minuten nach Eingang einer Meldung), ggf. speziell für vertrauenswürdige Hinweisgeber im Sinne von Artikel 19. Zudem sollte diese Verpflichtung nicht nur Hosting-Diensteanbieter (einschließlich Online-Plattformen) treffen, sondern auch solche Intermediäre, die nur die Vermittlung zu solchen Hosting-Angeboten ermöglichen. 

(2) Erweiterung des Erwggrd. 46 und des Art. 19: Eine rein horizontale Regelung für vertrauenswürdige Hinweisgeber reicht nicht aus. Die Besonderheiten der betroffenen Inhalte (insb. live/near-live) sollten stärker berücksichtigt werden. Zum einen sollten auch einzelne Rechteinhaber, die ihre Lizenznehmer kennen, den Status des vertrauenswürdigen Hinweisgebers erhalten können. Die Anforderung, dass Hinweisgeber kollektive Interessen verfolgen müssen, ist weder erforderlich noch zielführend. Zum anderen sollten nicht nur Online-Plattformen, sondern sämtliche Hosting-Diensteanbieter verpflichtend solche Hinweisgebersysteme vorhalten müssen, um auch bei diesen Diensten eine effektive Rechtsdurchsetzung (insb. im Fall von IP-Verletzungen) zu gewährleisten. 

(3) Erweiterung von Art. 22: Grundsätzlich ist der Vorschlag zur Verbesserung der Nachverfolgbarkeit von Unternehmen zu begrüßen. Es sollten aber zusätzliche Informationspflichten für alle Diensteanbieter vorgesehen werden. Neben Online-Plattformen müssten auch alle anderen Online-Vermittlungsdienste (z.B. Live-Streaming-Dienste) entsprechende Informationspflichten erfüllen, um eine Nachverfolgbarkeit strukturell rechtsverletzender Webseiten überhaupt erst möglich zu machen. 

Entsprechende Anpassungen wurden kürzlich durch eine Studie des Rechtsausschusses im Europäischen Parlament bestätigt („Challenges facing sports event organisers in the digital environment – A legal analysis“).

full_text:
www.efpia.eu 1

EFPIA POSITION PAPER ON THE DIGITAL SERVICES ACT

The European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA) represents the biopharmaceutical industry operating in Europe. Through its direct membership of 36 national associations, 39 leading pharmaceutical companies and a growing number of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), EFPIA's mission is to create a collaborative environment that enables our members to innovate, discover, develop and deliver new therapies and vaccines for people across Europe, as well as contribute to the European economy. More information on EFPIA can be found on our website https://www.efpia.eu/.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

- EFPIA welcomes the publication by the European Commission of the proposal for a Regulation on a Single Market for Digital Services (Digital Services Act or the DSA).

- Beyond the numerous provisions already outlined in the European Commission's proposal, EFPIA believes there are additional targeted measures needed to be taken to guarantee the protection of EU citizens against illicit/counterfeit medicines.

- It is very clear that everything which is forbidden offline should also be forbidden online. This principle should rule the entire DSA.

- In particular, EFPIA recommends the following measures be included in the DSA, as a means to further safeguard the health and safety of EU citizens:

o Introduction of a broader "KYBC" (Know Your Business Customer) principle, even truer for dangerous illegal content § "KYBC" requirements should apply to all providers of intermediary services § "KYBC" requirements should especially apply to domain names' registrars

o Introduction of binding obligations for all online intermediaries to avoid providing illegal content, at least for dangerous illegal content (general obligations should apply for all intermediaries, including small ones)

o Introduction of requirement for information sharing on delisted content, at least for dangerous illegal content (with the consumer/patient, the concerned pharmaceutical manufacturer and the law enforcement authorities)

- EFPIA continues to call for a safer Internet for EU citizens and a fair environment for genuine business activities to progress. With the below contribution to the consultation on the Digital Services Act, we reiterate our commitment to work towards achieving these objectives.

www.efpia.eu 2

I. CURRENT CONTEXT AND EFPIA'S GENERAL COMMENTS:

EFPIA members would like first and foremost to re-anchor the remind that illicit, substandard and falsified products have on patient safety and, overall, society. They seriously harm or kill patients, challenge healthcare systems and undermine people's trust in quality medicines. In the context of a global pandemic and vaccination campaign, we believe that this point should be high on the EU legislator's mind when drafting this Regulation. We have learned, even more in the current period, that trust is the key of a successful health strategy.

To give a worldwide context to the magnitude of the issue, according to the OECD/EUIPO (2019) study, the value of global trade in counterfeit pharmaceuticals was up to USD 4.4 billion in 2016 and direct and indirect job losses are estimated at more than 80 000 jobs in the EU1.

EFPIA, therefore, appreciates the Commission's great progress and achievement in this area especially regarding the proposal for a Regulation on a Single Market for Digital Services (Digital Services Act or the DSA).

This is undoubtedly a first step in the right direction.

Directive 2000/31/EC has proven to be evidently not sufficient to address all the issues linked to the online space and in particular to effectively protect consumer's safety. Moreover, the development of digital technology along with the spread of online illegal activities noticeably requires a new legal regime to adapt with the current context.

EFPIA fully understands and welcomes the philosophy of this text which is to:

- Better protect consumers and their fundamental rights online;
- Establish a powerful transparency and a clear accountability framework for online platforms;
- Foster innovation, growth and competitiveness within the single market.

Naturally, the right balance between these principles has to be found. But when it comes to the protection of consumers, the EU legislator has an obligation to protect EU citizens from the potential harm caused by the online purchase of illicit, substandard or falsified pharmaceutical products. It will really be a missed opportunity to let consumers continue to be at risk if we do not seize this opportunity to update more profoundly the 2000 e-commerce Directive.

Having reviewed the proposal for the DSA, we are nevertheless satisfied to see a number of welcome and interesting provisions, such as:

- Voluntary own-initiative investigations and legal compliance (Article 6);
- Obligation for legal representatives for all the online intermediaries (Article 10);
- Transparency reporting obligations for providers of intermediary services (Article 13);
- Notification of suspicions of criminal offences (Article 21);
- The publication of trader's information (Article 22) - even if we believe that in order to be efficient, this verification of the trader's information should not only be obtained but also be verified by the online platform and this provision should also apply to all intermediaries, and particularly, to domain names registrars;

www.efpia.eu 3

- Compliance officers (Article 32);
- The "European Board for Digital Services" and "Digital Services Coordinator of establishment" (Article 47).

That being said, EFPIA is of the opinion that there is room for improvement of the proposed act. Especially with regards to the protection of the patient who easily has access to any kind of illegal content related to pharmaceutical products putting his or her health at high risk.

There are various types of illegal content, but specific attention and therefore specific measures should be considered for illegal content related to dangerous products, namely "dangerous illegal content".

This point was mentioned very recently during the 25th European IP Forum organized by UNIFAB2.

At this occasion, Mr. Cédric O, French Secretary of State emphasized the particularities of dangerous contents and dangerous goods which "require a specific delimitation and response related to their dangerousness or the specific problems they raise" and thus, Mr. Cédric O believed that online platforms should have higher standards and obligations in the fight against these harmful products3.

Similarly, Mr. Olivier DUSSOPT, Deputy Minister in charge of publ ic Accounts, pointed to the seriousness of counterfeited medical products during the sanitary crisis, which " compromises the health and safety of consumers". Mr. DUSSOPT emphasized that "we need to follow through on proceedings where the health and safety of our citizens is at stake".4

Indeed, illicit, substandard or falsified medicines/medical devices put patients' and consumers' health and safety in danger. It also generates environmental high risks.

According to the General Product Safety Directive (Directive 2001/95/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 3 December 2001 on general product safety), only safe products should be placed on the market. It is common sense that falsified or substandard medicinal products are not safe for patients and consumers and these illicit products should not have access to the online market.

The sale of these products is per se dangerous as illegal content, which has a broader scope than Intellectual Property Rights infringement.

It is very clear that everything which is forbidden offline should also be forbidden online. This principle should rule the entire DSA.

However, today, this principle does not reflect that reality!

The online illicit sale of medicines is far from being a new issue. The Internet has become one of the preferred channels to circulate such products. The striking fact is that 96% of online pharmacies are illicit, which is equivalent to 35,000 illegal websites targeting consumers and patients every single day5. More than 50% of medicines purchased over the Internet from illegal sites that conceal their physical address have been found to be counterfeit (www.who.int/bulletin/volumes/88/4/10-020410/en/).

The situation increased in significance even more during the COVID-19 pandemic. For example, during March 2020, at least 100,000 new domain names were registered containing terms like "covid," "corona," and "virus", to sell masks or advertise COVID-related scams6. As reported by INTERPOL on their website concerning Operation Pangea XIII (March 2020), "Law enforcement agencies taking part in Operation Pangea found 2,000 online links advertising items related to COVID-19. The seizure of more than 34,000 counterfeit and substandard masks, "corona spray", "coronavirus packages" or "coronavirus medicine" reveals only the tip of the iceberg regarding this new trend in counterfeiting."

Furthermore, one of our members has performed an online monitoring in March 2020 which revealed that scams and misinformation related to COVID-19 treatments / vaccines were already prevalent at the very beginning of the pandemic. 66% of offers were for treatment scams; 34% for medical supplies, including diagnostic kits, personal protective equipment (masks, etc ).

At a very early stage of the pandemic, OLAF (European Anti-Fraud Office) had identified more than 800 suspicious companies acting as intermediaries or traders which resulted in the seizure or detention of more than 14 million counterfeit or substandard items linked to the COVID-19 pandemic, (i.e. masks, ventilators, or gloves) that flooded into the European market,7.

This undoubtedly demonstrates the link from the online environment to the physical world! It must be kept in mind that access to online dangerous illegal content means, at the end, de-facto access to offline dangerous illegal products (illegal content viewed online means dangerous illegal products being physically delivered)!

It is to be noted that this harm is even higher given that no patient would ever knowingly purchase counterfeit medicines online and will therefore take ("consume") the concerned product at the detriment of his or her health.

This is why this legislation should aim at avoiding that the illicit product reaches the patient's/consumer's hands in the first place. Furthermore, the online platforms should also systematically alert the patient/consumer when that patient/consumer has been unwillingly and unknowingly been a victim of such type of dangerous illegal content.

Just as a separate note, it must be underlined that some customers may buy counterfeits online to resell them. Besides there are also categories of online customers who are knowingly and illegally purchasing medicines online for off label use (opioids, hormone growth etc) expecting they would be genuine/diverted. In all cases, the harm would be the same for the final patient/consumer. II. EFPIA PROPOSALS TOWARDS THE PARTICULARITIES OF THE PHARMACEUTICAL SECTOR

The measures which are hereby proposed apply without prejudice to the existing pharmaceutical legislation which, as such, is not sufficient as it only gives the general framework of online sale of
