medicines but does not impose precise and specific obligations on online intermediaries who have unfortunately proven to be key actors as facilitators of those illicit activities.

Yet, in the online world where consumers are more easily vulnerable to counterfeit goods and frauds, the growth of illicit online sale of medicines must be regulated by strict and appropriate regulations applicable to online intermediaries to ensure the patients/consumers safety.

In general, Directive 2001/83/EC as amended by Directive 2011/62/EU on falsified medicines for human use and by the Implementing Regulation 699/2014 set out the legal background for the online sale of medicines. However, there is indeed a need for a specific regulation enhancing the obligations of all online intermediaries with regard to dangerous illegal content putting at risk the EU consumer and/or the environment.

The DSA, being horizontal, is a perfect instrument and this opportunity should not be missed in order to protect the EU consumer's safety.

1) Introduction of a broader "KYBC" (Know Your Business Customer) principle, even truer for dangerous illegal content

EFPIA supports the KYBC coalition on the fact that the "KYBC" principle or the principle of verifying the identity of sellers on a platform, as stated in Article 22, should apply to all online intermediaries. It is even more relevant for dangerous illegal content, as is detailed below, all the more as this verification could be done very easily when it comes to the sale of pharmaceutical products.

While almost all Member States allow the online sale of medicines, not every seller is authorized to sell medicines online. Some countries only allow the online sale of non-prescription medicines while other countries allow the online sale of prescription medicines with a requirement of the prescription.

In all cases and no matter if the product is under prescription or not, the online seller must be registered with the relevant national health authorities. This information can be easily checked on the EMA's website: https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/human-regulatory/overview/public-healththreats/falsified-medicines/buying-medicines-online.

Given this situation, EFPIA strongly advocates for the obligations to request and verify the registrant's and trader's competency to use the intermediary services for online sales of medicines. Naturally, this vetting obligation should, in our view, also apply to any dangerous illegal content.

a) "KYBC" requirements should apply to all providers of intermediary services: Indeed, when it comes to the illicit online sale of medicines (sale of medicines being per se a business regulated activity), it has been proven that most of the time, the recipient of the intermediary services, (excluding the final consumer), is an individual. When offering for sale pharmaceutical products, the individuals are business customers. It could be the case of the person who requests a domain name to be used for selling pharmaceutical products, or the person who offers for sale medicines on a market place or social media platform. In any case, when the illegal content is dangerous, all online intermediaries should apply the "KYBC" principle.

Our experience has outlined that criminals have a specific strategy which consists in dividing their activity into small pieces using a network of individuals with different roles.

www.efpia.eu 6

When traders (regardless if they are entities or individuals) list any medicines for sales on the websites, marketplaces, social media platforms and messaging applications, the providers of intermediary services shall request the trader to provide them with documents showing that the trader has the competence to sell or promote the sale of medicines in the EU.

If the registrant (trader) does not provide the intermediaries with the requested documents for verification, the intermediaries must refuse their services to the registrant or trader. From our standpoint, this verification in no way imposes a heavy duty on any intermediaries because the verification of the capacity of the online pharmacy in the EU c an be very easily checked on the European Medicines Agency website, as mentioned above8.

This level of obligation is an analogy to the obligation of service providers in Article 17 of Directive (EU) 2019/790 on copyright and related rights, in which the service providers must make best efforts to obtain an authorization from the right holders of the copyrighted contents. If the service providers fail to perform this obligation, they shall be held liable for unauthorized acts of communication to the public.

More specifically, we are providing suggestions/concrete proposals concerning domain names' registrars.

Indeed, one of the biggest issues the EU consumer is confronted with when it comes to the online sale of illicit, substandard or falsified medicines, is the sale done through illicit online pharmacies.

For the criminals to run their business, they need to have access to the websites on which they will offer for sale illicit, substandard or falsified medicines and to do so, they first need to obtain the registration of domain names.

b) "KYBC" requirements should especially apply to domain names' registrars

8 https://www.ema.europa.eu/en Criminals exploit the online phenomenon known as affiliate network marketing. Affiliate networks are set up by small groups of individuals, they can buy off the shelf software to set up their business and add the various components that are necessary to meet their requirements. For example, they can integrate with similarly ad hoc, independent service and product suppliers - pay per use customer services; bulk manufacturers to supply product; vast networks of independent dropshippers; web designers and programmers; high risk merchant account providers; etc.

The core network then attracts website owners to join the affiliate programme, in return for their Search Engine Optimisation investment, they receive commission payments based on transactions.

This type of network marketing developed from Amazon and was exploited into illicit pharmaceutical sales, illegal gambling and even pornography. Website owners who join these networks have no need to touch a product, find a manufacturer or interact with the customer. Their involvement tends to be limited to simply drawing in customer traffic. The core of the network ensures seamless functioning for the rest of the process.

www.efpia.eu 7

A joint industry initiative led by the Pharmaceutical Security Institute (PSI), which started in April 2020 with the monitoring of 27 medicines linked to the COVID-19 pandemic and offered by online pharmacies, showed similar trends as those identified by PSI in the previous three years concerning other medicines sold online demonstrating the role of the registrars.

More precisely, out of the more than 9100 traditional websites identified as selling COVID-19 related medicines, 338 have been targeted. More than 84% of these sites were from the same illicit online pharmacy networks, using the same domain name registrars that have already been actively engaged in the sales of fake medicines over the past three years (within the three precedent online disruption programs). This indicates the urgency to take immediate action!

It is known that certain domain name registrars knowingly sponsor illicit online pharmacy networks. These registrars do not allegedly comply with the Registrar Accreditation Agreement, ignore abuse notifications submitted by right holders and do not suspend the domain names of illicit online pharmacies.9

It has been showed that some registrars play a key role in this illicit business activity given that the registration of the domain name is Step 1. This is why the KYBC principle should be applied to the registrars when it comes to the registration of a domain name for a business activity of potentially dangerous content and this is why the entity that requests a domain name should be verified "at the gate".

Annex I lists a few precise proposals on how this verification could be done by the registrars.

Of course, this limitation alone would not be sufficient, because illicit online pharmacies are not the only source of the illicit online sales of medicines. The presence of illicit posts/offers for sale on marketplaces and social media platforms has shown an exponential growth and also requires an appropriate answer to tackle this significant threat for patient's health.

Our industry's aim is to avoid that the product reaches the patient's home which would mean that the posts/offers for sale are proactively delisted and where possible further investigated.

Reaching this goal should also be the aim of this legislation in protecting the EU consumers.

Therefore, online intermediaries have to play an active role and implement proactive measures. Failing to do so should make them held liable, as explained below.

2) Introduction of binding obligations for all online intermediaries to avoid providing illegal content, at least for dangerous illegal content

It has been enlightened that:

- The consumer/patient is hardly ever aware of buying illicit, substandard or falsified medicines and will take the concerned product and use it as a medication;

- To protect the consumer's/patient's health, actions should be taken to avoid that the product reaches the consumers / patients hands.

9 Id.

www.efpia.eu 8

One of these actions is to enlarge the KYBC principle to impose specific vetting obligations to online intermediaries, especially to registrars, as detailed above in point 1).

The second set of actions is to impose on online intermediaries specific proactive measures, including for small platforms, which, if they are falling short in these measures, would result in the online intermediaries' liability.

It is important to add, at this stage, that all the obligations (general and specific) should equally apply to all platforms, no matter their size, at least for dangerous illegal content. Indeed, the harm for the consumer's/patient's health is the same whether it is a small or a large online platform.

General obligations should equally apply to all intermediaries, including small ones.

The exclusion of small platforms from the obligations imposed to larger ones should not apply to dangerous illegal content, especially when it comes to the sale of illicit, substandard or falsified medicines.

Indeed, the actions led by our industry have highlighted that criminals are very agile and adapt very quickly to every new situation, as they have done it during the Covid-19 pandemic for instance.

It has been shown that those criminals use small entities with few persons and fragment the different stages of their activity to circumvent the obligations. It is also possible that they move from large platforms / registrars to small ones to avoid the obligations that apply to large platforms / registrars.

In such cases, small registrars or platforms may still play a significant role in the illegal activity because rogue registrars or non-compliant platforms are not always the big ones.

On top of that, we know from our experience that small platforms have less often entered into MoU's or put in place proactive measures or collaboration programs.

Annex II provides a list of specific obligations in relation to dangerous illegal content, as detailed in this paper, which should also equally apply to all platforms, including small ones.

3) Introduction of requirement for information sharing on delisted content, at least for dangerous illegal content

a) With the consumer/patient Once the patient has the product in hands, he or she cannot know whether it is genuine or not (we know that counterfeit pharmaceutical products look identical to the authentic product, i.e. same packaging, same batch number, same pills colors and shape, and 2D serialization code etc ). The probability of the patient taking a fake medicine is very high and this represents an immediate threat for the health of the patient and society as a whole.

There is also a risk for the patient deriving from the sale of illicit or diverted products coming for instance from Turkey or India. These products are not necessarily counterfeit but still illicit because the sellers do not have any authorization to sell medicines and do not follow the good distribution

www.efpia.eu 9

practices (no control of transportation and storage conditions which may alter the quality and efficacy of the products).

As already shared by different associations/entities, we also believe that consumers/patients should systematically be informed when the product they have purchased is a counterfeit or provided by an illicit seller. This is not the case currently.

This is very important even if done a posteriori so that the consumer/patient can take eventual verification measures with a doctor.

b) With the concerned pharmaceutical companies and/or with the law enforcement authorities Sharing this information with law enforcement authorities and/or the marketing authorization holder of the pharmaceutical product when this dangerous illegal content has been identified, is absolutely crucial for investigation purposes and threat assessments.

Collaboration between public and private sector is key in the fight against pharmaceutical crime and this has been proven very relevant at different occasions, in particular during the COVID-19 pandemic. Pharmaceutical associations, such as PSI and G5 Santé have frequently partnered or collaborated with law enforcement authorities in order to dismantle illicit networks.

This collaboration has for instance led to very efficient operational results very recently in the frame of a joint online monitoring conducted by 3 pharmaceutical companies of the G5 Santé on oncology products.

This operation resulted in the identification of a criminal network implanted in Europe based on a network of websites deployed in Europe and Turkey. The most relevant and exploitable elements were transmitted to the national law enforcement authorities and at the international level, through Operation SHIELD of EUROPOL.

As it is demonstrated by this example, offline investigations which lead to the arrest of criminals and to the dismantling of their illicit activities, nearly all the time start with an online investigation. That is why it is extremely important to share all the data related to the online illicit environment.

This information could be very easily shared by online intermediaries if the data is downloaded on a shared platform which could have the EU support, such as EU Observatory IPEP (Intellectual Property Enforcement Portal). III. EFPIA SUPPORTS OTHER GENERAL COMMENTS OF IP ASSOCIATIONS (not specifically related to dangerous illegal content)

Lastly, it must be noted that EFPIA supports the position of other associations, such as UNIFAB, on other parts of the DSA not commented above.

We have listed the main points below:

- The implementation of a "stay-down" mechanism, which would definitively ban illegal content and prevent it from continuously reappearing online and continuously harming consumers.

www.efpia.eu 10

o As proposed by other associations, "an illegal content that has been removed should not be able to come back online (even if it is posted by another user)". o It is a duty of the EU regulators to extend the compulsory stay-down mechanism to avoid the accessibility by the patient to any dangerous content that has already been removed.

- Repeat Infringer: We share the position of many associations as relayed by UNIFAB hereunder:

"UNIFAB believes that the current provisions of the DSA are too broad as it leaves too much margin for platforms to maneuver. Accordingly, we suggest advocating for the introduction of a rule whereby, after 3 posting of illegal content, the seller is permanently banned from the platform.

Implementing a well-defined policy to fight against repeat infringers would help avoid abusive behaviours of certain platforms such as: (a) several notifications from different right holders towards the same seller which are counted as one single notification; (b) repeat infringer policies that are never enforced; (c) several alerts from a right holder towards a seller which results in the blocking of sales of products concerning that specific right holder and not the blocking of all sales from that seller; etc."

- Trusted Flaggers in Article 19 The EFPIA welcomes the idea of this requirement. In the pharmaceutical industry, associations are used to make joint actions, such as in the frame of PSI and G5 Santé to maximize the effectiveness of each campaign. However, it is not always the case that pharmaceutical companies will join a program with others because each company may have their own strategy, in addition to the joint action.

Therefore, we would like to grant the status of Trusted flaggers to individual pharmaceutical companies or brand owners to (i) facilitate the submission of the reports without having to repeat the same process many times and (ii) be able to follow up on the process of the reports. In addition, companies and brand owners are at best positioned to assess and examine the illegal content, from which they can be proactive in the monitoring of the platforms as well as to calibrate their strategy. IV. CONCLUSION:

EFPIA's above listed proposals have as main purpose EU citizens' health and safety and we believe that this should be a common goal for all the Internet actors.

Nevertheless, it is also important to underline that the proliferation of online illegal content is not only harming the EU consumer's health and safety. Legitimate online pharmacies (which represent only 4% of all online pharmacies) are also heavily impacted and have almost no access to this online market.

When a patient/consumer is looking for a potential online purchase of medicines, the first results on search engines pages display a large number of illicit online pharmacies. This lack of visibility of the legitimate offer generates both uncertainty and unsafety for patients and prevents the development of legitimate online business activities.

EFPIA has always underlined the need for collaboration and involvement of all stakeholders and we want to reiterate, here, our industry's willingness to continue to actively collaborate with all and any actors.

www.efpia.eu 11

EFPIA has already engaged in discussions and collaboration with online platforms, and its candidacy as a member of the Memorandum of understanding (MoU) on the sale of counterfeit goods on the internet. We very much welcome voluntarily proactive measures already put in place by online platforms. Still, we do believe that an enhanced regulation will also benefit to the online intermediaries because it will increase the consumer's trust in the online intermediaries' ecosystem.

With the EFPIA's contribution to the DSA, we call for a safer Internet for EU citizens and a fair environment for genuine business activities to progress.

ANNEX I

KYBC principle - vetting obligation for registrars

The KYBC principle should be applied to the registrars when it comes to the registration of a domain name for a business activity of potentially dangerous content and this is why the entity that requests a domain name should be verified "at the gate".

We have listed below few precise proposals on how this verification could be done by the registrars:

1) To be accredited as registrars, their policy or terms and conditions shall include the obligation for the recipient of the service (in this specific case, the registrant) to acknowledge, in case the domain name is dedicated to a business activity of potentially dangerous content, that they are allowed to perform this activity and do comply with the concerned regulation.

If the registrant: o fails to provide the needed evidence or; o provides a document which is invalid or; o is not allowed to proceed with the activity for which it has requested the domain name § he will have to provide the correct evidence within 1 week at the latest. § If not, the registrar shall block access to the corresponding website either after his own check or after having been notified by any interested person. A specific online administrative procedure shall allow any interested person to oblige the registrar to block access to the website if the request has been considered as justified by a competent authority (to be defined). The repeatedly non-compliant registrars failing to comply with the Registrar Accreditation Agreement containing the above-mentioned obligation and/or ignoring abuse notifications shall lose their Accreditation (process to be defined including a definition of "repeatedly" / could be a number of ignored abuse notifications in a given period of time).

2) Additionally, when a registrant requests a domain name containing words such as hospital, pharmacy, doctor, etc in one of the Member States' language, the registrar should be obliged to ask the registrant to provide the supporting documents evidencing that the activity for which the domain will be used complies with the pharmaceutical regulation. The registrar shall have the obligation to proactively filter the domain name registration requests on the basis of a list of keywords that will be attached to the present regulation and regularly updated through the IP toolbox kit.

3) The same should apply if the domain name contains a medicine's name which appears on the list of product names if such list has been provided by the pharmaceutical companies or associations.

By doing so, we would limit the access to illicit online pharmacies "at the entrance gate" and give legal ground for action against the non-compliant registrars.

www.efpia.eu 13

ANNEX II

Specific obligations (=proactive measures) in relation to dangerous illegal content

If online platforms tolerate illegal content on their interfaces, they should be held liable and accountable for the risks they pose to consumers, especially when they tolerate dangerous illegal content.

The only way to exempt them from engaging their liability is to have implemented proactive measures to avoid providing dangerous illegal content.

Using the existing legal framework for the online sale of medicines and to facilitate the implementation of those proactive measures by platforms, we have proposed suggestions that are detailed below.

A common European legal framework for the online sale of medicines is set out in European Commission Directive 2001/83/EC as amended by Directive 2011/62/EU on falsified medicines for human use and by the Implementing Regulation 699/2014 on 24 June 2014.

Since the 1st of July 2015, national regulatory authorities in the EU are obliged to list all registered online medicine retailers in their country on their websites. Therefore, if a seller is not registered with the relevant national health authority, it is not authorized to sell medicines online. It should hence be automatically delisted.

Furthermore, online sale of prescription medicines is not authorized in all the EU Member States. Therefore, if a prescription drug is sold online in a Member State where it is not allowed, it should be automatically delisted.

Additionally, all online medicines retailers registered in the EU should display the common logo for all pharmaceutical products (either under prescription or not).

In summary, very easy checks can be done on the online platforms' side, provided that the pharmaceutical companies provide them with the needed information as detailed below.

This verification from the online platforms could take four parts:

1) On the nature of the product: under prescription or not?
2) Marketing authorization in the targeted country or not?
3) On the authorized status of the seller in the EU
4) Display of the common logo

In more details:
1) The pharmaceutical companies would provide the online platforms with the needed information, namely a list of products for which prescription is required and the corresponding list of countries where online sale of prescription drugs is not authorized.

www.efpia.eu 14

• If the prescription drug is sold online in a country where the online sale of prescription drugs is not authorized, there should be an automatic delisting.

2) The online platforms could have access to the list of authorized products (i.e. those which have a marketing authorization in the targeted national country/ies) on the national health agencies' or on the EMA's websites.

• If the product is offered for sale in a country where it has not any marketing authorization, there should be an automatic delisting.

3) The online platforms could have access to the list of all registered online medicine retailers in the EU, on a country by country basis, on the EMA's website: https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/human-regulatory/overview/public-health-threats/falsifiedmedicines/buying-medicines-online.

• If the seller is not authorized or recorded on the list maintained by each Member State national health authority in the country of the targeted consumer/patient, there should be an automatic delisting.

4) The online platforms should also verify that the retailer displays the common logo:.

• If the common logo does not appear, there should be an automatic delisting.

As soon as one criterion is missing, the online offer for sale is forbidden and should be automatically delisted, without any additional verification.

Finally, it is to be noted that the advertisement for prescription pharmaceutical products in the EU is forbidden - therefore, for social media online platforms, there should be an immediate automatic delisting.

The data coming from this delisting has to be shared with the pharmaceutical companies and law enforcement authorities for intelligence purposes.

As reported by INTERPOL on their website concerning Operation Pangea XIII (March 2020), "Law enforcement agencies taking part in Operation Pangea found 2,000 online links advertising items related to COVID-19. The seizure of more than 34,000 counterfeit and substandard masks, "corona spray", "coronavirus packages" or "coronavirus medicine" reveals only the tip of the iceberg regarding this new trend in counterfeiting."

Furthermore, one of our members has performed an online monitoring in March 2020 which revealed that scams and misinformation related to COVID-19 treatments / vaccines were already prevalent at the very beginning of the pandemic.

The seizure of more than 34,000 counterfeit and substandard masks, "corona spray", "coronavirus packages" or "coronavirus medicine" reveals only the tip of the iceberg regarding this new trend in counterfeiting."

Furthermore, one of our members has performed an online monitoring in March 2020 which revealed that scams and misinformation related to COVID-19 treatments / vaccines were already prevalent at the very beginning of the pandemic. 66% of offers were for treatment scams; 34% for medical supplies, including diagnostic kits, personal protective equipment (masks, etc ). At a very early stage of the pandemic, OLAF (European Anti-Fraud Office) had identified more than 800 suspicious companies acting as intermediaries or traders which resulted in the seizure or detention of more than 14 million counterfeit or substandard items linked to the COVID-19 pandemic, (i.e. masks, ventilators, or gloves) that flooded into the European market,7. This undoubtedly demonstrates the link from the online environment to the physical world! It must be kept in mind that access to online dangerous illegal content means, at the end, de-facto access to offline dangerous illegal products (illegal content viewed online means dangerous illegal products being physically delivered)! It is to be noted that this harm is even higher given that no patient would ever knowingly purchase counterfeit medicines online and will therefore take ("consume") the concerned product at the detriment of his or her health. This is why this legislation should aim at avoiding that the illicit product reaches the patient's/consumer's hands in the first place. Furthermore, the online platforms should also systematically alert the patient/consumer when that patient/consumer has been unwillingly and unknowingly been a victim of such type of dangerous illegal content. Just as a separate note, it must be underlined that some customers may buy counterfeits online to resell them. Besides there are also categories of online customers who are knowingly and illegally purchasing medicines online for off label use (opioids, hormone growth etc) expecting they would be genuine/diverted. In all cases, the harm would be the same for the final patient/consumer. II.

Besides there are also categories of online customers who are knowingly and illegally purchasing medicines online for off label use (opioids, hormone growth etc) expecting they would be genuine/diverted. In all cases, the harm would be the same for the final patient/consumer. II. EFPIA PROPOSALS TOWARDS THE PARTICULARITIES OF THE PHARMACEUTICAL SECTOR

The measures which are hereby proposed apply without prejudice to the existing pharmaceutical legislation which, as such, is not sufficient as it only gives the general framework of online sale of

6 Study published by ASOP Global - Alliance for Safe Online Pharmacies: https://buysaferx.pharmacy//wpcontent/uploads/2020/04/COVID-Scams-and-Domain-Industry-Accountability-Backgrounder1.pdf 7 PSI report mentioned in the Counterfeiting and Piracy Watch List: https://trade.ec.europa.eu/doclib/docs/2020/december/tradoc_159183.pdf

www.efpia.eu 5

medicines but does not impose precise and specific obligations on online intermediaries who have unfortunately proven to be key actors as facilitators of those illicit activities. Yet, in the online world where consumers are more easily vulnerable to counterfeit goods and frauds, the growth of illicit online sale of medicines must be regulated by strict and appropriate regulations applicable to online intermediaries to ensure the patients/consumers safety. In general, Directive 2001/83/EC as amended by Directive 2011/62/EU on falsified medicines for human use and by the Implementing Regulation 699/2014 set out the legal background for the online sale of medicines. However, there is indeed a need for a specific regulation enhancing the obligations of all online intermediaries with regard to dangerous illegal content putting at risk the EU consumer and/or the environment. The DSA, being horizontal, is a perfect instrument and this opportunity should not be missed in order to protect the EU consumer's safety. 1) Introduction of a broader "KYBC" (Know Your Business Customer) principle, even truer for dangerous illegal content

EFPIA supports the KYBC coalition on the fact that the "KYBC" principle or the principle of verifying the identity of sellers on a platform, as stated in Article 22, should apply to all online intermediaries. It is even more relevant for dangerous illegal content, as is detailed below, all the more as this verification could be done very easily when it comes to the sale of pharmaceutical products. While almost all Member States allow the online sale of medicines, not every seller is authorized to sell medicines online. Some countries only allow the online sale of non-prescription medicines while other countries allow the online sale of prescription medicines with a requirement of the prescription.

While almost all Member States allow the online sale of medicines, not every seller is authorized to sell medicines online. Some countries only allow the online sale of non-prescription medicines while other countries allow the online sale of prescription medicines with a requirement of the prescription. In all cases and no matter if the product is under prescription or not, the online seller must be registered with the relevant national health authorities. This information can be easily checked on the EMA's website: https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/human-regulatory/overview/public-healththreats/falsified-medicines/buying-medicines-online. Given this situation, EFPIA strongly advocates for the obligations to request and verify the registrant's and trader's competency to use the intermediary services for online sales of medicines. Naturally, this vetting obligation should, in our view, also apply to any dangerous illegal content. a) "KYBC" requirements should apply to all providers of intermediary services: Indeed, when it comes to the illicit online sale of medicines (sale of medicines being per se a business regulated activity), it has been proven that most of the time, the recipient of the intermediary services, (excluding the final consumer), is an individual. When offering for sale pharmaceutical products, the individuals are business customers. It could be the case of the person who requests a domain name to be used for selling pharmaceutical products, or the person who offers for sale medicines on a market place or social media platform. In any case, when the illegal content is dangerous, all online intermediaries should apply the "KYBC" principle. Our experience has outlined that criminals have a specific strategy which consists in dividing their activity into small pieces using a network of individuals with different roles. www.efpia.eu 6

When traders (regardless if they are entities or individuals) list any medicines for sales on the websites, marketplaces, social media platforms and messaging applications, the providers of intermediary services shall request the trader to provide them with documents showing that the trader has the competence to sell or promote the sale of medicines in the EU. If the registrant (trader) does not provide the intermediaries with the requested documents for verification, the intermediaries must refuse their services to the registrant or trader. From our standpoint, this verification in no way imposes a heavy duty on any intermediaries because the verification of the capacity of the online pharmacy in the EU c an be very easily checked on the European Medicines Agency website, as mentioned above8.

From our standpoint, this verification in no way imposes a heavy duty on any intermediaries because the verification of the capacity of the online pharmacy in the EU c an be very easily checked on the European Medicines Agency website, as mentioned above8. This level of obligation is an analogy to the obligation of service providers in Article 17 of Directive (EU) 2019/790 on copyright and related rights, in which the service providers must make best efforts to obtain an authorization from the right holders of the copyrighted contents. If the service providers fail to perform this obligation, they shall be held liable for unauthorized acts of communication to the public. More specifically, we are providing suggestions/concrete proposals concerning domain names' registrars. Indeed, one of the biggest issues the EU consumer is confronted with when it comes to the online sale of illicit, substandard or falsified medicines, is the sale done through illicit online pharmacies. For the criminals to run their business, they need to have access to the websites on which they will offer for sale illicit, substandard or falsified medicines and to do so, they first need to obtain the registration of domain names. b) "KYBC" requirements should especially apply to domain names' registrars

8 https://www.ema.europa.eu/en Criminals exploit the online phenomenon known as affiliate network marketing. Affiliate networks are set up by small groups of individuals, they can buy off the shelf software to set up their business and add the various components that are necessary to meet their requirements. For example, they can integrate with similarly ad hoc, independent service and product suppliers - pay per use customer services; bulk manufacturers to supply product; vast networks of independent dropshippers; web designers and programmers; high risk merchant account providers; etc. The core network then attracts website owners to join the affiliate programme, in return for their Search Engine Optimisation investment, they receive commission payments based on transactions. This type of network marketing developed from Amazon and was exploited into illicit pharmaceutical sales, illegal gambling and even pornography. Website owners who join these networks have no need to touch a product, find a manufacturer or interact with the customer. Their involvement tends to be limited to simply drawing in customer traffic. The core of the network ensures seamless functioning for the rest of the process.

Website owners who join these networks have no need to touch a product, find a manufacturer or interact with the customer. Their involvement tends to be limited to simply drawing in customer traffic. The core of the network ensures seamless functioning for the rest of the process. www.efpia.eu 7

A joint industry initiative led by the Pharmaceutical Security Institute (PSI), which started in April 2020 with the monitoring of 27 medicines linked to the COVID-19 pandemic and offered by online pharmacies, showed similar trends as those identified by PSI in the previous three years concerning other medicines sold online demonstrating the role of the registrars. More precisely, out of the more than 9100 traditional websites identified as selling COVID-19 related medicines, 338 have been targeted. More than 84% of these sites were from the same illicit online pharmacy networks, using the same domain name registrars that have already been actively engaged in the sales of fake medicines over the past three years (within the three precedent online disruption programs). This indicates the urgency to take immediate action! It is known that certain domain name registrars knowingly sponsor illicit online pharmacy networks. These registrars do not allegedly comply with the Registrar Accreditation Agreement, ignore abuse notifications submitted by right holders and do not suspend the domain names of illicit online pharmacies.9

It has been showed that some registrars play a key role in this illicit business activity given that the registration of the domain name is Step 1. This is why the KYBC principle should be applied to the registrars when it comes to the registration of a domain name for a business activity of potentially dangerous content and this is why the entity that requests a domain name should be verified "at the gate". Annex I lists a few precise proposals on how this verification could be done by the registrars. Of course, this limitation alone would not be sufficient, because illicit online pharmacies are not the only source of the illicit online sales of medicines. The presence of illicit posts/offers for sale on marketplaces and social media platforms has shown an exponential growth and also requires an appropriate answer to tackle this significant threat for patient's health. Our industry's aim is to avoid that the product reaches the patient's home which would mean that the posts/offers for sale are proactively delisted and where possible further investigated.

Our industry's aim is to avoid that the product reaches the patient's home which would mean that the posts/offers for sale are proactively delisted and where possible further investigated. Reaching this goal should also be the aim of this legislation in protecting the EU consumers. Therefore, online intermediaries have to play an active role and implement proactive measures. Failing to do so should make them held liable, as explained below. 2) Introduction of binding obligations for all online intermediaries to avoid providing illegal content, at least for dangerous illegal content

It has been enlightened that:

- The consumer/patient is hardly ever aware of buying illicit, substandard or falsified medicines and will take the concerned product and use it as a medication;

- To protect the consumer's/patient's health, actions should be taken to avoid that the product reaches the consumers / patients hands. 9 Id. www.efpia.eu 8

One of these actions is to enlarge the KYBC principle to impose specific vetting obligations to online intermediaries, especially to registrars, as detailed above in point 1). The second set of actions is to impose on online intermediaries specific proactive measures, including for small platforms, which, if they are falling short in these measures, would result in the online intermediaries' liability. It is important to add, at this stage, that all the obligations (general and specific) should equally apply to all platforms, no matter their size, at least for dangerous illegal content. Indeed, the harm for the consumer's/patient's health is the same whether it is a small or a large online platform. General obligations should equally apply to all intermediaries, including small ones. The exclusion of small platforms from the obligations imposed to larger ones should not apply to dangerous illegal content, especially when it comes to the sale of illicit, substandard or falsified medicines. Indeed, the actions led by our industry have highlighted that criminals are very agile and adapt very quickly to every new situation, as they have done it during the Covid-19 pandemic for instance. It has been shown that those criminals use small entities with few persons and fragment the different stages of their activity to circumvent the obligations. It is also possible that they move from large platforms / registrars to small ones to avoid the obligations that apply to large platforms / registrars.

It is also possible that they move from large platforms / registrars to small ones to avoid the obligations that apply to large platforms / registrars. In such cases, small registrars or platforms may still play a significant role in the illegal activity because rogue registrars or non-compliant platforms are not always the big ones. On top of that, we know from our experience that small platforms have less often entered into MoU's or put in place proactive measures or collaboration programs. Annex II provides a list of specific obligations in relation to dangerous illegal content, as detailed in this paper, which should also equally apply to all platforms, including small ones. 3) Introduction of requirement for information sharing on delisted content, at least for dangerous illegal content

a) With the consumer/patient Once the patient has the product in hands, he or she cannot know whether it is genuine or not (we know that counterfeit pharmaceutical products look identical to the authentic product, i.e. same packaging, same batch number, same pills colors and shape, and 2D serialization code etc ). The probability of the patient taking a fake medicine is very high and this represents an immediate threat for the health of the patient and society as a whole. There is also a risk for the patient deriving from the sale of illicit or diverted products coming for instance from Turkey or India. These products are not necessarily counterfeit but still illicit because the sellers do not have any authorization to sell medicines and do not follow the good distribution

www.efpia.eu 9

practices (no control of transportation and storage conditions which may alter the quality and efficacy of the products). As already shared by different associations/entities, we also believe that consumers/patients should systematically be informed when the product they have purchased is a counterfeit or provided by an illicit seller. This is not the case currently. This is very important even if done a posteriori so that the consumer/patient can take eventual verification measures with a doctor. b) With the concerned pharmaceutical companies and/or with the law enforcement authorities Sharing this information with law enforcement authorities and/or the marketing authorization holder of the pharmaceutical product when this dangerous illegal content has been identified, is absolutely crucial for investigation purposes and threat assessments.

b) With the concerned pharmaceutical companies and/or with the law enforcement authorities Sharing this information with law enforcement authorities and/or the marketing authorization holder of the pharmaceutical product when this dangerous illegal content has been identified, is absolutely crucial for investigation purposes and threat assessments. Collaboration between public and private sector is key in the fight against pharmaceutical crime and this has been proven very relevant at different occasions, in particular during the COVID-19 pandemic. Pharmaceutical associations, such as PSI and G5 Santé have frequently partnered or collaborated with law enforcement authorities in order to dismantle illicit networks. This collaboration has for instance led to very efficient operational results very recently in the frame of a joint online monitoring conducted by 3 pharmaceutical companies of the G5 Santé on oncology products. This operation resulted in the identification of a criminal network implanted in Europe based on a network of websites deployed in Europe and Turkey. The most relevant and exploitable elements were transmitted to the national law enforcement authorities and at the international level, through Operation SHIELD of EUROPOL. As it is demonstrated by this example, offline investigations which lead to the arrest of criminals and to the dismantling of their illicit activities, nearly all the time start with an online investigation. That is why it is extremely important to share all the data related to the online illicit environment. This information could be very easily shared by online intermediaries if the data is downloaded on a shared platform which could have the EU support, such as EU Observatory IPEP (Intellectual Property Enforcement Portal). III. EFPIA SUPPORTS OTHER GENERAL COMMENTS OF IP ASSOCIATIONS (not specifically related to dangerous illegal content)

Lastly, it must be noted that EFPIA supports the position of other associations, such as UNIFAB, on other parts of the DSA not commented above. We have listed the main points below:

- The implementation of a "stay-down" mechanism, which would definitively ban illegal content and prevent it from continuously reappearing online and continuously harming consumers. www.efpia.eu 10

o As proposed by other associations, "an illegal content that has been removed should not be able to come back online (even if it is posted by another user)". o It is a duty of the EU regulators to extend the compulsory stay-down mechanism to avoid the accessibility by the patient to any dangerous content that has already been removed.

o It is a duty of the EU regulators to extend the compulsory stay-down mechanism to avoid the accessibility by the patient to any dangerous content that has already been removed. - Repeat Infringer: We share the position of many associations as relayed by UNIFAB hereunder:

"UNIFAB believes that the current provisions of the DSA are too broad as it leaves too much margin for platforms to maneuver. Accordingly, we suggest advocating for the introduction of a rule whereby, after 3 posting of illegal content, the seller is permanently banned from the platform. Implementing a well-defined policy to fight against repeat infringers would help avoid abusive behaviours of certain platforms such as: (a) several notifications from different right holders towards the same seller which are counted as one single notification; (b) repeat infringer policies that are never enforced; (c) several alerts from a right holder towards a seller which results in the blocking of sales of products concerning that specific right holder and not the blocking of all sales from that seller; etc."

- Trusted Flaggers in Article 19 The EFPIA welcomes the idea of this requirement. In the pharmaceutical industry, associations are used to make joint actions, such as in the frame of PSI and G5 Santé to maximize the effectiveness of each campaign. However, it is not always the case that pharmaceutical companies will join a program with others because each company may have their own strategy, in addition to the joint action. Therefore, we would like to grant the status of Trusted flaggers to individual pharmaceutical companies or brand owners to (i) facilitate the submission of the reports without having to repeat the same process many times and (ii) be able to follow up on the process of the reports. In addition, companies and brand owners are at best positioned to assess and examine the illegal content, from which they can be proactive in the monitoring of the platforms as well as to calibrate their strategy. IV. CONCLUSION:

EFPIA's above listed proposals have as main purpose EU citizens' health and safety and we believe that this should be a common goal for all the Internet actors. Nevertheless, it is also important to underline that the proliferation of online illegal content is not only harming the EU consumer's health and safety.

Nevertheless, it is also important to underline that the proliferation of online illegal content is not only harming the EU consumer's health and safety. Legitimate online pharmacies (which represent only 4% of all online pharmacies) are also heavily impacted and have almost no access to this online market. When a patient/consumer is looking for a potential online purchase of medicines, the first results on search engines pages display a large number of illicit online pharmacies. This lack of visibility of the legitimate offer generates both uncertainty and unsafety for patients and prevents the development of legitimate online business activities. EFPIA has always underlined the need for collaboration and involvement of all stakeholders and we want to reiterate, here, our industry's willingness to continue to actively collaborate with all and any actors. www.efpia.eu 11

EFPIA has already engaged in discussions and collaboration with online platforms, and its candidacy as a member of the Memorandum of understanding (MoU) on the sale of counterfeit goods on the internet. We very much welcome voluntarily proactive measures already put in place by online platforms. Still, we do believe that an enhanced regulation will also benefit to the online intermediaries because it will increase the consumer's trust in the online intermediaries' ecosystem. With the EFPIA's contribution to the DSA, we call for a safer Internet for EU citizens and a fair environment for genuine business activities to progress. www.efpia.eu 12

ANNEX I

KYBC principle - vetting obligation for registrars

The KYBC principle should be applied to the registrars when it comes to the registration of a domain name for a business activity of potentially dangerous content and this is why the entity that requests a domain name should be verified "at the gate". We have listed below few precise proposals on how this verification could be done by the registrars:

1) To be accredited as registrars, their policy or terms and conditions shall include the obligation for the recipient of the service (in this specific case, the registrant) to acknowledge, in case the domain name is dedicated to a business activity of potentially dangerous content, that they are allowed to perform this activity and do comply with the concerned regulation.

We have listed below few precise proposals on how this verification could be done by the registrars:

1) To be accredited as registrars, their policy or terms and conditions shall include the obligation for the recipient of the service (in this specific case, the registrant) to acknowledge, in case the domain name is dedicated to a business activity of potentially dangerous content, that they are allowed to perform this activity and do comply with the concerned regulation. If the registrant: o fails to provide the needed evidence or; o provides a document which is invalid or; o is not allowed to proceed with the activity for which it has requested the domain name § he will have to provide the correct evidence within 1 week at the latest. § If not, the registrar shall block access to the corresponding website either after his own check or after having been notified by any interested person. A specific online administrative procedure shall allow any interested person to oblige the registrar to block access to the website if the request has been considered as justified by a competent authority (to be defined). The repeatedly non-compliant registrars failing to comply with the Registrar Accreditation Agreement containing the above-mentioned obligation and/or ignoring abuse notifications shall lose their Accreditation (process to be defined including a definition of "repeatedly" / could be a number of ignored abuse notifications in a given period of time). 2) Additionally, when a registrant requests a domain name containing words such as hospital, pharmacy, doctor, etc in one of the Member States' language, the registrar should be obliged to ask the registrant to provide the supporting documents evidencing that the activity for which the domain will be used complies with the pharmaceutical regulation. The registrar shall have the obligation to proactively filter the domain name registration requests on the basis of a list of keywords that will be attached to the present regulation and regularly updated through the IP toolbox kit. 3) The same should apply if the domain name contains a medicine's name which appears on the list of product names if such list has been provided by the pharmaceutical companies or associations. By doing so, we would limit the access to illicit online pharmacies "at the entrance gate" and give legal ground for action against the non-compliant registrars.

By doing so, we would limit the access to illicit online pharmacies "at the entrance gate" and give legal ground for action against the non-compliant registrars. www.efpia.eu 13

ANNEX II

Specific obligations (=proactive measures) in relation to dangerous illegal content

If online platforms tolerate illegal content on their interfaces, they should be held liable and accountable for the risks they pose to consumers, especially when they tolerate dangerous illegal content. The only way to exempt them from engaging their liability is to have implemented proactive measures to avoid providing dangerous illegal content. Using the existing legal framework for the online sale of medicines and to facilitate the implementation of those proactive measures by platforms, we have proposed suggestions that are detailed below. A common European legal framework for the online sale of medicines is set out in European Commission Directive 2001/83/EC as amended by Directive 2011/62/EU on falsified medicines for human use and by the Implementing Regulation 699/2014 on 24 June 2014. Since the 1st of July 2015, national regulatory authorities in the EU are obliged to list all registered online medicine retailers in their country on their websites. Therefore, if a seller is not registered with the relevant national health authority, it is not authorized to sell medicines online. It should hence be automatically delisted. Furthermore, online sale of prescription medicines is not authorized in all the EU Member States. Therefore, if a prescription drug is sold online in a Member State where it is not allowed, it should be automatically delisted. Additionally, all online medicines retailers registered in the EU should display the common logo for all pharmaceutical products (either under prescription or not). In summary, very easy checks can be done on the online platforms' side, provided that the pharmaceutical companies provide them with the needed information as detailed below. This verification from the online platforms could take four parts:

1) On the nature of the product: under prescription or not? 2) Marketing authorization in the targeted country or not? 3) On the authorized status of the seller in the EU
4) Display of the common logo

In more details:
1) The pharmaceutical companies would provide the online platforms with the needed information, namely a list of products for which prescription is required and the corresponding list of countries where online sale of prescription drugs is not authorized.

3) On the authorized status of the seller in the EU
4) Display of the common logo

In more details:
1) The pharmaceutical companies would provide the online platforms with the needed information, namely a list of products for which prescription is required and the corresponding list of countries where online sale of prescription drugs is not authorized. www.efpia.eu 14

• If the prescription drug is sold online in a country where the online sale of prescription drugs is not authorized, there should be an automatic delisting. 2) The online platforms could have access to the list of authorized products (i.e. those which have a marketing authorization in the targeted national country/ies) on the national health agencies' or on the EMA's websites. • If the product is offered for sale in a country where it has not any marketing authorization, there should be an automatic delisting. 3) The online platforms could have access to the list of all registered online medicine retailers in the EU, on a country by country basis, on the EMA's website: https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/human-regulatory/overview/public-health-threats/falsifiedmedicines/buying-medicines-online. • If the seller is not authorized or recorded on the list maintained by each Member State national health authority in the country of the targeted consumer/patient, there should be an automatic delisting. 4) The online platforms should also verify that the retailer displays the common logo:. • If the common logo does not appear, there should be an automatic delisting. As soon as one criterion is missing, the online offer for sale is forbidden and should be automatically delisted, without any additional verification. Finally, it is to be noted that the advertisement for prescription pharmaceutical products in the EU is forbidden - therefore, for social media online platforms, there should be an immediate automatic delisting. The data coming from this delisting has to be shared with the pharmaceutical companies and law enforcement authorities for intelligence purposes.

full_text:
Attached please find Verisgn's feedback on the Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on a Single Market For Digital Services (Digital Services Act) and amending Directive 2000/31/EC.

VERISIGN | 12061 Bluemont Way | Reston, VA 20190 Verisign.com

As the registry operator of the.COM,.NET,.NAME,.CC and.TV top-level domains (TLDs), and as an organization with a long history of helping to maintain the security, stability and resiliency of the Domain Name System (DNS) and the internet, VeriSign, Inc. ("Verisign"), welcomes the opportunity to provide feedback on the proposal for a Digital Services Act (DSA).

Comments on the Designation of TLD Registries as "Mere Conduits"

Verisign welcomes the DSA's treatment of TLD Registries and other DNS infrastructure providers as "providers of services establishing and facilitating the underlying logical architecture and proper functioning of the internet " who will benefit from the exemp tions from liability as set out in the DSA (Recital 27). To ensure a consistent application that perfects the intent of the European Commission, Verisign would suggest that the Commission explicitly classify TLD Registries as "mere conduits" in the text of the proposal for a Digital Services Act.

Comments on the Need to Differentiate Between "Technical Information Supporting the DNS" and Other Information

Regarding the is sue of distingui shing be tween in formation related to content and purely technical inf ormation sup porting the operational functionality o f the DNS, a clearer delineation between content-related information and "technical information supporting the DNS" in terms of expec tations and obligation s of various par ties would provide desirable clarity. Recital 12 's language could permit a flawed reading that even technical information received, processed and stored by a TLD Registry, and that is largely exchanged between computers to facilit ate automated processes, may nonetheless fall within the scope of th e term "information." That in turn could impose unintended requirements on TLD Registries and subvert the Comm ission's intent that the y be regar ded as mere conduits. To en sure a consistent application, Verisign would suggest that such differentiation be included in the text of the proposal for a Digital Services Act. This will help identify the appropriate escalation path for DNS abuse mitigation to most effectively and proportionally protect the consumer.

Comments Regarding Applicability of the "Know-Your-Business-Customer" Provision to DNS Infrastructure Providers

VERISIGN | 12061 Bluemont Way | Reston, VA 20190 Verisign.com This provision should not be expanded to gTLDs because they act as mere conduits and are not online platforms. Most generic TLD Registries do not facilitate distance contracts between traders and consumers but have only B2B relationships with ICANN accredited Registrars. Thin Registries do not hold consumer data and do not interact with consumers, as Registrars are the parties tha t provide domain registratio n and ren ewal services to consumers. full_text:
Please find attached Developers Alliance's feedback on the proposal for a Regulation on a Single Market For Digital Services (Digital Services Act) and amending Directive 2000/31/EC.

Developers Alliance is a global industry association that supports software developers as entrepreneurs, innovators, and creators. DevelopersAlliance.org policy@developersalliance.org March 30 2021 Developers Alliance Position On The Digital Services Act (DSA)
I. A Horizontal Regulation On A Single Market For Digital Services 1.The Digital Services Act represents an opportunity to have an updated and harmonized framework for providing digital services across the EU. This will benefit all internet businesses, including those of software developers. The aims of the regulation, as set out by art. 1.2, should guide the co-legislators in their efforts to reach a common agreement on the text. European startups and small and medium businesses depend on a cohesive Single Market to operate cross-border and to scale up. The DSA should help them overcome the diverse landscape of national legislation on content regulation and intermediary liability. In this regard, we are also concerned about new pieces of legislation being introduced across the EU (France, Germany, Austria, Poland, Hungary, and others), as this development goes against the idea of the EU's single market. 2.We support a horizontal approach and the objective to use technology-neutral requirements. A principle-based framework is the most efficient for regulating all digital services across the EU. However, the due diligence obligations are wide-ranging for different categories of services intermediaries, depending on their size and type. Many provisions seem quite prescriptive, while others are imprecise. While we recognize the need to avoid overburdening micro and small enterprises, and we welcome the proposed exceptions from certain obligations, the regulation should preserve a principle-based approach applicable to all current and future online services intermediaries and all issues (including the migration of bad actors from large platforms to smaller ones). The DSA should provide general principles and obligations and maintain flexible implementation guidelines for regulatory, co-, and self-regulatory measures. In this way, the Digital Services Act will serve as a stable, technology-neutral legislative framework for the next decade(s). In summary, the Developers Alliance supports a Digital Services Act that is a horizontal and harmonized framework provides legal clarity and certainty sets out the right incentives to tackle illegal content.

Developers Alliance is a global industry association that supports software developers as entrepreneurs, innovators, and creators. DevelopersAlliance.org policy@developersalliance.org II. A Clear Scope 1.It is currently not clear how the provisions would apply to certain types of services. Therefore the text could be amended to make clear the nature of the services within the scope. The provisions related to the KYBC principle ("Know your business customer") are intended for specific online platforms, mostly e-commerce providers, though the scope of art. 22 seems broader. 2.The scope of the regulation should be explicitly limited to illegal content and provide a clear legal basis to remove it. The ambiguous definition of art. 2.g), combined with other provisions on due diligence obligations (Chapter III) and enforcement (Chapter IV) would pose difficulties for services intermediaries when deciding which content should be removed and would lead to unintended consequences. The regulation should provide legal clarity, especially when it comes to tackling content that is not illegal in all Member States. 3.While we appreciate the advantages of an extraterritorial scope to capture off-shore content and foreign entities, the approach risks driving SMEs to leave the EU. Rather than risk conflicting content laws from inside and outside the EU, intermediaries might simply remove themselves from the EU's jurisdiction. The regulation's proposed obligation for a legal representative (art. 11) adds further uncertainty as to whose laws will be in play for global developers. III.A Plain Set Of Rules 1.The country of origin principle is a keystone in preserving the ability of small and medium businesses to operate cross-border and benefit from the Single Market. The proposed text affirms the principle but fails to offer guarantees that it would be viable in practice. The provisions on crossborder removal rules and the governance and oversight mechanism should be adjusted in this respect. 2.The rules should provide legal clarity and certainty, so to avoid the implementation of the DSA driving interminable legal disputes. Throughout the text, a series of terms and provisions require clarification (for ex. art. 2(g) - tightening the definition of illegal content by removing the "reference to an [illegal] activity", art. 14(3) - clarifying that notice formalities do not automatically give rise to knowledge and adding much-needed safeguards for data access). 3.We welcome the harmonized notice and action mechanism as a suitable framework for the notification of illegal content by third parties. While some provisions are prescriptive, including technical details which risks the future-proofness of the regulation (e.g. art.14.para 2 and 3), others are imprecise and lead to legal uncertainty (e.g. art. 14.3 - the exact moment when the provider is presumed to have "actual knowledge or awareness", relevant for art. 4.1.e) and art. 5.1.b)). Moreover, more legal clarity is required for provisions around out-of-court dispute settlement (art. 18) and statements of reasons (art. 15), which could open up avenues for abuse and weaken content moderation systems of online platforms. 4.The Voluntary own-initiative investigations (art. 6) and the interdiction of general monitoring obligation (art. 7) are two essential principles that will allow proactive and efficient content moderation while preserving the fundamental rights of users, especially freedom of speech. Both articles should be strengthened by unambiguous language and additional provisions concerning the enforcement and oversight mechanisms under Chapter IV. The providers of intermediary services should have clear legal protection for any of their voluntary efforts to moderate content and to prevent the proliferation of harmful and illegal content.

Developers Alliance is a global industry association that supports software developers as entrepreneurs, innovators, and creators. DevelopersAlliance.org policy@developersalliance.org The implementation of the obligations imposed by the regulation and the enforcement authorities should not lead to excessive use of automation (e.g. in many cases the obligation to "act expeditiously" or "without delay" can be fulfilled solely by utilising automated tools), or to unintended censorship of legal content. We welcome the policy option for self-regulation and co-regulation for addressing emerging risks. However, the text should be clear to prevent unintended consequences of undermining fundamental rights by pushing platforms to remove harmful but legal content (art. 26 - Risk Assessment, art. 35 - Codes of conduct). 5.The implementation of obligations should be coherent with the requirements of other EU legal acts, which are also mentioned by art. 1.5 and recitals 9 and 10. The transparency obligations should be correlated with the requirements of Regulation 2019/1150 (Platform to Business Regulation) and the Directive 2019/2161 on better enforcement and modernisation of Union consumer protection rules. National authorities' data gathering powers (art. 9) should contain necessary safeguards for national authorities to access user data and match the standards of the e-Evidence Regulation. 6.With regard to online advertising, we suggest a different approach to political versus commercial advertising, due to their different nature and potential risks. We fully support more transparency in the online advertising markets. However, the additional transparency obligations in art. 30 could lead to unintended consequences (potential risk of facilitating collusion), and therefore should be carefully assessed from the perspective of preserving healthy competition. Concerning the European Parliament's call for a ban on targeted online advertising, we emphasize that the benefits of personalized advertising for both small businesses and consumers can be preserved while respecting privacy. In-app advertising not only represents the main method of monetization for many developers, driving significant revenues but also an opportunity for free/low-cost access to diverse and high-quality digital products and services for users and the comfort of receiving the ads that respond to their preferences. Users should be able to make their choice. IV.Coherent Enforcement 1.The institution of "trusted flaggers", as well as the powers of enforcement authorities, should be subject to a proportional approach, with careful consideration for preserving democratic oversight and judicial scrutiny. Additional guarantees in this sense should be added. 2.The cooperation mechanisms between the Digital Services Coordinators, the European Commission and other authorities should be streamlined and clarified, to ensure efficient enforcement of the regulation. We reiterate the importance of preserving the country of origin principle. 3.We welcome the proposal to facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct, including for online advertising. For the latter, we suggest that art. 36 should fully reflect recital 70, regarding "the involvement of a wide range of stakeholders". 4.The date of application should be set with due consideration of the necessary arrangements that both economic operators and relevant authorities need to pursue to implement the regulation.

The Civil Liberties Union for Europe submits its position to give feedback to the European Commission about the Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on a Single Market For Digital Services (Digital Services Act). See the attachment in pdf.  We strongly support that the Digital Services Act (DSA) is not an updated version of the 20-year-old eCommerce Directive but instead delivers a new concept of data economy and digital ecosystem, introducing new rules on intermediary services and the enforcement of the law. We need new rules and measures to restore the equilibrium, where the fundamental rights of users, the digital market system, and innovations are in balance. We need big platforms to change, have accountability to users, and ensure that users’ fundamental rights are respected.

The role of the big platforms has changed significantly in the past years. They have grown into state-size companies with a huge influence on democratic institutions, such as public debate, the outcome of elections, freedom of expression, and privacy.  These big tech companies enjoy the ability to monitor users’ activities and create profiles to sell or use for targeted advertising, while at the same time they are able to set the rules for content curation, access to information, and, ultimately, freedom of expression. Because of their size and power, these companies also limit the possibility of free competition and for newcomers to enter the market. These companies are not only similar size-wise and financially to a state, but they also impose regulation on users through terms of services and act as privatized law enforcement entities to regulate speech and avoid liability for user content set out in the laws. Now DSA offers an opportunity to change this system for the better. 

In the attachment, Liberties analyzes the rules of the proposed DSA and flags the elements that need to be revised. Our approach is based on fundamental rights. We need legislation that serves to better protect consumers and fundamental rights online, establishing a powerful transparency and accountability framework for online platforms, and leading to fairer and more open digital markets.
