EMMA and ENPA's Position paper

on the proposal for a Regulation on a Single Market for Digital Services (COM(2020) 825) - hereafter the Digital Services Act (DSA): Version 12/03/2021

Executive Summary

1. Editorial platforms must be explicitly excluded from the scope of the new obligations of Chapter III DSA as they jeopardize the freedom of the press and editorial freedom

Newspapers and magazines depend on the possibility to offer third parties, their readers, the ability to comment or contribute to comment sections, editorial forums and communities in the context of their publications. These offerings are intermediary services according to the DSA. Such services are not merely optional add-ons that can be discontinued without any effect on the publications' journalistic and economic success. Rather, they are usually integral parts of the publication, indispensable to enable readers to engage in discussions with each other and with the editorial team.

The propose d content control obligations of Chapter III DSA woul d create disproportionate and impossible burdens for those editorial platforms and jeopardise editorial freedom. These platforms generally don't provide any direct revenue to publishers and therefore any additional burden would render them impossible to operate. As a result, spaces for qualitative and serious discussions online would be diminished and the gatekeeper platforms would entrench their control over the formation of opinion online.

We therefore call on all decision makers to exclude all editorial platforms from the scope of these obligations.

2. The DSA should not legally legitimize the arbitrary exclusion of legal publications from distribution on very large platforms

Digital platforms are increasingly indispensable distribution channels for the free, digital press. This is especially true for so-called gatekeeper platforms which play an important role in shaping the public opinion. Such gatekeep er platforms should not be allowed to exclude legitimate publications from public discussion on the basis of general terms and conditions. Publications which are legally available offline must also be available online on very large platforms.

Already today, these gatekeepers often decide arbitrarily which publication has a chance on the readers and advertising markets. It is therefore an essential prerequisite for the preservation of a free and pluralistic press to ensure fair and non-discriminatory distribution of all digital press publications on gatekeeper platforms. Instead of restoring or ensuring non-discriminatory distribution of press publications on gatekeeper platforms, however, the content control obligations, including those targeted for very large online platforms of the DSA would legitimise the fact that the boundaries of press freedom on those gatekeeper platforms are no longer the general laws, but the terms and conditions of gatekeeper platforms.

Therefore, what is legally available offline must also be legally available online on gatekeeper platforms. In addition, all legal editorial publications should be distributed in a non - discriminatory manner.

A. Main considerations and necessary changes

I. Editorial platforms must be explicitly excluded from the scope of the new obligations of Chapter III DSA as they jeopardize the freedom of the press and editorial freedom

It must be ensured that the disproportionate obligations of Chapter III DSA are not imposed on editorial platforms of press publishers. In Article 2(h) in combination with Recital 13, the proposal provides that comment sections of newspapers and magazines are excluded from certain obligations of Chapter III. This is however not enough to protect the free press. This exclusion must be extended to all obligations under Chapter III and include all editorial platforms, including reader communities and discussions forums.

The existing obligations under Directive 2000/31/EC (ECD) to immediately remove or block unlawful content such as unlawful reader comments, etc. and to take reasonable steps to prevent a recurrence, already impose significant and entirely sufficient obligations on publishers and their platform offerings to deploy capacities for the monitoring and often complex factual and legal assessment of user content and t he implementation of corresponding assessments on discussion forums, comment sections, editorial communities, etc. We therefore are opposed to the extension of the obligations laid down in Chapter III DS A to all intermediary services, including the editorial platforms such as comment sections, readers' forums, editorial communities, etc.

Press publishers which provide their readers with opportunities to express themselves on editorial platforms do so in exercise of their own fundamental rights and freedoms. Publishers and editors are therefore free, on the basis of their own fundamental rights and their editorial freedom, to decide to what extent and under what conditions they admit reader comments, and to what extent they want to review user complaints about denied opportunities to express themselves, etc.

The far-reaching obligations set out in Section 1, 2 and 3 of Chapter III DSA would however also apply to these integral components of the digital press and constitute a disproportionate restriction of the fundamental communication rights and editorial freedom of editorial platforms. The fundamental freedom of the press includes both the freedom to allow any legal commentary and, according to its own editorial standards, not to allow legally admissible comments from the outset or to remove them after publication. In practice, publishers often apply higher standards than the mere compliance with general laws. This generally applies to both the content itself, as well as the form of comment. For example, disparaging remarks can generally be made inadmissible on the editorial platforms, although criticism of disparaging nature is often legal. The respective editorial orientation of the publisher or publication can lead to the inadmissibility of certain legal statements that would appear unproblematic with a different editorial orientation. All this is protected by press freedom.

Yet, the obligations in Chapter III, for example Articles 12 to 19 DSA would impose disproportionate obligations on editorial platforms by obliging them t o lay out all content moderation policies in the general terms and conditions and publish at least once a year a detailed report on the content moderation enforced. It would also oblige publishers to set up a harmonized notice and action mechanism and an obligation to provide a statement of reason for any removed or disabled reader comment etc. These editorial platforms, while they are integral parts of the digital press and indispensable for the success of a digital publication are generally not generating revenues.

Hence, the mere obligation to increase staff in order to comply with the obligations would render these platforms impossible to operate and would most likely have to be discontinued. In addition, these editorial platforms play an important role in the formation of public opinion. Any reduction of such offers

on the market would only further shift the formation of public opinion online to the few gatekeeper platforms.

Concrete examples of forums and reader communities which handle the necessary content control in a situation-specific and efficient manner and which would be endangered, both journalistically and economically, by any additional content control procedures and harmonized complaint mechanisms:

1. The forum of a house and garden magazine serves the primary objective of giving readers the possibility to exchange experiences about gardens, gardening etc. It exists since 15 years and has now 3.5 million contributions and 185,000 users. The forum has a netiquette to which the users must adhere. Problematic contributions are rare. The moderation is handled by long-time forum members who are appointed moderators by the editorial staff. Only in exceptional cases does the editorial staff moderate, delete or comment on contributions. If the editorial staff would have to set up and operate a dedicated and formalized content control system, a full-time employee for the forum would be required. In such a scenario the forum would no longer be able to cover its costs and would most likely have to be closed and discontinued.

2. The online community of a computer magazine exists since 1995 and is thus even older than the digital version of the magazine itself. As a forum in today's sense, the platform has existed for at least 23 yea rs (1998). Today the forum has more than 2 million registered accounts and several hundred thousand active users. The platform is maintained by a part-time employee who is supported by long-time forum members on a voluntary basis. The forum is very important for readers of both the digital and printed versions of the magazine. If a dedicated and formalized content or complaint management system would be imposed, the forum would be required to hire one or two additional employees. These additional costs could not be generated and covered by the forum and would as a consequence have to be closed.

3. The forum of an IT magazine's online publication exists for more than 20 years and has around 670,000 registered users who during this period have posted more than 37 million contributions on all conceivable technical, economic, social and political aspects of the digital world. During peak times of the day, three contributions per second are posted on the forum. The several million readers of user posts generate around 30 million page views per month. The posted content is not only used for discussion among readers. It also provides valuable suggestions and corrections for the editorial team. The forum is managed by the editors responsible for respective topics, who are supported by forum members on a voluntary basis. An obligation to introduce a formalized content control system with organizational or procedural obligations would in fact only be possible with the support of additional personnel and additional cos ts. Such additional human and financial resources would exceed the possibilities of the publisher and could not be afforded. Considering the fact that the forum has only dealt with a handful of complaints over the past years, such content control systems would neither be necessary nor appropriate.

4. The online-discussion platform focused on law and taxation has been operated by a specialised press publisher since 2009. The platform, which is designed for professional exchanges amongst experts, could not continue to exist in this form if content controls with administrative and procedural requirements were imposed on the publisher, as the additional personnel required to comply with the new obligations, and thus ultimately the costs relating to the necessa ry changes, would be disproportionate to the economic value generated by the platform.

We therefore call on all decision makers to exclude all editorial platforms from the scope of these obligations.

II. Non-discriminatory distribution of the press online - the DSA should not legitimize by law the arbitrary deletion of legal publications on very large platforms. Publications available offline must also be available online on very large platforms

Furthermore, we believe that the DSA will endang er the freedom and diversity of the press on the regulated very large platforms, which are increasingly important distributions channels for the digital press.

In fact, these gatekeeper platforms - or very large platforms according to Section 4 of the DSA - due to their size and reach often represent a part of the public space. As such, access to this very digital public space is almost indispensable for any actor involved in the formation of public opinion. It is therefore of utmost importance that such gatekeeper platforms cannot control and restrict this public opinion market by enforcing its own political, ideological or religious tendencies according to its terms and conditions. Publications which are legally available offline and sold and distribute d in kiosks etc. must also be available online in the same manner. Ensuring fair and non-discriminatory distribution of all legal press publications on gatekeeper platforms is therefore an essential prerequisite for maintaining a free and pluralistic press in a world increasingly dominated by such quasi-monopolies.

Ideally, such very large platforms should be prohibited from limiting press freedom on their gatekeeper platforms by deleting and excluding legal publications on the basis of their own general terms and conditions. Should such practices however not be prohibited explicitly, it would be unacceptable if a law would actually legitimize and encourage this practice of very large platforms.

Unfortunately, this is exactly what the DSA seems to provide: the DSA explicitly authorizes very large platforms to block legal publications or show them with reduced visibility based on their own T&Cs.

Articles 12 and 13 entail transparency and reporting obligations in relation to terms and conditions as well as content moderation. These provisions de facto grant very large platforms the right to block, delete, etc. legal content and publications on the basis of their own terms and conditions. Such platforms would only have to provide transparency according to w hich guidelines, procedures, etc. the content is approved or deleted. This right for gatekeepers is incompatible with the necessary fair and non-discriminatory distribution of all legal publications.

In addition, Article 29 DSA is limited to very large pl atforms and provides additional transparency obligations in the terms and conditions for the applied recommender systems. This provision would again authorise gatekeeper platforms to block legal publications or to show them with reduced visibility on the basis of their own terms and conditions. Merely obliging such very large platforms to be more transparent about the exclusion of legal publications from their gatekeeper platforms does in no way safeguard press freedom. Such recommender systems of such gate keeper platforms must be designed in a non-discriminatory manner and based on non-discriminatory parameter. Otherwise, gatekeeper platforms could exclude publications from competition at their own discretion and thus determine the journalistic and economic success of a publication.

We also have concerns with the current proposal on crisis protocols in Article 37 DSA. In particular paragraph 2a provides the possibility to highlight certain information provided by public authorities on gatekeeper platforms. Without a clear limitation in scope such a general provision is concerning and unacceptable, as we cannot see how it can be sufficiently ensured that such crisis protocols would

not favour publicly provided information over comparable offerings by the free press on gatekeeper platforms. Safeguarding freedom of the press must also be ensured in this context.

In conclusion, we believe that the DSA would further jeopardize press freedom on those gatekeeper platforms. The fact that the EU or a member state grants a monopoly platforms the right to decide which legal speech and publications protected by fundamental rights are admissible and which are not in such an important p art of the public sphere does not seem acceptable. It would endanger the preservation of a pluralistic and free press. If a proposal aims to regulate this aspect, it must on the contrary ensure that what is legally available offline must also be legally available online on such gatekeeper platforms, and that all legal editorial publications are distributed in a non-discriminatory manner thereon.

III. Disproportionate obligations also for commercial platforms of publishers

Also important for publishers are complementary commercial platforms that have substituted formerly typical lines of business in publishing such as classified ads and emerged as new business models (e.g. career portals of newspapers and magazines) or otherwise expand the publishing business in the context of the publication and its competence (e.g. rating and comparison platforms, vertical product search, etc.).

These complementary commercial platforms are indispensable for many publishers but generally do not have high profit margins. Additional costs imposed due to the necessity to comply with politically imposed additional obligations could therefore hardly be borne. In this they differ from the gatekeeper platforms, which easily shoulder any burden of cont rol with their monopoly profits. As such, these gatekeeper platforms would even be strengthened due the anticompetitive effects of such obligations.

The obligations imposed on those commercial platforms under the current ECD already ensure that publishers must take adequate precautions to be able to respond to complaints in a timely manner. Otherwise, publishers would become liable for the illegal third-party content. However, the rigid content control requirements now envisaged in Chapter III DSA place a disproportionate burden on these publishers' commercial platforms. Such additional requirements would make it even more difficult for publishers to maintain their media activities in the future.

IV. Chapter II DSA - Liability of providers of intermediary services

Articles 3, 4, 5 and 7 DSA replace Article 10 to 15 of the ECD. The proposal basically maintains the liability concept for online intermediaries and continues to distinguish between "mere conduit", "caching" and "hosting" services. This liability concept is correct and remains indispensable for democracy and a free press. In contrast, any legal tightening of the editors' liability for reader comments etc. would hit the free press hard without any comprehensible reason or recognisable justification.

It is also to be welcomed that Article 6 DSA states that voluntary measures against illegal content may not in themselves lead to the loss of liability privileges.

With regard to Articles 8 DSA, it is not clear whether this constitutes a new exception to Article 3 ECD. Questions arise in particular from Recital 33 DSA, which states that orders addressed to providers established in another Member State do not in principle restrict the freedom of these providers to provide their services across borders, and that therefore the provisions of Article 3 of the

ECD should not apply to such orders. In any case, it must be ensured that cross-border orders may only concern the dissemination of content in the issuing state and never prohibit the dissemination in the service provider's home country. It is the legitimate purpose of the exceptions to the country of origin principle in Article 3 ECD that a state must be able to prohibit unlawful publications in its territory even if they are sent from another member state. On the other hand, it would unacceptable if the issuing state of such order could also prevent communication in the home country of the provider.

B. Considerations on specific provisions

• Definition of online platform (Article 2.h)

We believe that no new additional legal responsibilities or obligations are necessary or proportionate for publishers' platforms. Therefore, publishers' editorial and commercial platforms should not fall under the new obligations for intermediaries, hosting providers or online platforms. This is in particular true for the different editorial platforms of press publishers, which are integral parts of the digital free press and are protected by press freedom.

The exception of ancillary features in Article 2 (h) and Recital 13 seems to exclude comment sections from the scope of the definition and "online platforms". This is insufficient, as obligations for intermediaries and hosting providers would still apply. Secondly, and equally important, discussion forums and reader communities would not be covered by this exception and would still be obliged to implement all these obligations.

• Orders to act against illegal content and to provide information (Articles 8 and 9)

As a preliminary remark, we must stress the importance of preserving the country of origin principle which establishes that any publication can operate across the single market, insofar as it complies with the legal requirements of its country of establishment. Maintaining this principle is essential in a networked digital environment, where online publications can be accessed in all 27 European Member States.

While Article 8 and 9 are unclear and ambiguous, it is fundamental that conditions of cross-border cooperation do not impose on intermediary services to respond to requests from any Member State.

• Points of contact (Article 10)

When it comes to mega-platforms, we believe that one single point of contact for all Member States would not be appropriate. Instead, such platforms should have a presence in each of the Member States where they are operating.

• Terms and conditions and transparency reporting obligations (Articles 12 and 13)

Additional transparency and further obligations on terms and conditions would impose a disproportionate burden on publishers' platforms and undermine press and editorial freedom. It would be sheer impossible for press publishers to continue operating editorial platforms which generally do not provide revenue streams but constitute an integral part of the digital press. (see A.I above)

In addition, when it comes to gate-keeper platforms, publications which are legally available offline must also be available online. Already today, the se gatekeepers often decide arbitrarily which

publication has a chance on the readers and advertising markets. It is therefore an essential prerequisite for the preservation of a free and pluralistic press to ensure fair and non-discriminatory distribution of all digital press publications on gatekeeper platforms. Instead of restoring or ensuring non-discriminatory distribution of press publications on gatekeeper platforms, however, the content control obligations, including those targeted for very large online platforms of the DSA would actually legitimise the fact that the boundaries of press freedom on those gatekeeper platforms are no longer the general laws, but the terms and conditions of gatekeeper platforms.

• Notice and action mechanisms and statement of reasons (Articles 14 and 15)

The new obligations, including a rigid and harmonized notice and action mechanism in combination with the obligation to provide statements of reason would render indispensable parts of the digital press more expen sive and difficult to operate. This is especially problematic since the se editorial platforms largely provide no revenue streams and the digital press generally has no financial leeway for further costs or burdens. Even the mere necessity to increase staff to comply with such obligations could force publishers to close such offers. The press sector and their editorial and commercial offerings should therefore be excluded from such burdensome obligations. Already today, press publishers under the current E-Commerce Directive ensure that adequate precautions and actions are taken in order to respond to complaints in a timely manner. If such an obligation would nonetheless be imposed, it must be necessarily limited to very large megaplatforms.

• Internal complaint-handling mechanism and out of court dispute settlement (Articles 17 and 18)

The establishment of an internal complaint-handling and out of court dispute settlement mechanisms would be costly to set up and operate therefore further undermining the financing opportunities for the editorial work of the publishers. The proposal also provides that the cost are essentially in every case shouldered by the publisher, should it come to such a dispute settlement. In addition, it is up to the courts, and not private platforms, to decide whether content is illegal or not, and which measures should be taken to address it. Ultimately, the specific obligations on how to deal with a sufficiently substantiated complaint, the urgency of the situation and its remedies etc. are decided by the courts, which in each specific case consider all fundamental rights and circumstances at stake.

Therefore, imposing additional burdens on editorial platforms through imposing specific procedures or other obligations would not be justified. On the contrary, it would be a disproportionate and even counterproductive restriction of press freedom.

• Trusted flaggers (Article 19)

Legally obliging platforms, including editorial platforms, to cooperate with trusted flaggers would be disproportionate and raises a number of important questions, for example on which basis and by what standards should such a decision be taken? How can it be ensured that such flaggers are in no way biased when it comes to content? Who determines the illegality of content?

Such obligations seem prone to establish a mixture of private and state control over the boundaries of freedom of expression. We therefore firmly oppose such content policing which would impose a severe risk on press freedom and freedom of expression.

• Online advertising transparency (Article 24)

Current advertising systems do not always allow such identification. In many cases, the information requested (under Article 24.c) is held by the advertiser provider and not by the platform on which the advertisement is displayed. These new obligations wou ld apply to our editorial communities as well as on our commercial platforms which feed and finance the editorial content.

In addition, we firmly believe that advertising issues should not be discussed within the DSA.

• Recommender systems (Article 29)

We believe that more transparency in relation to recommender systems deployed by very large online platforms are not enough. Instead, and in order to avoid the concerns raised in section II b) of this paper, the regulation must ensure that such recommender systems by gatekeeper platforms are not only transparent, but also non-discriminatory. Recommender systems should therefore be able to offer content based on non-discriminatory parameters such as performance data, topical filters etc, but i t would be a serios risk for press freedom if such recommender systems of gatekeeper platforms enable the discrimination between legal publications, for example, by favouring or demoting legal publications that third parties consider to be trustworthy or not.

• Codes of conduct (Articles 35 and 36)

As a principle, we do not support any measure going beyond self-regulation and would therefore be opposed to any imposition on mega-platforms to develop codes of practice.

• Crisis protocols (Article 37)

Press publishers are concerned about the prospect of promoting public communications and announcements, including on gatekeeper platforms and even if limited to "extraordinary circumstances affecting public security or public health ". It is not clear to us how such provisions ensure that information provided through crisis protocols is not favoured on gatekeeper platforms compared to comparable offers of the free press.

In addition, Article 37.2 extends the potential imposition to "other online platforms". Suh an imposition of content on the press would constitute a severe breach of editorial freedom and be incompatible with press freedom. In relation to other platforms, such measures would under mine freedom of expression and potentially other fundamental rights.

• Powers of the Digital Services Coordinators (Articles 38 and 41)

We believe that the powers of investigations of the Digital Services Coordinators as invested in Article 41 are disproportionate and too far-reaching.

In addition, the appointment by national authorities of Digital Services Coordinators would be particularly problematic in Member States where the plurality of views in the media is being challenged by governments. This body and its far-reaching invested powers would be used as a tool to curtail press freedom.

We therefore call on all decision makers to exclude all editorial platforms from the scope of these obligations. 2. The DSA should not legally legitimize the arbitrary exclusion of legal publications from distribution on very large platforms

Digital platforms are increasingly indispensable distribution channels for the free, digital press. This is especially true for so-called gatekeeper platforms which play an important role in shaping the public opinion. Such gatekeep er platforms should not be allowed to exclude legitimate publications from public discussion on the basis of general terms and conditions. Publications which are legally available offline must also be available online on very large platforms. Already today, these gatekeepers often decide arbitrarily which publication has a chance on the readers and advertising markets. It is therefore an essential prerequisite for the preservation of a free and pluralistic press to ensure fair and non-discriminatory distribution of all digital press publications on gatekeeper platforms. Instead of restoring or ensuring non-discriminatory distribution of press publications on gatekeeper platforms, however, the content control obligations, including those targeted for very large online platforms of the DSA would legitimise the fact that the boundaries of press freedom on those gatekeeper platforms are no longer the general laws, but the terms and conditions of gatekeeper platforms. Therefore, what is legally available offline must also be legally available online on gatekeeper platforms. In addition, all legal editorial publications should be distributed in a non - discriminatory manner. A. Main considerations and necessary changes

I. Editorial platforms must be explicitly excluded from the scope of the new obligations of Chapter III DSA as they jeopardize the freedom of the press and editorial freedom

It must be ensured that the disproportionate obligations of Chapter III DSA are not imposed on editorial platforms of press publishers. In Article 2(h) in combination with Recital 13, the proposal provides that comment sections of newspapers and magazines are excluded from certain obligations of Chapter III. This is however not enough to protect the free press. This exclusion must be extended to all obligations under Chapter III and include all editorial platforms, including reader communities and discussions forums. The existing obligations under Directive 2000/31/EC (ECD) to immediately remove or block unlawful content such as unlawful reader comments, etc.

This exclusion must be extended to all obligations under Chapter III and include all editorial platforms, including reader communities and discussions forums. The existing obligations under Directive 2000/31/EC (ECD) to immediately remove or block unlawful content such as unlawful reader comments, etc. and to take reasonable steps to prevent a recurrence, already impose significant and entirely sufficient obligations on publishers and their platform offerings to deploy capacities for the monitoring and often complex factual and legal assessment of user content and t he implementation of corresponding assessments on discussion forums, comment sections, editorial communities, etc. We therefore are opposed to the extension of the obligations laid down in Chapter III DS A to all intermediary services, including the editorial platforms such as comment sections, readers' forums, editorial communities, etc. Press publishers which provide their readers with opportunities to express themselves on editorial platforms do so in exercise of their own fundamental rights and freedoms. Publishers and editors are therefore free, on the basis of their own fundamental rights and their editorial freedom, to decide to what extent and under what conditions they admit reader comments, and to what extent they want to review user complaints about denied opportunities to express themselves, etc. The far-reaching obligations set out in Section 1, 2 and 3 of Chapter III DSA would however also apply to these integral components of the digital press and constitute a disproportionate restriction of the fundamental communication rights and editorial freedom of editorial platforms. The fundamental freedom of the press includes both the freedom to allow any legal commentary and, according to its own editorial standards, not to allow legally admissible comments from the outset or to remove them after publication. In practice, publishers often apply higher standards than the mere compliance with general laws. This generally applies to both the content itself, as well as the form of comment. For example, disparaging remarks can generally be made inadmissible on the editorial platforms, although criticism of disparaging nature is often legal. The respective editorial orientation of the publisher or publication can lead to the inadmissibility of certain legal statements that would appear unproblematic with a different editorial orientation. All this is protected by press freedom.

All this is protected by press freedom. Yet, the obligations in Chapter III, for example Articles 12 to 19 DSA would impose disproportionate obligations on editorial platforms by obliging them t o lay out all content moderation policies in the general terms and conditions and publish at least once a year a detailed report on the content moderation enforced. It would also oblige publishers to set up a harmonized notice and action mechanism and an obligation to provide a statement of reason for any removed or disabled reader comment etc. These editorial platforms, while they are integral parts of the digital press and indispensable for the success of a digital publication are generally not generating revenues. Hence, the mere obligation to increase staff in order to comply with the obligations would render these platforms impossible to operate and would most likely have to be discontinued. In addition, these editorial platforms play an important role in the formation of public opinion. Any reduction of such offers

on the market would only further shift the formation of public opinion online to the few gatekeeper platforms. If the editorial staff would have to set up and operate a dedicated and formalized content control system, a full-time employee for the forum would be required. As a forum in today's sense, the platform has existed for at least 23 yea rs (1998). Today the forum has more than 2 million registered accounts and several hundred thousand active users. The platform is maintained by a part-time employee who is supported by long-time forum members on a voluntary basis. The forum is very important for readers of both the digital and printed versions of the magazine. These additional costs could not be generated and covered by the forum and would as a consequence have to be closed. 3. The posted content is not only used for discussion among readers. It also provides valuable suggestions and corrections for the editorial team. The forum is managed by the editors responsible for respective topics, who are supported by forum members on a voluntary basis. INDICAM accoglie positivamente la proposta “Digital Services Act” (DSA) della Commissione Europea, come primo importante passo per assicurare un ambiente digitale più trasparente e sicuro per i consumatori e più attento alla tutela dei diritti di proprietà intellettuale e al know-how delle aziende, senza con ciò limitare i diritti e le libertà fondamentali.

Rispetto al contenuto della proposta, riteniamo che sia rilevante, al fine di perseguire in maniera efficace gli obiettivi che il DSA si prepone:
- includere un obbligo di implementazione di misure proattive per prevenire la comparsa di prodotti illeciti sul web; purtroppo, le sole azioni volontarie non risultano essere uno strumento sufficiente per arginare il fenomeno del commercio illegale
- prevedere un meccanismo di "stay-down" che impedisca ai contenuti illegali già accertati come tali di riapparire continuamente sulle piattaforme; omettere una simile misura comporta un enorme dispendio di risorse, soprattutto in capo a chi subisce il danno

INDICAM POSITION - DIGITAL SERVICES ACT

INDICAM accoglie positivamente la proposta " Digital Services Act " (DSA) della Commissione Europea, come primo importante passo per assicurare un ambiente digitale più trasparente e sicuro per i consumatori e più attento alla tutela dei diritti di proprietà intellettuale e al know-how delle aziende, senza con ciò limitare i diritti e le libertà fondamentali. Le trasformazioni che da vent'anni a questa parte hanno interessato il mondo online hanno garantito opportunità di business e sono state stimolo per la conoscenz a, la crescita e lo sviluppo di nuove forme di impresa e accesso a beni e servizi per il pubblico. Tuttavia, è innegabile che l'era digitale abbia presentato, allo stesso tempo, rischi e sfide sotto il profilo della sicurezza dei prodotti offerti sul web, sollecitando la comunità di portatori di interesse a chiedersi cosa potesse essere migliorato nel corrente assetto normativo per garantire agli utenti di fruire delle opportunità di Internet senza l'ombra di un'informazione opaca e ingannevole e della minaccia posta da cybercrimes e commercio illegale. Per tale motivo, il DSA rappresenta un'occasione cruciale per assicurare da un lato la protezione dei consumatori nell'accesso a prodotti leciti e sicuri, dall'altro la tutela delle imprese e del loro patrimonio di investimenti, perché, come affermato dalla stessa Commissione, "ciò che è illegale offline deve essere illegale online " e i fornitori di servizi digitali costituiscono un tassello essenziale per garantire ciò. A tal proposito, è importante rilevare la sussistenza di una profonda separazione tra prevenzione del commercio di prodotti illegali e tutela della libertà di espressione: includere misure proattive tra le misure richieste agli online service providers per mantenere un ecosistema digital e sicuro e trasparente è qualcosa di significativamente differente dal monitoraggio sulle opinioni o i contenuti generati dagli utenti. Un prodotto illecito non può costituire nulla di controverso dal momento in cui la sua illiceità sia stata accertata e, d'altro lato, tali garanzie sono le medesime cui devono sottostare i venditori tradizionali: non ci sono quindi ragioni per cui le regole dovrebbero essere differenti quando parliamo di e-commerce. Per il medesimo motivo, si ritiene che, per assicurare l'accesso ad un mercato pulito da beni illeciti, a prescindere dalla grandezza, tutti i fornitori di servizi digitali siano tenuti a garantire la tutela del consumatore e dei diritti di proprietà intellettuale: e questo è p ossibile solo attraverso una appropriata due diligence per avere contezza di chi sono i soggetti che sfruttano tali servizi digitali (il c.d. protocollo " Know your Business Customer ") e trasparenza nei confronti degli utenti. Sono elementi che dovrebbero costituire la soglia minima da sostenere per fare business, indipendentemente dal fatto che si tratti di piccole, medie o grandi piattaforme. Infatti, se è impensabile un qualsiasi tipo di esenzione per le piattaforme più piccole in caso di traffico di stupefacenti o armi, lo stesso deve valere anche per i prodotti contraffatti, parimenti rischiosi sotto il profilo della salute e della sicurezza. È poi sicuramente da lodare l'introduzione di un obbligo per le piattaforme di raccogliere e verificare determinate informazioni sui venditori che utilizzano i loro servizi, ma per ottenere i risultati cui la proposta legislativa ambisce - un ambiente digitale giusto, sicuro, trasparente - si ritiene opportuno estendere il novero di soggetti tenuti a tale due diligence.

Qualunque soggetto voglia sfruttare il web per business, ha bisogno, per esempio, di un nome a dominio, di un sito web accessibile agli utenti, di pubblicità e di un servizio di pagamento: tali intermediari dovrebbero essere tenuti a verificare l'identità della persona con cui entrano in affari, a sapere che si tratta di qualcuno di affidabile che si muove nel rispetto delle rego le. Non si tratta di un controllo sul comportamento del cliente, ma di una semplice verifica sull'identità dello stesso, anche sulla base di dati disponibili pubblicamente. Qualora sia accertato che il soggetto menta sulle proprie generalità, è importante che tali intermediari interrompano i loro servizi e informino le autorità. D'altro canto, i titolari di diritto non hanno contezza circa l'identità di un richiedente di nome a dominio che apre il proprio sito web per ven dere prodotti illegali o di un venditore che sfrutta una piattaforma di e-commerce per pubblicizzare merce contraffatta. Tali dati sono visibili solamente ai fornitori di servizi digitali, che, nel rispetto delle norme applicabili, devono essere tenuti a condividere i contatti e l'identità del trasgressore con titolari di diritto e forze dell'ordine. Se davvero vogliamo vedere una riduzione significativa - se non una scomparsa definitiva - dei prodotti illeciti online, ciascun anello della catena che si interpone tra bad actor e consumatore finale deve essere coinvolto. Pertanto, se un fornitore di servizi digita li non intenda verificare l'identità dei suoi clienti, non dovrebbe essere ammesso al regime di esenzione di responsabilità. Si ricorda, infine, come già l'Art. 5 della stessa Direttiva E-Commerce, spesso rimasto inapplicato, prevedeva tali obblighi informativi. Tornando alla proposta della Commissione, l 'Art. 5 condiziona, correttamente, l'esenzione di responsabilità all'assenza di un ruolo attivo da parte del digital service provider. Sarebbe però utile chiarire quando si profili un ruolo attivo in capo alla piattaforma. Un ulteriore punto cruciale, che risulta tuttavia assente nel testo della proposta, è l'introduzione di misure proattive e preventive obbligatorie per contrastare il traffico di prodotti illegali. Se ciò che è illecito offline è illecito online, come i rivenditori nell'ambiente fisico sono tenuti a offrire e vendere beni leciti e a far fronte ad eventuali infiltrazioni di prodotti vietati dalla legge, la medesima considerazione dovrebbe essere richiesta agli operatori digitali. La previsione di misure "volontarie" svolte "in buona fede e in maniera diligente", come recita il consideranda 25, non può essere sufficiente nella lotta al mercato illegale: è necessario che vi sia una regola vincolante che obblighi i fornitori di servizi online al medesimo duty of care richiesto ai venditori offline. Inoltre, se a seguito di (1) una misura posta proattivamente in atto dalla piattaforma, (2) un ordine di una corte di giustizia, (3) una notifica del titolare di diritto che accerta la natura illecita di un prodotto, quest'ultimo viene rimosso, si ritiene sia necessario anche impedire che prodotti identici riappaiono subito dopo la rimozione. In questo modo si eviterebbe uno spreco di risorse per la piattaforma che pone in essere controlli e blocchi, per il tribunale che deve emettere un nuovo ordine per ciascun listing in violazione, per il titolare di diritto che con ingenti dispendi economici deve effettuare un monitoraggio costante e procedere a notificare le offerte illecite in maniera continuativa. È evidente che un meccanismo di c.d. " stay-down", specifico, limitato e proporzionato, sarebbe compatibile con il divieto di monitoraggio generale proposto dalla Commissione e assolutamente fattibile sul piano pratico, se guardiamo agli strumenti tecnologici già in uso tra le piattaforme (basati su parole chiave e riconoscimento immagine, ad esempio).

Accogliamo poi positivamente l'introduzione di meccanismi di "notice & take down" più snelli e accessibili, aggiungendo che sarebbe utile permett ere di notificare il seller trasgressore e a cascata tutti i listings cui questo fanno capo. In tale contesto, sarebbe altresì apprezzabile includere un obbligo di inform azione al consumatore che abbia acquistato un prodotto illecito, rendendolo edotto della rimozione dell'annuncio e della ragione sottostante tale rimozione. Non si deve assumere che gli utenti siano sempre consapevoli della natura illegale dei beni che acquistano. Inoltre, sensibilizzare i consumatori sull'esistenza d i prodotti illeciti sui canali online nei quali rimettono massima fiducia, significa renderli più attenti a futuri raggiri e contribuire a spezzare l'ultimo anello della catena del mercato illegale, che mette la merce direttamente nelle mani dell'utente finale. Guardando alle misure di trasparenza previste a beneficio dei venditori circa la ragione della rimozione di un contenuto in seguito a notifica, si assiste ad una certa asimmetria tra quanto richiesto al ti tolare di diritto che notifica un annuncio in violazione e il seller che asserisce invece che la merce che vende è lecita, ponendo l'onere della prova in capo al primo, senza invece esigere lo stesso obbligo informativo dal secondo.

Inoltre, se da un lato risulta apprezzabile l'istituzione della categoria " segnalatori affidabili", dall'altro si ritiene opportuno includervi anche i titolari di diritto e non solo le organizzazioni che li rappresentano: nel caso della contraffazione, proprio i brand owner sono i soggetti in grado di confermare la natura autentica o meno del prodotto, velocizzando in tal mondo il processo di rimozione.

Per quanto concerne i trasgressori recidivi, si chiede che sia prevista, insieme alla sospensione, la possibilità di estromettere definitivamente dalla piattaforma il soggetto che abbia attuato reiterate condotte illecite. Fare altrimenti significherebbe non porre alcun vero deterrente a chi agisce in maniera impropria sul web, mettendo in pericolo la salute e sicurezza degli utenti. Per la medesima ragione, tali soggetti non dovrebbero in alcun modo essere avvertiti, di nuovo, della loro imminente sospensione, mentre dall'altro lato chi subisce il danno spende ingenti risorse per contrastare la comparsa di prodotti illegali online, non solo a proprio beneficio, ma anche, se non soprattutto, per tutelare i consumatori. Obbligare le piattaforme ad una verifica dell'identità dei seller serve proprio a questo, per evitare che uno stesso soggetto con diversi account offra merce in violazione sottraendosi alle sanzioni e moltiplicando i guadagni.

La contraffazione rappresenta un fenomeno di portata globale, che altera la concorrenza, danneggia l'economia lecita e mette a rischio la salute e sicurezza dei consumatori, alimentando allo stesso tempo le casse della criminalità organizzata. Nel 2016 il valore della merce contraffatta circolante nel mondo era di quasi 510 miliardi di euro, di cui 121 miliardi riferiti al contesto europeo. E Internet ha rappresentato un canale perfetto per incrementare gli affari illegali e dilatare i profitti. Per questo motivo la proposta DSA costituisce un'occasione unica per migliorare le regole alla base del mercato digitale. Un deciso cambio di rotta che meritano gli utenti che credono e investono nell'esperienza online, le imprese che si presentano in maniera legittima per offrire i propri beni e servizi e l'Europa stessa, per diventare presenza leader dell'era digitale.

Guardando alle misure di trasparenza previste a beneficio dei venditori circa la ragione della rimozione di un contenuto in seguito a notifica, si assiste ad una certa asimmetria tra quanto richiesto al ti tolare di diritto che notifica un annuncio in violazione e il seller che asserisce invece che la merce che vende è lecita, ponendo l'onere della prova in capo al primo, senza invece esigere lo stesso obbligo informativo dal secondo. Inoltre, se da un lato risulta apprezzabile l'istituzione della categoria " segnalatori affidabili", dall'altro si ritiene opportuno includervi anche i titolari di diritto e non solo le organizzazioni che li rappresentano: nel caso della contraffazione, proprio i brand owner sono i soggetti in grado di confermare la natura autentica o meno del prodotto, velocizzando in tal mondo il processo di rimozione. Per quanto concerne i trasgressori recidivi, si chiede che sia prevista, insieme alla sospensione, la possibilità di estromettere definitivamente dalla piattaforma il soggetto che abbia attuato reiterate condotte illecite. Fare altrimenti significherebbe non porre alcun vero deterrente a chi agisce in maniera impropria sul web, mettendo in pericolo la salute e sicurezza degli utenti. Per la medesima ragione, tali soggetti non dovrebbero in alcun modo essere avvertiti, di nuovo, della loro imminente sospensione, mentre dall'altro lato chi subisce il danno spende ingenti risorse per contrastare la comparsa di prodotti illegali online, non solo a proprio beneficio, ma anche, se non soprattutto, per tutelare i consumatori. Obbligare le piattaforme ad una verifica dell'identità dei seller serve proprio a questo, per evitare che uno stesso soggetto con diversi account offra merce in violazione sottraendosi alle sanzioni e moltiplicando i guadagni. La contraffazione rappresenta un fenomeno di portata globale, che altera la concorrenza, danneggia l'economia lecita e mette a rischio la salute e sicurezza dei consumatori, alimentando allo stesso tempo le casse della criminalità organizzata. Nel 2016 il valore della merce contraffatta circolante nel mondo era di quasi 510 miliardi di euro, di cui 121 miliardi riferiti al contesto europeo. 19.03.21 The Danish Rights Alliance1 submission: The consultation on the Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on a Single Market for Digital Services COM(2020) 825 final

The Danish Rights Alliance herewith submits a short response to the Commission's consultation on the Proposal for a Regulation: Digital Services Act (the 'proposal' in the following).

The Danish Rights Alliance welcomes the proposal which we believe has a number of positive elements that will contribute to a much safer and legal Internet and improving a better enforcement of intellectual property rights on the digital platform services. The platforms have a key role in this respect and therefore we welcome the obligations to remove illegal content in a faster and more efficient way in particular by the institutionalization by nomination of a Trusted Flagger by a public authority. Experience has demonstrated that this kind of public-private partnership is very efficient2.. At the same time, the introduction of the much-needed requirement for digital services to obtain verified knowledge of their business customers seems to need to some improvements before this requirement can fully contribute to the Internet as a more legal and safe environment for consumers.

Our key observations are the following:

1) 'Trusted flaggers'

The proposal introduces in Article 19 a formalized use of 'trusted flaggers' by legally introducing the use of a trusted flagger designated by a public authority.

This provision supports the Rights Alliance's effort to create a safe and legal Internet and we urge the Commission and the EP to preserve these provisions. In particular, the designation by public authorities is important to ensure transparency and public confidence in the system also when it comes to intellectual property rights.

The pivotal elements in the provision are the criteria for being designated as trusted notifier. Concerning intellectual property rights, an organization representing right-holders should only be awarded trusted flagger status when it complies with following:

a. It has expertise and competence for the purposes of detecting, identifying and notifying illegal content.

1 https://rettighedsalliancen.com/ 2 E.g. the Danish Dialogue Forum operated by the Ministry of Culture with participation by relevant stakeholders.

+45 60 56 63 64  mail@rettighedsalliancen.dk

b. It represents collective interests and is independent of any online platform.
c. It carries out its activities for the purposes of submitting notices in a timely, diligent and objective manner i.e., the entity has demonstrated that it has competence in tackling illegal content., We further suggest that the wording in Recital 46 and preferable also in Article 19 is amended to reflect that:
1. The combination of being independent of platforms, being non-commercial and having proven competence as well as experience implies by default a high degree of credibility and trustworthiness for a designated flagger.
2. Therefore, the level of trustworthiness should explicitly enable co-operation with the enforcement authorities and the legal system including notifications of illegal activities to be ex ante accepted as valid and justified.
3. In the area of illegal services infringing IPR it is preferential that only one designated flagger is nominated in the national market for digital services to avoid redundant, conflicting or 'competing' notifications which may weaken the system and reduce its credibility.

The priority awarded to notifications by trusted flaggers and the access to fast-track procedures by the platforms for handling the illegal content is evenly important.

2) Traceability or 'KYBC' (Know your business customer).

Article 22 of the proposal introduces a requirement that online platforms must know and verify the identity of the providers of services on the platform, the so-called 'traders'. While the obligation is an obvious requirement to ensure a transparent and safe market place the scope of the obligation to verify service providers which follows from the concept of 'traders' is overly restrictive.

The obligation can only be applied to 'traders' as defined by Article 2e in conjunction with the premise set out in Article 22.1 which says the obligation only applies where an online platform allows consumers to 'conclude distance contracts with traders'. This implies a narrow application as it only addresses a subset of the platform's non-residential customers.

To ensure consumer protection and to effectively fight illegal activities a wider concept rather than 'traders' should be applied. We suggest the concept 'business users of online intermediation services' as defined by Regulation 2019/11503 should be considered. While this definition in article 2.2 of 2019/1150 as such is equal to the definition in the proposal's article 2e of 'trader' it is not restricted by the requirement of 'conclude distance contracts', in other words the 'business user' may not necessarily be involved in any direct relation with end users cf.:

Article 2.1) 'business user' means any private individual acting in a commercial or professional capacity who, or any legal person which, through online intermediation services offers goods or services to consumers for purposes relating to its trade, business, craft or profession.

3 Regulation (EU) 2019/1150 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019 on promoting fairness and transparency for business users of online intermediation services

+45 60 56 63 64  mail@rettighedsalliancen.dk

Also, the derived obligation in 2019/1150 to check identity is relevant:

Article 3.5) Providers of online intermediation services shall ensure that the identity of the business user providing the goods or services on the online intermediation services is clearly visible.

A mandatory and detailed obligation accompanied by sanctions if not complied with for trusted verification of business users could be introduced to the relevant intermediaries who provide digital services including but not limited to providers of platform services, of domain names and of hosting services. Such a requirement will help to at least significantly curb the presence of illegal Internet services e.g. infringing copyright.

This requirement is for example applied in practice in Denmark at DK Hostmaster to verify users of.dk domain names.

3) Digital Services Coordinators

The proposal requires Member States to designate a public authority as the 'Digital Services Coordinator' (DSC) to be part of a network where decisions and information must be exchanged at EU level. We find the introduction of a national DSC is an important element of the proposal since the DSC:

1. Establishes in Article 38.2 a single point of responsibility for the provisions of the proposal which is likely to contribute significantly to the effectiveness and transparency of platform regulation.

2. Acts as the public authority that appoints a trusted flagger.

We suggest that concerning appointment of trusted flaggers that the proposal emphasizes this nomination in particular when it comes to IPR infringements should constitute a public-private partnership and thus call for an active involvement by the DSC to create a safe and legal Internet4.

3. Holds the power to order intermediaries to cease infringements, including the imposition of sanctions to ensure that orders are implemented in Article 41.

We suggest it should be explicitly clarified if the power entrusted to the DSC in article 41.2 also may cover instances where intermediaries of digitals services such as ISPs (Internet Service Providers) provide access to illegal services and thus can be ordered by the DSC to block such access.

The Danish Rights Alliance will finally once more emphasize that in the final version of the Regulation maintaining the proposal's provisions regarding 'trusted flaggers ' and ' DSC' is key to ensure significant improvements of the legality ad safety of the digital services on the Internet.

4 We refer to the Danish Dialogue Forum that coins out 'follow-the-money' approach to illegal services as well as the ShareWithCare initiative which involves ISP in blocking of illegal services.

La Fédération Française du bâtiment accueille favorablement la proposition de règlement relatif à un marché intérieur des services numériques dans la mesure où il entend définir les responsabilités incombant aux plateformes en ligne en tant que fournisseurs de services intermédiaires.
Lors de la consultation européenne relative au futur paquet de mesures sur les services numériques menée à l’été 2020, la Fédération Française du Bâtiment avait identifié trois principales actions à engager :
- harmoniser un système d’alerte spécifique aux produits illicites et/ou contrefaisants, qui doit pouvoir être déclenchée tant par le détenteur des droits de propriété intellectuelle ou le propriétaire du bien contrefait, que par le client (même potentiel) ;
- responsabiliser les plateformes numériques de mise en relation vis-à-vis des utilisateurs professionnels avec, par exemple, des vérifications de leur existence légale, de leurs qualifications professionnelles, voire des assurances contractées au regard de leur activité ;
- normaliser la méthode de recueil et de publication des avis de consommateurs afin d’éviter la publication de commentaires mensongers et de favoriser la transparence.
À ce titre et au regard de la proposition de règlement présentée par la Commission européenne, la FFB souhaiterait apporter des commentaires sur deux articles.
Contrairement à ce que prévoit l’article 7, la FFB demande l’instauration d’une obligation générale de surveillance ou de recherche active de faits ou de circonstances révélant des activités illicites soit imposée aux plateformes en ligne. En effet, dans une démarche de responsabilisation des plateformes, qu’il s’agisse de places de marché pour la vente de biens ou de services d’intermédiation avec des professionnels, il apparait opportun qu’elles développent des procédures de contrôle et de vérification, en amont, de la licéité des produits vendus et/ou des professionnels avec lesquels elles collaborent. 
Dans cette optique, l’article 22, qui prévoit qu’une plateforme obtienne, préalablement à l’utilisation de ses services, des informations sur les professionnels avec lesquels elles collaborent et en assurent une évaluation, constitue une avancée. 
Toutefois, la FFB regrette que cet article se restreigne à la conclusion de contrats à distance entre des consommateurs et des professionnels utilisant les services de ladite plateforme. Le cadre juridique du contrat à distance ne s’applique pas, par exemple, à une prestation de travaux qui requiert en général une visite du professionnel et l’élaboration d’un devis avant la conclusion du contrat. Or, la mise en relation a été initiée par la plateforme d’intermédiation et la confiance du consommateur s’appuie sur celle-ci.
Pour la FFB, il conviendrait donc d’élargir le champ de l’article 22 pour tout utilisateur professionnel qui propose des produits ou services par l’intermédiaire d’une plateforme en ligne. De plus, la plateforme devrait également procéder à une vérification non seulement de l’existence légale des professionnels utilisateurs de ses services, mais aussi des qualifications professionnelles dont ils se prévalent, voire des assurances contractées au regard de leur activité.

full_text:
Brussels, March 2021 1040 Brussels W bsa.org Belgium EU Register of Interest Representa tives 75039383277-48

BSA Position Paper on the Digital Services Act

BSA | The Software Alliance (BSA) 1 welcomes the opportunity to provide input to the Commission's draft Digital Services Act (DSA). BSA is the leading advocate for the global software industry. Our Members are at the forefront of software-enabled innovation that is fueling global economic growth by helping enterprises in every sector of the economy operate more efficiently. BSA supp orts the development of relevant policy instruments and smart regulation that strengthen the Digital Single Market in Europe. In this context, we welcome the Commission's proposal for a DSA as a good starting point to update the rules provided by the 2000 E-Commerce Directive, and as it strives to strike the right balance between ensuring online responsibility and accountability, while allowing digital businesses to continue to grow and innovate. The 2000 E-Commerce Directive has played a fundamental role in the development of the DSM, providing a flexible regulatory framework and accounting of the different features and layers of the technology industry. The draft DSA introduces a number of important modifications, such as the so-called Go od Samaritan Clause, while safeguarding several of the key elements of the 2000 E-Commerce Directive, such as the intermediary liability principles, the Country of Origin principle and tailored approach to requirements for different types of digital servic es. The establishment of new categories of digital services such as online platforms and very large online platforms (VLOPs) subject to a set of enhanced rules, is a step in the right direction to ensure safeguards and legal certainty, though additional clarifications on the concept of dissemination to the public would be necessary to ensure that the draft DSA achieves its objectives. Overall, BSA calls upon the Commission and the other co-legislators, to ensure that the Digital Services Act does not esta blish obligations that would conflict with requirements of other EU Legislation, pending or proposed. The EU body of law offers strong safeguards and protection, as well as legal obligations and requirements for service providers. Any new requirements that were to be added by the draft DSA should take into account existing and proposed legislation to ensure harmonization and legal certainty. More specifically, BSA would like to highlight the following elements:

1) Dissemination to the public BSA urges the co-legislators to provide additional clarity around the concept of dissemination to the public, which is instrumental in the distinction between hosting providers and online platforms. The objective of the proposal is to ensure that digital services have clear and effective rules, while providing proportionate responsibilities

1 BSA | The Software Alliance (www.bsa.org) is the leading advocate for the global software industry before governments and in the international marketplace. Its members are among the world's most innovative companies, creating software solutions that spark the economy and improve modern life. Wit h headquarters in Washington, DC, and operations in more than 30 countries, BSA pioneers compliance programs that promote legal software use and advocates for public policies that foster technology innovation and drive growth in the digital economy. BSA's members include: Adobe, Akamai, Atlassian, Autodesk, Bentley Systems, Box, Cloudflare, CNC/Mastercam, DocuSign, Dropbox, IBM, Informatica, Intel, Intuit, MathWorks, McAfee, Microsoft, Okta, Oracle, PTC, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Siemens Industry Software In c., Slack, Splunk, Trend Micro, Trimble Solutions Corporation, Twilio, and Workday.

1040 Brussels W bsa.org Belgium EU Register of Interest Representa tives 75039383277-48 which are tailored to a specific digital service and risk profile. The current language used to describe the concept of dissemination to the public does not provide the necessary clarifications for all those services that host user-generated content whose defining characteristic is not the dissemination of content. In t his context, BSA would recommend that the Regulation makes it clear that the dissemination to the public of content, as a condition to qualify as an online platform, should be an essential characteristic of the service. Moreover, the dissemination should h appen on the service that is to be qualified as a platform, not elsewhere. This clarification would also be closely linked with the language included at the end of Recital 14 of the proposal, whereby "[i]nformation should be considered disseminated to the public within the meaning of this Regulation only where that occurs upon the direct request by the recipient of the service that provided the information." Recital 14 implies a direct involvement of the recipient of the service to disseminate the content, but it does not clarify that such dissemination should happen on the service itself, in order to qualify as an online platform.

2) Tailored approach to different digital services BSA welcomes the Commission's decision to maintain, in the draft DSA proposal, the structure of the E-Commerce Directive, taking a tailored-approach to the different obligations and requirements for different digital services.

It is essential that the Commission ensures that this structure is maintained during the legislative proc ess. A one-size-fits-all approach that would impose the same rules on all digital services would create disproportionate burdens for many businesses that do not have the ability to view, access or moderate content, or do not disseminate content to the publ ic. Many B2B services providers, for example, do not offer content sharing services for end-consumers or the general public, and therefore may not have the ability to control, edit or curate user-generated content that may appear online. A one-size-fitsall approach would therefore limit the uptake of cloud technologies across businesses and damage the broader data economy.

Furthermore, many B2B services - in particular IaaS - could be classified as hosting service under the proposal, which would entail compliance with the updated notice and action requirements and removal and information orders (Articles 8 and 9 of the draft proposal). Enterprise cloud providers are often not in a position to identify which of their cloud customers' users is associated w ith content posted online. As a result, an enterprise cloud provider does not always have a direct relationship with the user uploading the alleged illegal content and may not have the ability to take action on the data that is made public. For these reasons, BSA recommends that the proposal includes language clarifying that requests should be sent to the cloud customers first, and only in second instance to the enterprise software provider, to ensure that action can be taken swiftly and by the most appropr iate entity.

3) Know Your Business Customer principle BSA strongly supports the European Commission's approach to the so called Know Your Business Customer (KYBC) principle. By taking a tailored approach and identifying the specific conduct that it intends to address, the Commission ensures the

1040 Brussels W bsa.org Belgium EU Register of Interest Representa tives 75039383277-48 protection of consumers by preventing dishonest businesses selling illegal products online, while avoiding applying inappropriate cons traints on business - to-business services. Setting stronger consumer protection rules should first take into account whether the digital services actively provide a business-to-consumer good or service, while balancing the need to safeguard the smoothness a nd speed of online business operations.

We would caution policymakers against expanding the proposed scope of these KYBC provisions and requiring that such obligations should be horizontally implemented by all digital services beyond online platforms. The provision of core services to regulated sectors such as operators of essential services depends entirely on the ability to provide robust cloud solutions that are neither designed nor intended for consumers. Enterprise cloud-based solutions are often offered on a "Pay as You Go" principle, which has contributed to the success and security of the cloud, particularly among small businesses and developers. A large number of those businesses rely on the scalability of cloud solutions to provide their services to their customers, therefore requiring extensive ex ante identification and verification checks on all businesses subscribing to cloud services, would create significant barriers to the delivery of cloud services in Europe. Moreover, m any B2B cloud servi ces already implement strong safeguards to prevent fraudulent businesses from using cloud services (e.g. contractual obligations in service contracts, security-based services against fraud). Additional and disproportionate KY BC requirements may not only ra ise privacy and business confidentiality concerns, but could discourage companies, particularly SMEs and start-ups, from moving to the cloud, if held up from accessing services pending clearance.

4) Intermediary Liability BSA also supports the Commission's d ecision to maintain the core principles of intermediary liability, as they were established by the E-Commerce Directive. The Directive has greatly contributed to the success of the digital ecosystem, from the internet to cloud services, and the current int ermediary liability system - with clearly defined conditions - remains a fundamental aspect of the Digital Single Market. In this respect, we also welcome the decision to maintain the E-Commerce Directive's ban on general monitoring obligations.

5) Country of origin In addition, the Commission's draft DSA proposal correctly provides for the so-called Country of Origin principle, which has proven to be a fundamental aspect of EU Legislation, originally in the 2000 E-Commerce Directive, and also in the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). BSA recommends ensuring that the Country of Origin principle is retained throughout the legislative process, as it mirrors the mechanism established by the E-Commerce Directive and GDPR, and would ensure better compliance for all digital service providers. The Country of Origin principle is a long established mechanism to ensure legal certainty for digital services operators, and is applied effectively in diverse sectors across the EU. Retaining the Country of Origin principle in the draft DSA proposal would ensure continuity of regulation between the 2000 E-Commerce Directive, reducing compliance costs and obligations for service
